cards.question: §61.103 - Eligibility requirements: General
cards.answer:
To be eligible for a private pilot certificate, a person must:

(a) Be at least 17 years of age for a rating in other than a glider or balloon.
(b) Be at least 16 years of age for a rating in a glider or balloon.
(c) Be able to read, speak, write, and understand the English language.
(d) Receive a logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor who conducted the training or reviewed the person's home study on the aeronautical knowledge areas listed in §61.105(b) and certified that the person is prepared for the required knowledge test.
(e) Pass the required knowledge test on the aeronautical knowledge areas listed in §61.105(b).
(f) Receive flight training and a logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor who conducted the training in the areas of operation listed in §61.107(b) and certified that the person is prepared for the required practical test.
(g) Meet the aeronautical experience requirements of this part that apply to the aircraft rating sought before applying for the practical test.
(h) Pass a practical test on the areas of operation listed in §61.107(b) that apply to the aircraft rating sought.
(i) Comply with the appropriate sections of this part that apply to the aircraft category and class rating sought.
(j) Hold a U.S. student pilot certificate, sport pilot certificate, or recreational pilot certificate.

cards.question: §61.109(a) - Aeronautical experience for airplane single-engine rating
cards.answer:
A person who applies for a private pilot certificate with an airplane category and single-engine class rating must log at least 40 hours of flight time that includes at least 20 hours of flight training from an authorized instructor and 10 hours of solo flight training in the areas of operation listed in §61.107(b)(1), and the training must include at least:

(1) 3 hours of cross-country flight training in a single-engine airplane;
(2) 3 hours of night flight training in a single-engine airplane that includes:
    (i) One cross-country flight of over 100 nautical miles total distance; and
    (ii) 10 takeoffs and 10 landings to a full stop (with each landing involving a flight in the traffic pattern) at an airport.
(3) 3 hours of flight training in a single-engine airplane on the control and maneuvering of an airplane solely by reference to instruments, including straight and level flight, constant airspeed climbs and descents, turns to a heading, recovery from unusual flight attitudes, radio communications, and the use of navigation systems/facilities and radar services appropriate to instrument flight;
(4) 3 hours of flight training with an authorized instructor in a single-engine airplane in preparation for the practical test, which must have been performed within the preceding 2 calendar months from the month of the test; and
(5) 10 hours of solo flight time in a single-engine airplane, consisting of at least:
    (i) 5 hours of solo cross-country time;
    (ii) One solo cross country flight of 150 nautical miles total distance, with full-stop landings at three points, and one segment of the flight consisting of a straight-line distance of more than 50 nautical miles between the takeoff and landing locations; and
    (iii) Three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop (with each landing involving a flight in the traffic pattern) at an airport with an operating control tower.
glance: 40 hours total flight time
20 hours dual (flight training) · 10 hours solo
Dual must include: 3 hr cross-country · 3 hr night · 3 hr instrument · 3 hr checkride prep (within 2 calendar months)
Night: one XC over 100 NM total + 10 full-stop takeoffs & landings
Solo: 5 hr solo XC · one 150 NM XC, full-stop landings at 3 points, one leg over 50 NM straight-line
Solo: 3 full-stop takeoffs & landings at a towered airport

cards.question: Part 141 Appendix B - Private Pilot Certification Course (Airplane)
cards.answer:
For a combined private pilot certification and instrument rating course involving a single-engine airplane:

Flight training: 35 hours minimum, including:
• 20 hours of flight training from an authorized instructor on the approved areas of operation
• 5 hours of solo flight training in the approved areas of operation

Solo flight training must include:
• One solo cross-country flight of at least 100 nautical miles with landings at a minimum of three points, and one segment of the flight consisting of a straight-line distance of at least 50 nautical miles between takeoff and landing locations
• Three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop (with each landing involving a flight in the traffic pattern) at an airport with an operating control tower

cards.question: §61.109(a)(2) - Night flight training requirements
cards.answer:
3 hours of night flight training in a single-engine airplane that includes:

(i) One cross-country flight of over 100 nautical miles total distance; and
(ii) 10 takeoffs and 10 landings to a full stop (with each landing involving a flight in the traffic pattern) at an airport.
glance: 3 hours night flight training
One XC over 100 NM total distance
10 takeoffs & 10 full-stop landings (pattern)

cards.question: §61.109(a)(3) - Instrument training requirements for Private Pilot
cards.answer:
3 hours of flight training in a single-engine airplane on the control and maneuvering of an airplane solely by reference to instruments, including:

• Straight and level flight
• Constant airspeed climbs and descents
• Turns to a heading
• Recovery from unusual flight attitudes
• Radio communications
• The use of navigation systems/facilities and radar services appropriate to instrument flight

cards.question: §61.57(a) - General experience (passenger-carrying currency)
cards.answer:
No person may act as a pilot in command of an aircraft carrying passengers or of an aircraft certificated for more than one pilot flight crewmember unless that person has made at least three takeoffs and three landings within the preceding 90 days, and:

(1) The person acted as the sole manipulator of the flight controls; and
(2) The required takeoffs and landings were performed in an aircraft of the same category, class, and type (if a type rating is required).

For tailwheel airplanes: The landings must be made to a full stop in an airplane with a tailwheel.
glance: Carrying passengers: 3 takeoffs & 3 landings in the preceding 90 days
Sole manipulator of the controls
Same category, class, and type (if type rating required)
Tailwheel: landings to a full stop

cards.question: §61.57(b) - Night takeoff and landing experience
cards.answer:
No person may act as pilot in command of an aircraft carrying passengers during the period beginning 1 hour after sunset and ending 1 hour before sunrise, unless within the preceding 90 days that person has made at least three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop during the period beginning 1 hour after sunset and ending 1 hour before sunrise, and:

(1) That person acted as sole manipulator of the flight controls; and
(2) The required takeoffs and landings were performed in an aircraft of the same category, class, and type (if a type rating is required).
glance: Night passengers: 3 takeoffs & 3 full-stop landings in the preceding 90 days
Done between 1 hr after sunset and 1 hr before sunrise
Sole manipulator · same category, class, and type

cards.question: §61.56 - Flight review
cards.answer:
No person may act as pilot in command of an aircraft unless, since the beginning of the 24th calendar month before the month in which that pilot acts as pilot in command, that person has:

(1) Accomplished a flight review given in an aircraft for which that pilot is rated by an authorized instructor; and
(2) A logbook endorsed from an authorized instructor who gave the review certifying that the person has satisfactorily completed the review.

The flight review consists of a minimum of 1 hour of flight training and 1 hour of ground training that includes:
(i) A review of the current general operating and flight rules of part 91; and
(ii) A review of those maneuvers and procedures that, at the discretion of the person giving the review, are necessary for the pilot to demonstrate the safe exercise of the privileges of the pilot certificate.
glance: Every 24 calendar months
Minimum 1 hr ground + 1 hr flight
Part 91 rules review + maneuvers at instructor's discretion
Logbook endorsement from the instructor

cards.question: §61.31(i) - Additional training required for operating tailwheel airplanes
cards.answer:
No person may act as pilot in command of a tailwheel airplane unless that person has received and logged flight training from an authorized instructor in a tailwheel airplane and received an endorsement in the person's logbook from an authorized instructor who found the person proficient in the operation of a tailwheel airplane. The flight training must include at least the following maneuvers and procedures:

(1) Normal and crosswind takeoffs and landings;
(2) Wheel landings (unless the manufacturer has recommended against such landings); and
(3) Go-around procedures.

cards.question: §61.31(e) - Additional training required for operating complex airplanes
cards.answer:
No person may act as pilot in command of a complex airplane unless the person has:

(1) Received and logged ground and flight training from an authorized instructor in a complex airplane, or in a full flight simulator or flight training device that is representative of a complex airplane, and has been found proficient in the operation and systems of the airplane; and
(2) Received a one-time endorsement in the pilot's logbook from an authorized instructor who certifies the person is proficient to operate a complex airplane.

Complex airplane means an airplane that has a retractable landing gear, flaps, and a controllable pitch propeller, including airplanes equipped with an engine control system consisting of a digital computer and associated accessories for controlling the engine and propeller, such as a full authority digital engine control; or, in the case of a seaplane, flaps and a controllable pitch propeller.

cards.question: §61.31(f) - Additional training required for operating high-performance airplanes
cards.answer:
No person may act as pilot in command of a high-performance airplane unless the person has:

(1) Received and logged ground and flight training from an authorized instructor in a high-performance airplane, or in a full flight simulator or flight training device that is representative of a high-performance airplane, and has been found proficient in the operation and systems of the airplane; and
(2) Received a one-time endorsement in the pilot's logbook from an authorized instructor who certifies the person is proficient to operate a high-performance airplane.

High-performance airplane means an airplane with an engine of more than 200 horsepower.

cards.question: §61.31(g) - Additional training required for operating pressurized aircraft
§61.113(a) - Private pilot privileges and limitations: General
cards.answer: Except as provided in paragraphs (b) through (h) of this section, no person who holds a private pilot certificate may act as pilot in command of an aircraft that is carrying passengers or property for compensation or hire; nor may that person, for compensation or hire, act as pilot in command of an aircraft.

cards.question: §61.113(c) - Private pilot: Sharing operating expenses
cards.answer: A private pilot may not pay less than the pro rata share of the operating expenses of a flight with passengers, provided the expenses involve only fuel, oil, airport expenditures, or rental fees.

cards.question: §61.113 - Exceptions allowing compensation for private pilots
§61.87(b) - Aeronautical knowledge for student pilots (pre-solo)
cards.answer:
Prior to conducting a solo flight, a student pilot must have demonstrated satisfactory aeronautical knowledge on a knowledge test that is administered by the student's authorized instructor on the following aeronautical knowledge areas:

(1) Applicable sections of parts 61 and 91 of this chapter;
(2) Airspace rules and procedures for the airport where the solo flight will be performed; and
(3) Flight characteristics and operational limitations for the make and model of aircraft to be flown.

The authorized instructor who administers the test must, at the conclusion of the test, review all incorrect answers with the student before authorizing that student to conduct a solo flight.

cards.question: §61.87(d) - Maneuvers and procedures for pre-solo flight training (airplanes)
§61.87(n) & (p) - Student pilot endorsement requirements
cards.answer:
§61.87(n) - A student pilot must have the following endorsements from an authorized instructor in the student's logbook:

(1) An endorsement that the student has received training in the make and model of aircraft to be flown, and has been found proficient to make solo flights in that make and model.
(2) An endorsement dated within 90 days of the solo flight, certifying that the student has received the required training and is prepared to make the solo flight.

§61.87(p) - An endorsement for a student pilot to operate an aircraft in solo flight is valid for 90 days from the date it is issued. Upon expiration of the 90-day period, each additional 90-day period must be authorized by an endorsement.

cards.question: §61.87(o) - Night solo flight requirements for student pilots
cards.answer:
A student pilot may not operate an aircraft in solo flight at night unless that student pilot has received:

(1) Flight training at night on night flying procedures that includes takeoffs, approaches, landings, and go-arounds at night at the airport where the solo flight will be conducted;
(2) Navigation training at night in the vicinity of the airport where the solo flight will be conducted; and
(3) An endorsement in the student's logbook for the specific make and model aircraft to be flown for night solo flight by an authorized instructor who gave the training within the 90-day period preceding the date of the flight.

cards.question: 49 CFR §830.2 - Definition of Aircraft Accident
cards.answer: Aircraft accident means an occurrence associated with the operation of an aircraft which takes place between the time any person boards the aircraft with the intention of flight and all such persons have disembarked, and in which any person suffers death or serious injury, or in which the aircraft receives substantial damage.

cards.question: 49 CFR §830.2 - Definition of Serious Injury
49 CFR §830.2 - Definition of Substantial Damage
cards.answer:
Substantial damage means damage or failure which adversely affects the structural strength, performance, or flight characteristics of the aircraft, and which would normally require major repair or replacement of the affected component.

Engine failure or damage limited to an engine if only one engine fails or is damaged, bent fairings or cowling, dented skin, small punctured holes in the skin or fabric, ground damage to rotor or propeller blades, and damage to landing gear, wheels, tires, flaps, engine accessories, brakes, or wingtips are not considered substantial damage.

cards.question: 49 CFR §830.2 - Definition of Aircraft Incident
cards.answer: Incident means an occurrence other than an accident, associated with the operation of an aircraft, which affects or could affect the safety of operations.

cards.question: 49 CFR §830.5 - Immediate notification required
14 CFR §21.197 - Special flight permits
cards.answer:
A special flight permit may be issued for an aircraft that may not currently meet applicable airworthiness requirements but is capable of safe flight, for the following purposes:

(a) Flying the aircraft to a base where repairs, alterations, or maintenance are to be performed, or to a point of storage.
(b) Delivering or exporting the aircraft.
(c) Production flight testing new production aircraft.
(d) Evacuating aircraft from areas of impending danger.
(e) Conducting customer demonstration flights in new production aircraft that have satisfactorily completed production flight tests.

cards.question: 14 CFR §1.1 - Category, Class, and Type definitions
cards.answer:
Category:
(1) As used with respect to the certification, ratings, privileges, and limitations of airmen, means a broad classification of aircraft. Examples: airplane, rotorcraft, glider, lighter-than-air.
(2) As used with respect to the certification of aircraft, means a grouping of aircraft based upon intended use or operating limitations. Examples: transport, normal, utility, acrobatic, limited, restricted, provisional.

Class:
(1) As used with respect to the certification, ratings, privileges, and limitations of airmen, means a classification of aircraft within a category having similar operating characteristics. Examples: single engine, multi-engine, land, water, gyroplane, helicopter, airship, free balloon.
(2) As used with respect to the certification of aircraft, means a broad grouping of aircraft having similar characteristics of propulsion, flight, or landing. Examples: airplane, rotorcraft, glider, balloon, landplane, seaplane.

Type:
(1) As used with respect to the certification, ratings, privileges, and limitations of airmen, means a specific make and basic model of aircraft, including modifications thereto that do not change its handling or flight characteristics. Examples: DC-7, 1049, F-27.
(2) As used with respect to the certification of aircraft, means those aircraft which are similar in design. Examples: DC-7 and DC-7C, 1049G and 1049H.

cards.question: §61.3 - Required pilot certificate and documents
§91.203 - Civil aircraft: Certifications required
cards.answer:
No person may operate a civil aircraft unless it has within it the following:

(a) An appropriate and current airworthiness certificate.
(b) An effective U.S. registration certificate issued to its owner or, for operation within the United States, the second copy of the Aircraft Registration Application as provided for in §47.31(c), a Certificate of Aircraft Registration as provided for in part 48, or a registration certification issued under the laws of a foreign country.
(c) An approved Airplane or Rotorcraft Flight Manual, approved manual material, markings, and placards, or any combination thereof.
(d) Weight and balance data, either the original or copy.

Mnemonic: ARROW (Airworthiness certificate, Registration, Radio station license [international only], Operating limitations/manual, Weight and balance)

cards.question: §61.60 - Change of address
cards.answer: The holder of a pilot, flight instructor, or ground instructor certificate who has made a change in permanent mailing address may not, after 30 days from that date, exercise the privileges of the certificate unless the holder has notified in writing the FAA, Airman Certification Branch, of the new permanent mailing address, or current residential address if the permanent mailing address includes a post office box number.

cards.question: §91.151 - Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions
cards.answer:
No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed:

(a) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or
(b) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.

cards.question: §91.409 - Inspections (Annual and 100-hour)
cards.answer:
No person may operate an aircraft unless, within the preceding 12 calendar months, it has had:

(a) An annual inspection in accordance with part 43 and has been approved for return to service by a person authorized by §43.7; or
(b) An inspection for the issuance of an airworthiness certificate.

§91.409(b) - 100-hour inspection:
No person may operate an aircraft carrying any person (other than a crewmember) for hire, or operate any aircraft for flight instruction for hire, unless within the preceding 100 hours of time in service the aircraft has received an annual or 100-hour inspection and been approved for return to service.

The 100-hour limitation may be exceeded by not more than 10 hours while en route to reach a place where the inspection can be done. The excess time must be included in computing the next 100 hours of time in service.
glance: Annual: within the preceding 12 calendar months
100-hour: for hire (passengers or flight instruction you provide)
May exceed 100 hr by up to 10 hr to reach an inspection; excess counts toward the next 100

cards.question: §91.171 - VOR equipment check for IFR operations
cards.answer:
No person may operate a civil aircraft under IFR using the VOR system of radio navigation unless the VOR equipment of that aircraft:

(a) Is maintained, checked, and inspected under an approved procedure; or
(b) Has been operationally checked within the preceding 30 days, and was found to be within the allowable limits of bearing error:

(1) VOT signal: ±4°
(2) VOR test facility ground checkpoint: ±4°
(3) VOR ground checkpoint established by the Administrator or the aircraft owner: ±4°
(4) VOR airborne checkpoint established by the Administrator: ±6°
(5) If dual VOR systems, cross-check one against the other: ±4° difference between the two

Each person making the VOR operational check shall enter the date, place, bearing error, and sign the aircraft log or other record.

cards.question: §91.411 & §91.413 - Altimeter and transponder inspections
cards.answer:
§91.411 - Altimeter system and altitude reporting equipment tests and inspections:
No person may operate an airplane, or helicopter, in controlled airspace under IFR unless within the preceding 24 calendar months, each static pressure system, each altimeter instrument, and each automatic pressure altitude reporting system has been tested and inspected and found to comply with appendix E of part 43.

§91.413 - ATC transponder tests and inspections:
No persons may use an ATC transponder unless within the preceding 24 calendar months the ATC transponder has been tested and inspected and found to comply with appendix F of part 43.

cards.question: §91.207 - Emergency locator transmitters (ELT)
cards.answer:
No person may operate a U.S.-registered civil airplane unless there is attached to the airplane an approved automatic type emergency locator transmitter that is in operable condition (with exceptions for training flights within 50 NM, design/production flight tests, ferry flights, and certain agricultural aircraft).

Each ELT required must be inspected within 12 calendar months after the last inspection for:
(1) Proper installation;
(2) Battery corrosion;
(3) Operation of the controls and crash sensor; and
(4) The presence of a sufficient signal radiated from its antenna.

Batteries used in ELTs must be replaced (or recharged, if the battery is rechargeable):
(1) When the transmitter has been in use for more than 1 cumulative hour; or
(2) When 50 percent of their useful life (or, for rechargeable batteries, 50 percent of their useful life of charge) has expired.

cards.question: §91.205(b) - Visual flight rules (day) required instruments and equipment
cards.answer:
For VFR flight during the day, the following instruments and equipment are required:

(1) Airspeed indicator.
(2) Altimeter.
(3) Magnetic direction indicator (compass).
(4) Tachometer for each engine.
(5) Oil pressure gauge for each engine using pressure system.
(6) Temperature gauge for each liquid-cooled engine.
(7) Oil temperature gauge for each air-cooled engine.
(8) Manifold pressure gauge for each altitude engine.
(9) Fuel gauge indicating the quantity of fuel in each tank.
(10) Landing gear position indicator, if the aircraft has a retractable landing gear.
(11) For small civil airplanes certificated after March 11, 1996, an approved aviation red or aviation white anticollision light system.
(12) If the aircraft is operated for hire over water and beyond power-off gliding distance from shore, approved flotation gear readily available to each occupant and at least one pyrotechnic signaling device.
(13) An approved safety belt with an approved metal-to-metal latching device for each occupant 2 years of age or older.
(14) For small civil airplanes manufactured after July 18, 1978, an approved shoulder harness for each front seat.
(15) An emergency locator transmitter, if required by §91.207.

Mnemonic: A TOMATO FLAMES (Airspeed, Tachometer, Oil pressure, Manifold pressure, Altimeter, Temperature, Oil temperature, Fuel gauge, Landing gear indicator, Anti-collision lights, Magnetic compass, ELT, Seatbelts)

cards.question: §91.205(c) - Visual flight rules (night) required instruments and equipment
cards.answer:
For VFR flight at night, the following instruments and equipment are required in addition to the day VFR equipment:

(1) Approved position lights (navigation lights).
(2) An approved aviation red or aviation white anticollision light system on all U.S.-registered civil aircraft.
(3) If the aircraft is operated for hire, one electric landing light.
(4) An adequate source of electrical energy for all installed electrical and radio equipment.
(5) One spare set of fuses, or three spare fuses of each kind required, that are accessible to the pilot in flight.

Mnemonic: FLAPS (Fuses, Landing light [if for hire], Anti-collision lights, Position lights, Source of electrical power)

cards.question: §91.103 - Preflight action
cards.answer:
Each pilot in command shall, before beginning a flight, become familiar with all available information concerning that flight. This information must include:

(a) For a flight under IFR or a flight not in the vicinity of an airport, weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, alternatives available if the planned flight cannot be completed, and any known traffic delays of which the pilot in command has been advised by ATC;

(b) For any flight, runway lengths at airports of intended use, and the following takeoff and landing distance information:
(1) For civil aircraft for which an approved Airplane or Rotorcraft Flight Manual containing takeoff and landing distance data is required, the takeoff and landing distance data contained therein; and
(2) For civil aircraft other than those specified in paragraph (b)(1), other reliable information appropriate to the aircraft, relating to aircraft performance under expected values of airport elevation and runway slope, aircraft gross weight, and wind and temperature.

Mnemonic: NWKRAFT (NOTAMs, Weather, Known traffic delays, Runway lengths, Alternatives, Fuel requirements, Takeoff and landing data)

cards.question: §91.213 - Inoperative instruments and equipment
cards.answer:
No person may take off an aircraft with inoperative instruments or equipment installed unless the following conditions are met:

(d) For aircraft not having a Master Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) or approved operations specifications:

(1) The flight operation is conducted in a rotorcraft, nonturbine-powered airplane, glider, lighter-than-air aircraft, powered parachute, or weight-shift-control aircraft, for which a master minimum equipment list has not been developed; and

(2) The inoperative instrument or equipment does not make the aircraft unairworthy under an airworthiness directive.

(3) The inoperative instruments and equipment are not:
    (i) Part of the VFR-day type certification instruments and equipment prescribed in the applicable airworthiness regulations under which the aircraft was type certificated;
    (ii) Indicated as required on the aircraft's equipment list, or on the Kinds of Operations Equipment List for the kind of flight operation being conducted;
    (iii) Required by §91.205 or any other rule of this part for the specific kind of flight operation being conducted; or
    (iv) Required to be operational by an airworthiness directive;

(4) The inoperative instruments and equipment are removed from the aircraft, the cockpit control placarded, and the maintenance recorded in accordance with §43.9, or deactivated and placarded 'Inoperative.'

(5) A determination is made by a pilot, who is certificated and appropriately rated under part 61 of this chapter, or by a person, who is certificated and appropriately rated to perform maintenance on the aircraft, that the inoperative instrument or equipment does not constitute a hazard to the aircraft.

cards.question: §91.17 - Alcohol or drugs
IMSAFE Checklist - Pilot fitness for flight
cards.answer:
Before each flight, pilots should assess their fitness using the IMSAFE checklist:

I - Illness: Am I suffering from any illness or symptom of an illness?
M - Medication: Am I currently taking any drugs (prescription or over-the-counter) that might affect my judgment or make me drowsy?
S - Stress: Am I under psychological pressure from the job, worried about financial matters, health problems, or family discord?
A - Alcohol: Have I been drinking within 8 hours? Within 24 hours?
F - Fatigue: Am I tired and not adequately rested?
E - Eating/Emotion: Am I adequately nourished? Am I emotionally upset?

Per §91.17, no person may act as a crewmember within 8 hours of consuming alcohol or while under its influence.

cards.question: §91.113(b) - General right-of-way rules
cards.answer:
When weather conditions permit, regardless of whether an operation is conducted under instrument flight rules or visual flight rules, vigilance shall be maintained by each person operating an aircraft so as to see and avoid other aircraft.

When a rule of this section gives another aircraft the right-of-way, the pilot shall give way to that aircraft and may not pass over, under, or ahead of it unless well clear.

cards.question: §91.113(c) - In distress right-of-way
cards.answer: An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other air traffic.

cards.question: §91.113(d) - Converging aircraft right-of-way
§91.113(e) - Approaching head-on
cards.answer: When aircraft are approaching each other head-on, or nearly so, each pilot of each aircraft shall alter course to the right.

cards.question: §91.113(f) - Overtaking
cards.answer: Each aircraft that is being overtaken has the right-of-way and each pilot of an overtaking aircraft shall alter course to the right to pass well clear.

cards.question: §91.113(g) - Landing right-of-way
cards.answer:
Aircraft, while on final approach to land or while landing, have the right-of-way over other aircraft in flight or operating on the surface, except that they shall not take advantage of this rule to force an aircraft off the runway surface which has already landed and is attempting to make way for an aircraft on final approach.

When two or more aircraft are approaching an airport for the purpose of landing, the aircraft at the lower altitude has the right-of-way, but it shall not take advantage of this rule to cut in front of another which is on final approach to land or to overtake that aircraft.

cards.question: §91.159 - VFR cruising altitude or flight level
cards.answer:
Except while holding in a holding pattern of 2 minutes or less, or while turning, each person operating an aircraft under VFR in level cruising flight more than 3,000 feet above the surface shall maintain the appropriate altitude or flight level:

Below 18,000 feet MSL:
• Magnetic courses 0° through 179°: Odd thousands MSL, plus 500 feet (3,500, 5,500, 7,500, etc.)
• Magnetic courses 180° through 359°: Even thousands MSL, plus 500 feet (4,500, 6,500, 8,500, etc.)

Above 18,000 feet MSL to FL290:
• Magnetic courses 0° through 179°: Odd Flight Levels, plus 500 feet (FL195, FL215, FL235, etc.)
• Magnetic courses 180° through 359°: Even Flight Levels, plus 500 feet (FL185, FL205, FL225, etc.)

Mnemonic: Odd + 500 going East, Even + 500 going West

cards.question: §91.117 - Aircraft speed limits
cards.answer:
Unless otherwise authorized by the Administrator:

(a) No person may operate an aircraft below 10,000 feet MSL at an indicated airspeed of more than 250 knots (288 mph).

(b) Unless otherwise authorized or required by ATC, no person may operate an aircraft at or below 2,500 feet above the surface within 4 nautical miles of the primary airport of a Class C or Class D airspace area at an indicated airspeed of more than 200 knots (230 mph).

(c) No person may operate an aircraft in the airspace underlying a Class B airspace area designated for an airport or in a VFR corridor designated through such a Class B airspace area, at an indicated airspeed of more than 200 knots (230 mph).

(d) If the minimum safe airspeed for any particular operation is greater than the maximum speed prescribed in this section, the aircraft may be operated at that minimum speed.

cards.question: §91.119 - Minimum safe altitudes: General
cards.answer:
Except when necessary for takeoff or landing, no person may operate an aircraft below the following altitudes:

(a) Anywhere: An altitude allowing, if a power unit fails, an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property on the surface.

(b) Over congested areas: Over any congested area of a city, town, or settlement, or over any open air assembly of persons, an altitude of 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal radius of 2,000 feet of the aircraft.

(c) Over other than congested areas: An altitude of 500 feet above the surface, except over open water or sparsely populated areas. In those cases, the aircraft may not be operated closer than 500 feet to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure.

(d) Helicopters, powered parachutes, and weight-shift-control aircraft: May be operated at less than the minimums prescribed in paragraph (b) or (c) if the operation is conducted without hazard to persons or property on the surface.

cards.question: §91.155 - Basic VFR weather minimums (Class G airspace)
cards.answer:
Class G Airspace VFR Weather Minimums:

DAY (1,200 feet AGL or less):
• Visibility: 1 statute mile
• Cloud clearance: Clear of clouds

DAY (More than 1,200 feet AGL, but less than 10,000 feet MSL):
• Visibility: 1 statute mile
• Cloud clearance: 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, 2,000 feet horizontal

NIGHT (1,200 feet AGL or less):
• Visibility: 3 statute miles
• Cloud clearance: 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, 2,000 feet horizontal

NIGHT (More than 1,200 feet AGL, but less than 10,000 feet MSL):
• Visibility: 3 statute miles
• Cloud clearance: 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, 2,000 feet horizontal

At or above 10,000 feet MSL:
• Visibility: 5 statute miles
• Cloud clearance: 1,000 feet below, 1,000 feet above, 1 statute mile horizontal

cards.question: §91.155 - Basic VFR weather minimums (Class E airspace)
cards.answer:
Class E Airspace VFR Weather Minimums:

Less than 10,000 feet MSL:
• Visibility: 3 statute miles
• Cloud clearance: 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, 2,000 feet horizontal

At or above 10,000 feet MSL:
• Visibility: 5 statute miles
• Cloud clearance: 1,000 feet below, 1,000 feet above, 1 statute mile horizontal

cards.question: §91.155 - Basic VFR weather minimums (Class B, C, D airspace)
cards.answer:
Class B Airspace VFR Weather Minimums:
• Visibility: 3 statute miles
• Cloud clearance: Clear of clouds

Class C Airspace VFR Weather Minimums:
• Visibility: 3 statute miles
• Cloud clearance: 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, 2,000 feet horizontal

Class D Airspace VFR Weather Minimums:
• Visibility: 3 statute miles
• Cloud clearance: 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, 2,000 feet horizontal

cards.question: §91.157 - Special VFR weather minimums
cards.answer:
Special VFR operations may be conducted under the weather minimums and requirements of this section, instead of those contained in §91.155, within the lateral boundaries of controlled airspace designated to the surface for an airport.

(a) Special VFR operations may only be conducted:
(1) With an ATC clearance;
(2) Clear of clouds;
(3) Except for helicopters, when flight visibility is at least 1 statute mile; and
(4) Except for helicopters, between sunrise and sunset (or in Alaska, when the sun is 6 degrees or more below the horizon) unless:
    (i) The person being granted the ATC clearance meets the applicable requirements for instrument flight under part 61; and
    (ii) The aircraft is instrument equipped.

No person may take off or land an aircraft (other than a helicopter) under special VFR unless ground visibility is at least 1 statute mile, or if ground visibility is not reported, unless flight visibility is at least 1 statute mile.

cards.question: Class A Airspace - Characteristics and requirements
cards.answer:
Class A Airspace:

• Vertical extent: From 18,000 feet MSL up to and including FL600 (60,000 feet)
• Horizontal extent: Generally overlies the 48 contiguous states and Alaska, including waters within 12 NM of the coast

Operating requirements:
• IFR flight plan required
• ATC clearance required
• Two-way radio communication required
• Transponder with Mode C required
• Instrument rating required
• VFR flight is NOT permitted

Altimeter setting: 29.92 inches Hg (standard pressure)

cards.question: Class B Airspace - Characteristics and requirements
cards.answer:
Class B Airspace:

• Location: Surrounds the nation's busiest airports (generally airports with airline service)
• Shape: Individually tailored, generally resembles upside-down wedding cake
• Vertical extent: Surface to typically 10,000 feet MSL

Operating requirements:
• ATC clearance required prior to entry ('Cleared into Class Bravo')
• Two-way radio communication required
• Transponder with Mode C required
• Private pilot certificate required (or student with endorsement per §61.95)

VFR weather minimums:
• Visibility: 3 statute miles
• Cloud clearance: Clear of clouds

Speed limit: 200 knots below Class B or in VFR corridor; 250 knots at or below 10,000 feet MSL

cards.question: Class C Airspace - Characteristics and requirements
cards.answer:
Class C Airspace:

• Location: Airports with an operational control tower, radar approach control, and a certain level of IFR operations or passenger traffic
• Shape: Typically a 5 NM radius surface area and a 10 NM radius shelf area
• Vertical extent: Surface to typically 4,000 feet AGL

Operating requirements:
• Two-way radio communication required (must establish communication prior to entry)
• Transponder with Mode C required within and above Class C, and within 30 NM of the primary airport below 10,000 feet MSL

VFR weather minimums:
• Visibility: 3 statute miles
• Cloud clearance: 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, 2,000 feet horizontal

Speed limit: 200 knots at or below 2,500 feet AGL within 4 NM of primary airport

cards.question: Class D Airspace - Characteristics and requirements
cards.answer:
Class D Airspace:

• Location: Airports with an operational control tower
• Shape: Typically a 4 NM radius (can be larger based on instrument procedures)
• Vertical extent: Surface to typically 2,500 feet AGL

Operating requirements:
• Two-way radio communication required (must establish communication prior to entry)
• No transponder requirement (unless required by §91.215)

VFR weather minimums:
• Visibility: 3 statute miles
• Cloud clearance: 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, 2,000 feet horizontal

Speed limit: 200 knots at or below 2,500 feet AGL within 4 NM of primary airport

Note: When the control tower is not in operation, Class D reverts to Class E or G airspace.

cards.question: Class E Airspace - Characteristics and requirements
cards.answer:
Class E Airspace:

• The controlled airspace that is not Class A, B, C, or D
• Exists at various altitudes throughout the NAS

Common Class E configurations:
• Surface areas: Designated for airports without an operating control tower but with approved instrument approach procedures
• Transition areas: Extend upward from 700 feet or 1,200 feet AGL to provide controlled airspace for IFR transitions
• En route: Begins at 14,500 feet MSL over the continental US (excluding airspace below 1,500 feet AGL)
• Federal airways: 4 NM either side of centerline from 1,200 feet AGL up to but not including 18,000 feet MSL

Operating requirements:
• Two-way radio communication NOT required for VFR
• Transponder with Mode C required above 10,000 feet MSL

VFR weather minimums vary by altitude (see §91.155).

cards.question: Class G Airspace - Characteristics and requirements
cards.answer:
Class G Airspace:

• Uncontrolled airspace
• That portion of the airspace that has not been designated as Class A, B, C, D, or E

Typical locations:
• Below 700 feet or 1,200 feet AGL in most areas
• Below 14,500 feet MSL in areas more than 1,500 feet AGL over terrain

Operating requirements:
• No ATC clearance or communication required
• No transponder required (below 10,000 feet MSL)
• Pilot certificate NOT required (ultralight vehicles)

VFR weather minimums (below 10,000 feet MSL):
• Day (1,200 feet AGL or less): 1 SM visibility, clear of clouds
• Day (above 1,200 feet AGL): 1 SM visibility, 500 below/1,000 above/2,000 horizontal
• Night: 3 SM visibility, 500 below/1,000 above/2,000 horizontal

cards.question: §91.215 - ATC transponder and altitude reporting equipment
§91.225 - Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) Out equipment
§91.211 - Supplemental oxygen requirements
cards.answer:
No person may operate a civil aircraft of U.S. registry:

(a) At cabin pressure altitudes above 12,500 feet MSL up to and including 14,000 feet MSL unless the required minimum flight crew is provided with and uses supplemental oxygen for that part of the flight at those altitudes that is of more than 30 minutes duration;

(b) At cabin pressure altitudes above 14,000 feet MSL unless the required minimum flight crew is provided with and uses supplemental oxygen during the entire flight time at those altitudes; and

(c) At cabin pressure altitudes above 15,000 feet MSL unless each occupant of the aircraft is provided with supplemental oxygen.

Summary:
• 12,500-14,000 feet: Crew uses O2 after 30 minutes
• Above 14,000 feet: Crew uses O2 the entire time
• Above 15,000 feet: ALL occupants must have O2 available

cards.question: §91.107 - Use of safety belts, shoulder harnesses, and child restraint systems
cards.answer:
No pilot may take off a U.S.-registered civil aircraft unless the pilot in command of that aircraft ensures that each person on board is briefed on how to fasten and unfasten that person's safety belt and, if installed, shoulder harness.

No pilot may cause to be moved on the surface, take off, or land a civil aircraft unless the pilot in command of that aircraft ensures that each person on board has been notified to fasten his or her safety belt and, if installed, shoulder harness.

During the takeoff and landing of a U.S.-registered civil aircraft, each person on board the aircraft must occupy a seat or berth with a safety belt and, if installed, shoulder harness properly secured about him or her.

Exceptions:
• Children under 2 years of age may be held by an adult
• Persons engaged in necessary duties (flight attendants, parachutists)
• Persons using approved child restraint systems

cards.question: §91.303 - Aerobatic flight
§91.307 - Parachutes and parachuting
cards.answer:
No pilot of a civil aircraft may allow a parachute that is available for emergency use to be carried in that aircraft unless it is an approved type and:

(1) If a chair pack or chest pack parachute: has been packed by a certificated and appropriately rated parachute rigger within the preceding 180 days; or
(2) If any other type: has been packed by a certificated and appropriately rated parachute rigger within the preceding 180 days, or within the preceding 60 days if a composite material parachute.

(c) Unless each occupant of the aircraft is wearing an approved parachute, no pilot of a civil aircraft carrying any person (other than a crewmember) may execute any intentional maneuver that exceeds:
(1) A bank of 60 degrees relative to the horizon; or
(2) A nose-up or nose-down attitude of 30 degrees relative to the horizon.

Exceptions: Flight tests, spins for certification, and aircraft certificated for aerobatics (occupants are pilot and examiner/instructor).

cards.question: §91.111 - Operating near other aircraft
cards.answer:
(a) No person may operate an aircraft so close to another aircraft as to create a collision hazard.

(b) No person may operate an aircraft in formation flight except by arrangement with the pilot in command of each aircraft in the formation.

(c) No person may operate an aircraft, carrying passengers for hire, in formation flight.

cards.question: §91.15 - Dropping objects
cards.answer:
No pilot in command of a civil aircraft may allow any object to be dropped from that aircraft in flight that creates a hazard to persons or property.

However, this section does not prohibit the dropping of any object if reasonable precautions are taken to avoid injury or damage to persons or property.

cards.question: §91.21 - Portable electronic devices
AIM 4-3-13 - ATC Light Gun Signals
cards.answer:
Light Gun Signals from ATC:

AIRCRAFT ON THE GROUND:
• Steady Green: Cleared for takeoff
• Flashing Green: Cleared to taxi
• Steady Red: Stop
• Flashing Red: Taxi clear of runway in use
• Flashing White: Return to starting point on airport
• Alternating Red and Green: Exercise extreme caution

AIRCRAFT IN FLIGHT:
• Steady Green: Cleared to land
• Flashing Green: Return for landing (to be followed by steady green at proper time)
• Steady Red: Give way to other aircraft and continue circling
• Flashing Red: Airport unsafe, do not land
• Alternating Red and Green: Exercise extreme caution

Acknowledge light signals:
• During day: Rock wings or move ailerons/rudder
• During night: Flash landing light twice or blink navigation lights

cards.question: AIM 4-3-3 - Traffic pattern operations
cards.answer:
Standard traffic pattern:
• All turns are made to the LEFT unless otherwise indicated by visual markings, light signals, or ATC instructions.
• Standard traffic pattern altitude is typically 1,000 feet AGL (unless otherwise specified).

Components of the traffic pattern:
(1) Upwind leg: Parallel to the runway in the direction of landing
(2) Crosswind leg: Perpendicular to the runway at the departure end
(3) Downwind leg: Parallel to the runway, opposite the direction of landing
(4) Base leg: Perpendicular to the runway, begins the approach to landing
(5) Final approach: Aligned with the runway for landing

Pattern entry:
• Enter at pattern altitude at a 45° angle to the downwind leg at midfield
• Or enter straight-in or crosswind when appropriate

A right traffic pattern is indicated by a segmented circle or noted on charts.

cards.question: AIM 7-4-6 - Wake turbulence avoidance
cards.answer:
Wake turbulence is generated by all aircraft in flight. The greatest vortex strength occurs when the generating aircraft is:
• Heavy
• Clean (flaps/gear retracted)
• Slow

Vortex behavior:
• Vortices sink at 400-500 feet per minute
• Vortices tend to level off about 900 feet below the flight path
• Vortices drift with the wind
• In ground effect, vortices move laterally at about 5 knots

Avoidance procedures:

Landing behind a larger aircraft on the same runway:
• Stay at or above the larger aircraft's final approach path
• Land beyond its touchdown point

Landing behind a departing larger aircraft on the same runway:
• Land prior to the larger aircraft's rotation point

Departing behind a larger aircraft:
• Rotate prior to the larger aircraft's rotation point
• Climb above and upwind of the larger aircraft's climb path

En route: Avoid flight below and behind a larger aircraft.

cards.question: AIM 7-1-25 - Wind shear
cards.answer:
Wind shear is a change in wind speed and/or wind direction in a short distance resulting in a tearing or shearing effect. It can exist in a horizontal or vertical direction and occasionally in both.

Common sources of wind shear:
• Frontal activity (especially fast-moving cold fronts)
• Thunderstorms (microbursts and gust fronts)
• Temperature inversions
• Surface obstructions

Microburst characteristics:
• Downdrafts as strong as 6,000 feet per minute
• Horizontal winds near the surface may exceed 45 knots
• Typically last 5-15 minutes
• May occur anywhere convective activity is present

Pilot actions:
• If wind shear is encountered on approach:
  - Apply maximum thrust
  - Adjust pitch to stop descent/begin climb
  - Do not retract flaps or gear until out of the shear
• Report all wind shear encounters to ATC
• Use PIREPs to warn other pilots

cards.question: AIM 8-1-8 - Scanning for other aircraft (see and avoid)
cards.answer:
Effective scanning is accomplished with a series of short, regularly spaced eye movements that bring successive areas of the sky into the central visual field. Each movement should not exceed 10 degrees, and each area should be observed for at least 1 second.

Effective visual scanning:
• Move eyes in small sectors (10°), pause for at least 1 second per sector
• Most important areas: ±60° of your flight path
• Focus at infinity, then refocus at specific distances
• Be aware of visual limitations at night

Factors that reduce effectiveness:
• Empty-field myopia (eyes focus 10-30 feet without visual reference)
• Narrow field of focus (central vision is only 10-15°)
• Head colds, fatigue, medications
• Dirty or scratched windscreens
• Atmospheric conditions (haze, glare)

Collision course indicators:
• No apparent relative motion
• Aircraft appears to stay in same spot on windscreen
• Aircraft grows larger without moving

cards.question: §91.3 - Responsibility and authority of the pilot in command
cards.answer:
(a) The pilot in command of an aircraft is directly responsible for, and is the final authority as to, the operation of that aircraft.

(b) In an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action, the pilot in command may deviate from any rule of this part to the extent required to meet that emergency.

(c) Each pilot in command who deviates from a rule under paragraph (b) of this section shall, upon the request of the Administrator, send a written report of that deviation to the Administrator.

This regulation establishes the PIC as the final authority and allows deviation from ANY rule when an emergency requires immediate action. The key requirement is that the deviation must be necessary to meet the emergency.

cards.question: Emergency frequencies and transponder codes
cards.answer:
Emergency Frequencies:
• 121.5 MHz: International aeronautical emergency frequency (civil)
• 243.0 MHz: Military emergency frequency
• Guard frequency: 121.5 is monitored by ATC facilities and many aircraft

Emergency Transponder Codes:
• 7500: Hijack (unlawful interference)
• 7600: Lost communications (radio failure)
• 7700: Emergency (general emergency)

Mnemonic for codes:
• 75 - Taken alive (hijack)
• 76 - Technical tricks (radio problems)
• 77 - Going to heaven (emergency)

When to declare an emergency:
• The pilot in command has the authority to declare an emergency at any time
• Declaration gets you priority handling from ATC
• When in doubt, declare - it's better to have help available

cards.question: AIM 6-2-3 - Distress and urgency procedures
cards.answer:
MAYDAY (Distress) - Used when threatened by serious and/or imminent danger and requires immediate assistance.

PAN-PAN (Urgency) - Used when the safety of the aircraft or some person on board or within sight is concerned, but does not require immediate assistance.

If you become lost:
1. Maintain aircraft control - fly the airplane first
2. Climb if possible (better radio/radar coverage, see further)
3. Confess - contact ATC on current frequency or 121.5
4. Communicate - provide: aircraft ID, position (last known), altitude, fuel remaining, souls on board, nature of distress
5. Comply with ATC instructions
6. Squawk 7700 if appropriate

Four C's: Climb, Communicate, Confess, Comply

ATC can provide:
• Radar vectors to nearest airport
• DF (Direction Finding) steers
• No-gyro approaches if instruments failed

cards.question: §91.153 & §91.169 - VFR and IFR flight plan requirements
cards.answer:
VFR Flight Plans (§91.153):
• Not required by regulation for VFR flights (except when crossing ADIZ or FIR boundaries)
• Highly recommended for cross-country flights
• Provides search and rescue protection if overdue
• Must include: aircraft identification, type, true airspeed, departure point and time, route, destination, fuel on board, number aboard, pilot's name/address
• Remains open until you close it (failure to close triggers search and rescue)

IFR Flight Plans (§91.169):
• Required for all IFR operations
• Must be filed at least 30 minutes before proposed departure time for electronic flight plans
• Must include: aircraft identification/type/equipment suffix, true airspeed, departure point/time, altitude, route, destination, ETE, fuel, alternate airport (if required), pilot's name/phone

Closing flight plans:
• VFR: Close with FSS (radio, phone, or online)
• IFR: Automatically closed by ATC upon landing at airports with operating control towers; pilot must close at non-towered airports

cards.question: §91.7 - Civil aircraft airworthiness
cards.answer:
(a) No person may operate a civil aircraft unless it is in an airworthy condition.

(b) The pilot in command of a civil aircraft is responsible for determining whether that aircraft is in condition for safe flight. The pilot in command shall discontinue the flight when unairworthy mechanical, electrical, or structural conditions occur.

This regulation places the final responsibility for airworthiness determination on the PIC, not mechanics or aircraft owners. Even if the aircraft has current inspections and proper logbook entries, the PIC must determine before each flight that the aircraft is in a condition for safe flight.

cards.question: 14 CFR Part 43 Appendix A - Preventive maintenance (pilot-performed)
cards.answer:
A certificated pilot (private or higher) may perform preventive maintenance on any aircraft owned or operated by that pilot which is not used in air carrier service. Preventive maintenance items include:

(1) Removal, installation, and repair of landing gear tires
(2) Replacing elastic shock absorber cords on landing gear
(3) Servicing landing gear shock struts by adding oil, air, or both
(4) Servicing landing gear wheel bearings (cleaning and greasing)
(5) Replacing defective safety wiring or cotter keys
(6) Lubrication not requiring disassembly other than removal of non-structural items such as cover plates, cowlings, and fairings
(7) Making simple fabric patches not requiring rib stitching or the removal of structural parts or control surfaces
(8) Replenishing hydraulic fluid in the hydraulic reservoir
(9) Refinishing decorative coating of fuselage, wings, tail group surfaces (excluding balanced control surfaces) when not requiring disassembly
(10) Replacing side windows where that work does not interfere with the structure or any operating system
(11) Replacing safety belts
(12) Replacing seats or seat parts not involving disassembly of any primary structure or operating system
(13) Troubleshooting and repairing broken circuits in landing light wiring circuits
(14) Replacing bulbs, reflectors, and lenses of position and landing lights
(15) Replacing spark plugs (and setting spark plug gap)
(16) Replacing hoses, and replacing or cleaning filters
(17) Replacing batteries and checking fluid level and specific gravity
(18) Cleaning or replacing fuel and oil strainers or filter elements
(19) Replacing and servicing ELT batteries

Note: All preventive maintenance must be recorded in the aircraft maintenance records.

cards.question: §61.23 - Medical certificates: Required class and duration
cards.answer:
Medical certificate classes and required operations:

• First-Class: Required for ATP privileges (airline transport pilot acting as PIC)
• Second-Class: Required for commercial pilot privileges
• Third-Class: Required for private pilot, recreational pilot, flight instructor, and student pilot privileges

Duration of medical certificates:

First-Class (under age 40):
• ATP privileges: 12 calendar months
• Commercial privileges: 12 calendar months
• Private privileges: 60 calendar months

First-Class (age 40 or older):
• ATP privileges: 6 calendar months
• Commercial privileges: 12 calendar months
• Private privileges: 24 calendar months

Second-Class (under age 40):
• Commercial privileges: 12 calendar months
• Private privileges: 60 calendar months

Second-Class (age 40 or older):
• Commercial privileges: 12 calendar months
• Private privileges: 24 calendar months

Third-Class (under age 40): 60 calendar months
Third-Class (age 40 or older): 24 calendar months

Note: BasicMed (§61.113(i)) may be used as an alternative to a third-class medical for certain operations.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-1 - Weight and balance terminology
cards.answer:
Datum: An imaginary vertical plane or line from which all measurements of arm are taken. The datum is established by the manufacturer.

Arm: The horizontal distance in inches from the reference datum line to the center of gravity of an item.

Moment: The product of the weight of an item multiplied by its arm (Moment = Weight × Arm). Moments are expressed in pound-inches.

Center of Gravity (CG): The point at which an airplane would balance if it were suspended at that point. The CG is found by dividing total moment by total weight.

Station: A location in the aircraft identified by a number designating its distance in inches from the datum.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-1 - Types of aircraft weight
cards.answer:
Standard Empty Weight: The weight of the airframe, engines, and all items of operating equipment that have fixed locations and are permanently installed in the airplane. Includes unusable fuel and full operating fluids including engine oil.

Basic Empty Weight: Standard empty weight plus the weight of optional and special equipment that have been installed.

Useful Load: The difference between maximum ramp weight (or maximum takeoff weight if ramp weight is not listed) and basic empty weight. Includes usable fuel, passengers, baggage, and cargo.

Payload: The weight of occupants, cargo, and baggage.

Maximum Ramp Weight: The maximum weight approved for ground maneuver. It includes weight of fuel used for start, taxi, and runup.

Maximum Takeoff Weight: The maximum allowable weight for takeoff.

Maximum Landing Weight: The maximum weight approved for the landing touchdown.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-1 - Effects of CG position on aircraft stability
cards.answer:
Forward CG:
• More stable (greater longitudinal stability)
• Less fuel efficient (requires more tail-down force, creating more induced drag)
• Higher stall speed (effective wing loading increased)
• Better stall/spin recovery characteristics
• May require excessive back pressure on yoke

Aft CG:
• Less stable (reduced longitudinal stability)
• More fuel efficient (less induced drag)
• Lower stall speed
• Poor stall/spin recovery characteristics (reduced elevator authority)
• May be difficult or impossible to recover from stall/spin
• Lighter control forces (may feel overly sensitive)

An airplane loaded with the CG aft of the approved limits may be impossible to control.

cards.question: AC 00-6 - Atmospheric stability characteristics
cards.answer:
Stable Atmosphere Characteristics:
• Stratiform clouds and fog
• Smooth air (little or no turbulence)
• Continuous precipitation (drizzle)
• Fair to poor visibility in haze and smoke
• Temperature decreases slowly with altitude

Unstable Atmosphere Characteristics:
• Cumuliform clouds
• Turbulent air
• Showery precipitation
• Good visibility (except in precipitation)
• Temperature decreases rapidly with altitude
• Strong vertical development

Stability is determined by comparing the temperature of a rising air parcel with the temperature of the surrounding air. If the parcel is cooler than the surrounding air, it will sink (stable). If warmer, it will continue to rise (unstable).

cards.question: AC 00-6 - Temperature inversion
cards.answer:
A temperature inversion occurs when temperature increases with altitude instead of the normal decrease. Inversions are extremely stable and suppress vertical motion.

Conditions associated with inversions:
• Smooth flying conditions
• Poor visibility (haze, smoke, and pollutants trapped below inversion)
• Fog formation likely if sufficient moisture present
• Low stratus clouds
• Drizzle

Inversions form by:
• Surface cooling (radiation fog conditions)
• Warm air overrunning cold air (warm front)
• Subsidence (sinking air in high pressure systems)

Inversions are significant hazards because they can trap fog, smoke, and pollution at low levels, severely reducing visibility.

cards.question: AC 00-6 - Cold front characteristics
cards.answer:
A cold front forms when a cold air mass advances and replaces a warmer air mass. The cold air, being denser, wedges under the warm air, forcing it aloft.

Characteristics:
• Cumuliform clouds (due to steep frontal slope causing rapid lifting)
• Showery precipitation in narrow band
• Good visibility after frontal passage (except in precipitation)
• Turbulence
• Possible thunderstorms, especially with fast-moving cold fronts
• Rapid weather changes
• Wind shift (clockwise in Northern Hemisphere)
• Temperature drop
• Pressure rise after passage

Fast-moving cold fronts produce the most severe weather and may have squall lines 50-200 miles ahead of the front containing severe thunderstorms.

cards.question: AC 00-6 - Warm front characteristics
cards.answer:
A warm front forms when a warm air mass advances and replaces a cooler air mass. The warm air, being less dense, rides up and over the cold air.

Characteristics:
• Stratiform clouds (due to gradual frontal slope)
• Steady, widespread precipitation ahead of front
• Poor visibility in precipitation and fog
• Smooth air (unless thunderstorms embedded)
• Low ceilings
• Wind shift (clockwise in Northern Hemisphere)
• Temperature rise after passage
• Pressure fall then rise

Clouds progress in order: cirrus, cirrostratus, altostratus, nimbostratus, stratus. Precipitation may begin 200-300 miles ahead of surface front.

Thunderstorms may be embedded in stratiform clouds during summer, making them particularly dangerous because they cannot be visually detected.

cards.question: AC 00-6 - Types of fog
cards.answer:
Radiation Fog: Forms on clear, calm nights when ground cools by radiation. Requires light winds (under 5 knots), clear skies, and moist air. Common in valleys. Burns off after sunrise.

Advection Fog: Forms when warm, moist air moves over cooler surface. Requires wind for formation. Can persist day and night. Common along coastlines.

Upslope Fog: Forms when moist, stable air is forced up sloping terrain, cooling to dewpoint. Requires upward terrain slope and wind. Common on eastern slopes of Rockies.

Steam Fog (Arctic Sea Smoke): Forms when cold, dry air moves over warm water. Water evaporates, saturating cold air. Low-level turbulence and icing possible.

Precipitation-Induced Fog: Forms when warm rain falls through cool air, saturating it. Common with warm fronts.

Ice Fog: Occurs in extremely cold temperatures (below -25°F) when water vapor sublimates directly into ice crystals.

cards.question: AC 00-6 - Pressure systems and associated weather
cards.answer:
High Pressure Systems (Anticyclones):
• Air descends and warms (prevents cloud formation)
• Generally fair weather
• Clear or scattered clouds
• Light winds
• Good visibility (unless inversion traps haze)
• Winds flow clockwise and outward (Northern Hemisphere)

Low Pressure Systems (Cyclones):
• Air rises and cools (promotes cloud formation)
• Clouds, precipitation, poor visibility
• Strong winds
• Turbulence
• Winds flow counterclockwise and inward (Northern Hemisphere)

Trough: Elongated area of low pressure. Creates convergence and lifting. Often associated with fronts. Weather similar to low pressure.

Ridge: Elongated area of high pressure. Creates divergence and sinking. Generally fair weather.

cards.question: AC 00-6 - Three stages of thunderstorm development
cards.answer:
Cumulus (Building) Stage:
• Characterized by updrafts throughout the cell
• Rising air creates cumulus clouds with strong vertical development
• Lasts 15-30 minutes
• Usually no precipitation at surface

Mature Stage:
• Characterized by presence of both updrafts AND downdrafts
• Most violent stage
• Heavy precipitation, possibly hail
• Lightning most intense
• Anvil top forms
• Strong gusty surface winds from downdraft spreading out
• Maximum turbulence and icing

Dissipating Stage:
• Characterized by downdrafts throughout the cell
• Precipitation decreases
• Anvil may spread out
• Light turbulence
• Cell dies as downdrafts cut off updraft supply

A cell typically progresses through all three stages in 1-2 hours.

cards.question: AIM 7-1-26 - Microbursts
cards.answer:
A microburst is a small-scale, intense downdraft that spreads outward from its center upon reaching the surface. It is typically less than 2.5 miles in diameter.

Characteristics:
• Downdrafts can reach 6,000 feet per minute
• Horizontal winds near surface can exceed 45 knots
• Wind speed changes of 90 knots have been recorded
• Peak intensity typically lasts only 2-4 minutes
• Maximum duration is 15 minutes
• May or may not produce precipitation at ground

Hazard to aircraft:
• Initial headwind increases performance (false sense of security)
• Aircraft enters downdraft, losing altitude
• Tailwind develops, causing rapid loss of airspeed and lift
• At low altitudes (takeoff/landing), insufficient time/altitude to recover

Microbursts should be avoided. If encountered, apply maximum power and maintain attitude.

cards.question: AIM 7-1-25 - Wind shear
cards.answer:
Wind shear is a change in wind speed and/or direction over a short distance. It can occur in horizontal or vertical planes.

Common sources:
• Frontal systems (especially fast-moving cold fronts)
• Thunderstorms and microbursts
• Temperature inversions (low-level jet)
• Surface obstructions
• Mountain waves

Hazards:
• Sudden loss of airspeed and lift
• Sudden increase in airspeed (potential overspeed)
• Rapid altitude deviations
• Most dangerous at low altitude during takeoff and landing

Recovery:
• Apply maximum power immediately
• Maintain or increase pitch to stop descent
• Do NOT retract flaps or gear until clear of shear
• Be prepared for rapid airspeed fluctuations

All wind shear encounters should be reported to ATC via PIREPs.

cards.question: AC 00-6 - Types of structural icing
cards.answer:
Clear Ice:
• Glossy, transparent ice
• Forms from large supercooled water droplets that flow over the surface before freezing
• Dense and hard
• Difficult to remove
• Most serious type of icing
• Common in temperatures 0°C to -10°C

Rime Ice:
• Rough, milky, opaque ice
• Forms from small supercooled droplets that freeze immediately on contact
• Lighter and less dense than clear ice
• Easier to remove
• Rough surface disrupts airflow
• Common in temperatures -10°C to -20°C

Mixed Ice:
• Combination of clear and rime ice
• Forms when droplet sizes vary or temperatures fluctuate
• Has properties of both types

Frost:
• Forms through sublimation when surface is below freezing and below dewpoint
• Must be removed before flight - disrupts smooth airflow over wing
• Can increase stall speed 5-10%

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Carburetor icing
cards.answer:
Carburetor icing can occur at ambient temperatures between 20°F and 70°F (-7°C to 21°C) when there is visible moisture or high humidity.

How it forms:
• Fuel vaporization and air expansion in carburetor venturi cause temperature drop of 60-70°F
• Moisture freezes on throttle valve and carburetor interior
• Most likely at temperatures between 32°F and 50°F with high humidity

Indications:
• Fixed-pitch propeller: RPM decrease
• Constant-speed propeller: Manifold pressure decrease
• Rough engine operation

Use of carburetor heat:
• Apply full carburetor heat (partial heat can worsen icing)
• Expect initial RPM/power decrease (heated air is less dense)
• RPM/power should increase as ice melts
• Engine may run rough as ice passes through
• Use before reducing power for descent
• Refer to POH for specific aircraft procedures

cards.question: AIM 2-3-8 - Mandatory instruction signs (red background)
cards.answer:
Mandatory instruction signs have a red background with white inscription. They denote an entrance to a runway, critical area, or prohibited area.

Types:
• Runway Holding Position: Designates runway or runway/runway intersection (e.g., '15-33' or '4-APCH'). Do not cross without ATC clearance.

• Runway Approach Area Hold: 'APCH' indicates holding position for approach area. Hold for aircraft on approach.

• ILS Critical Area Hold: Indicates boundary of ILS critical area. Do not enter when instructed to hold short of ILS critical area.

• No Entry: Red circle with white horizontal bar. Identifies areas where aircraft entry is prohibited.

NEVER cross a red sign without ATC clearance at a towered airport. At non-towered airports, verify runway is clear before crossing.

cards.question: AIM 2-3-9 - Location signs (black background)
cards.answer:
Location signs have a black background with yellow inscription and a yellow border. They identify your current location.

Types:
• Taxiway Location: Single letter or letter-number (e.g., 'A' or 'A2'). Identifies taxiway you are on.

• Runway Location: Runway numbers (e.g., '22'). Identifies runway you are on or entering.

• Runway Boundary: Yellow runway number on black background. Indicates you are leaving runway and entering taxiway.

• ILS Critical Area Boundary: Identifies exit from ILS critical area.

• Runway Distance Remaining: Black sign with white number indicating remaining runway length in 1,000-foot increments (e.g., '7' = 7,000 feet remaining).

Location signs tell you WHERE YOU ARE. They do not give instructions or directions.

cards.question: AIM 2-3-10 - Direction and destination signs (yellow background)
cards.answer:
Direction/Destination signs have a yellow background with black inscription. They provide routing information.

Direction Signs:
• Show direction to taxiways and runways
• Include arrow indicating direction of turn
• Letters/numbers indicate taxiway or runway designation
• Example: '← A' means Taxiway A to the left

Destination Signs:
• Identify general destinations on airport
• Common destinations: FBO, Terminal, Parking, Runways
• Usually include arrows pointing toward destination

Sign arrays combine location (black/yellow) and direction (yellow/black) signs at intersections to show both current position and available routes.

Remember: Yellow signs give directions/information. Black signs show your location.

cards.question: AIM 2-3-3 - Runway markings
cards.answer:
Runway markings are WHITE.

Runway Designator: Magnetic heading rounded to nearest 10° (omit last zero). Parallel runways add L, C, or R.

Centerline: Single dashed white line running full length of runway.

Threshold: White stripes across beginning of landing portion.

Displaced Threshold: White arrows point toward usable landing threshold. Area before threshold can be used for takeoff, landing rollout, and taxiing, but not for landing.

Aiming Point: Two broad white stripes approximately 1,000 feet from threshold (on runways 4,000+ feet).

Touchdown Zone: Series of stripes beginning 500 feet from threshold (on precision runways).

Edge Markings: Continuous white lines along runway edges.

Blast Pad/Stopway: Yellow chevrons. Not for aircraft use.

cards.question: AIM 2-3-5 - Taxiway markings
cards.answer:
Taxiway markings are YELLOW.

Centerline: Continuous yellow line on taxiway center.

Edge Markings: Double yellow lines (continuous for pavement edge, dashed for shoulder).

Holding Position Markings: Four yellow lines (two solid, two dashed) across taxiway. Solid lines on side where aircraft must hold. Never cross solid lines without clearance at towered airport.

Runway Holding Position: Hold short of runway.

ILS Critical Area: Hold short of ILS critical area when in use.

Surface Painted Holding Position Signs: Supplement elevated signs with same information painted on pavement.

Taxiway/Taxiway Intersection Marking: Yellow dashes indicate intersection.

Enhanced Taxiway Centerline: Dashed yellow centerline within runway hold position marking area.

cards.question: AIM 2-1-2 - Visual Approach Slope Indicator (VASI/PAPI)
cards.answer:
VASI (Visual Approach Slope Indicator):
2-bar VASI standard indications:
• Both bars WHITE: Too high (more than 3.5°)
• Near bar RED, far bar WHITE: On glidepath (3°)
• Both bars RED: Too low (less than 2.5°)

Mnemonic: 'Red over white, you're alright. Red over red, you're dead. White over white, you're high as a kite.'

PAPI (Precision Approach Path Indicator):
4-light single row system:
• 4 WHITE: High (more than 3.5°)
• 3 WHITE, 1 RED: Slightly high
• 2 WHITE, 2 RED: On glidepath (3°)
• 1 WHITE, 3 RED: Slightly low
• 4 RED: Low (less than 2.5°)

These systems provide visual glidepath guidance for approach. Standard glidepath is 3°. Always maintain at or above glidepath, especially at night or over water.

cards.question: AIM 2-1-4 - Airport beacon characteristics
cards.answer:
Airport beacons identify airport location and type during night and marginal weather conditions.

Beacon Color Combinations:
• White and Green: Civilian land airport
• White and Yellow: Water airport (seaplane base)
• Green, Yellow, and White: Heliport
• Two quick White flashes then Green flash: Military airport
• White and Green alternating: Lighted land airport

Beacon Operation:
• Beacons operate sunset to sunrise
• At airports with control towers, beacon ON during day indicates weather below VFR minimums (ceiling less than 1,000 feet and/or visibility less than 3 miles)

Rotation rate is approximately 12-30 times per minute, creating distinctive flashing pattern visible for many miles.

cards.question: AIM 4-3-3 - Traffic pattern procedures
cards.answer:
Standard Traffic Pattern:
• All turns are to the LEFT unless otherwise indicated by visual markings, light signals, or ATC instructions
• Standard pattern altitude is 1,000 feet AGL (unless otherwise specified)

Pattern Components:
1. Departure leg: Parallel to runway, direction of takeoff
2. Crosswind leg: Perpendicular to runway, turned within 300 feet of pattern altitude
3. Downwind leg: Parallel to runway, opposite direction of landing
4. Base leg: Perpendicular to runway, descended from pattern altitude
5. Final approach: Aligned with runway centerline

Pattern Entry:
• Enter at 45° angle to downwind leg at midfield, at pattern altitude
• Avoid flying over airport unless at least 500 feet above pattern altitude
• Straight-in approaches should be avoided if other traffic in pattern

Right traffic pattern indicated by: visual markings (segmented circle), chart notation, or ATC instructions.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Four forces of flight
cards.answer:
The four forces acting on an aircraft in flight:

Lift: The upward force created by the wing as a result of pressure differential between upper and lower surfaces. Lift acts perpendicular to the relative wind.

Weight (Gravity): The downward force due to the aircraft's mass acted upon by gravity. Acts toward the center of the Earth.

Thrust: The forward force produced by the engine/propeller. Overcomes drag to provide forward motion.

Drag: The rearward (retarding) force caused by disruption of airflow over the aircraft. Acts parallel and opposite to direction of flight.

Straight and level unaccelerated flight: Lift = Weight, Thrust = Drag

Types of Drag:
• Parasite drag: Increases with airspeed squared. Includes form, skin friction, and interference drag.
• Induced drag: Decreases with airspeed. Byproduct of lift (wingtip vortices).

Total drag is minimum at L/D max airspeed.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Left-turning tendencies
cards.answer:
Four factors cause left-turning tendency in single-engine propeller aircraft (clockwise rotation as viewed from cockpit):

1. Torque: Newton's Third Law - as propeller rotates clockwise, aircraft tends to rotate counterclockwise. Most noticeable during high-power, low-airspeed conditions.

2. P-Factor (Asymmetric Propeller Loading): At high angles of attack, descending (right) blade has greater angle of attack than ascending (left) blade, producing more thrust on right side, yawing aircraft left.

3. Spiraling Slipstream: Propeller wash spirals around fuselage, striking left side of vertical stabilizer, pushing tail right and yawing nose left.

4. Gyroscopic Precession: Propeller acts as gyroscope. Force applied to gyroscope is manifested 90° ahead in direction of rotation. During pitch changes (especially tailwheel takeoff), creates yawing force.

Compensated by rudder pressure, especially during takeoff and climb.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Stall recognition and recovery
cards.answer:
A stall is a rapid decrease in lift caused by the separation of airflow from the wing's surface brought on by exceeding the critical angle of attack.

Key Points:
• A stall can occur at ANY airspeed and ANY attitude
• The wing always stalls at the same critical angle of attack (typically 16-20°)
• Higher weight increases stall speed
• Load factor increases stall speed (stall speed × √load factor)
• Bank angle increases load factor and stall speed

Stall Recognition:
• Aerodynamic buffeting
• Reduced control effectiveness
• Stall warning horn/light
• Nose drops despite back pressure
• High sink rate

Stall Recovery (standard):
1. Reduce angle of attack (lower nose)
2. Add power as needed
3. Level wings
4. Return to desired flight path

Minimize altitude loss while avoiding secondary stall.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Spins: Entry, phases, and recovery
cards.answer:
A spin is an aggravated stall resulting in autorotation. Requires both a stall and yaw (uncoordinated flight).

Spin Entry Requirements:
• Wing must be stalled
• Yawing moment present (uncoordinated flight)

Spin Phases:
1. Entry: Stall with yaw
2. Incipient: First 2 rotations, disorientation likely
3. Developed: Stabilized spin, consistent rotation rate
4. Recovery: Intentional recovery actions

Standard Spin Recovery (PARE):
• Power: Idle (reduces P-factor and gyroscopic effects)
• Ailerons: Neutral
• Rudder: Full opposite to direction of spin
• Elevator: Forward to break stall
• Hold until rotation stops, then neutralize rudder
• Smoothly recover from dive

ALWAYS consult POH for aircraft-specific recovery procedures. Some aircraft have different or prohibited spin recovery techniques.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Load factor and maneuvering speed
cards.answer:
Load Factor: The ratio of lift to weight, measured in G's. In straight and level flight, load factor is 1G.

Load Factor in Turns:
• 30° bank = 1.15 G's
• 45° bank = 1.41 G's
• 60° bank = 2.0 G's
• 75° bank = 3.86 G's

Load factor increases stall speed: Stall speed in turn = 1G stall speed × √load factor

Maneuvering Speed (VA):
• Maximum speed at which full deflection of any one control will not cause structural damage
• At VA, aircraft will stall before exceeding structural limits
• VA decreases with weight (lower weight = lower VA)
• Rule: Reduce VA approximately 1% for each 2% reduction in weight below max gross

VA provides no protection against:
• Multiple control inputs simultaneously
• Gust loads
• Aerodynamic flutter

cards.question: AIM 7-4-6 - Wake turbulence avoidance
cards.answer:
