Wake turbulence consists of wingtip vortices generated by all aircraft in flight. Vortices are most severe when generating aircraft is:
• Heavy
• Clean (gear and flaps retracted)
• Slow

Vortex Behavior:
• Vortices sink at 400-500 feet per minute
• Level off approximately 900 feet below flight path
• Drift with wind
• In ground effect, move laterally at approximately 5 knots

Avoidance Procedures:

Landing behind larger aircraft (same runway):
• Stay at or above approach path
• Land beyond touchdown point

Landing behind departing larger aircraft (same runway):
• Land prior to rotation point

Departing behind larger aircraft (same runway):
• Rotate prior to their rotation point
• Climb above and upwind of their flight path

En route: Avoid flight below and behind larger aircraft. If crossing behind, pass at or above their altitude.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Reciprocating engine operation
cards.answer:
Four-Stroke Cycle:
1. Intake: Piston moves down, intake valve opens, fuel-air mixture enters cylinder
2. Compression: Both valves closed, piston moves up, compressing mixture
3. Power: Spark plug ignites mixture, expanding gases push piston down
4. Exhaust: Exhaust valve opens, piston moves up, expelling burned gases

Dual Ignition System:
• Two separate magnetos provide independent ignition
• Each cylinder has two spark plugs
• If one magneto fails, engine continues on other
• Both magnetos firing together provides more efficient combustion
• Magneto check during runup verifies both systems operating

Magneto Safety:
• Magnetos generate their own electricity
• Do not depend on aircraft electrical system
• Engine can start if propeller is moved and ignition is ON or P-lead is broken
• Always treat propeller as if ignition is live

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Aircraft electrical system
cards.answer:
Main Components:

Alternator/Generator: Produces electrical power when engine running. Alternator produces AC current (converted to DC), lighter weight, produces power at lower RPM. Generator produces DC directly, requires higher RPM.

Battery: Stores electrical energy. Provides power for starting and backup if alternator fails. Typical capacity: 30-60 minutes depending on electrical load.

Voltage Regulator: Controls alternator output to prevent overcharging battery and damaging equipment.

Ammeter: Shows battery charging (+) or discharging (-). Zero indicates battery neither charging nor discharging.

Loadmeter: Shows alternator output as percentage of capacity or in amps. Zero indicates no alternator output (alternator failure).

Bus Bar: Distribution point for electrical power to aircraft systems.

Circuit Breakers/Fuses: Protect circuits from overload. If breaker pops, wait before resetting. If it pops again, leave it out.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Fuel system components
cards.answer:
Main Components:

Fuel Tanks: Store fuel. May be wing tanks, fuselage tanks, or tip tanks. Check for water and sediment during preflight.

Fuel Selector: Allows pilot to select which tank supplies fuel or to shut off fuel. Common positions: LEFT, RIGHT, BOTH, OFF.

Fuel Strainer/Sump: Collects water and sediment. Drain during preflight and periodically during operation.

Engine-Driven Fuel Pump: Primary fuel pump, operates mechanically off engine.

Electric Fuel Pump: Backup pump. Used for starting, takeoff, landing, and suspected fuel pump failure. Also helps prevent vapor lock.

Fuel Primer: Manually pumps fuel directly into cylinders for cold starts. Must be locked after use.

Mixture Control: Adjusts fuel-to-air ratio. Lean for cruise (less fuel), enrich for high power operations.

Fuel Types:
• 100LL (Low Lead): Blue color, most common
• 100: Green color
• Jet-A: Clear to straw color - NEVER use in piston engines

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Engine problems: Detonation and preignition
cards.answer:
Detonation:
• Uncontrolled, explosive ignition of fuel-air mixture after normal ignition
• Causes severe stress on engine components
• Can cause engine failure

Causes:
• Using lower octane fuel than specified
• High manifold pressure with low RPM
• Lean mixture at high power
• High engine temperatures

Signs: Rough running, high CHT/EGT, loss of power

Preignition:
• Fuel-air mixture ignites before spark plug fires
• Caused by hot spot in combustion chamber (carbon deposits, damaged spark plug, overheated valve)

Signs: Rough running, high temperatures, loss of power

Both conditions can cause:
• Engine damage or failure
• Should prompt immediate power reduction and enrichment of mixture
• Land as soon as practical for inspection

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Pitot-static system instruments
cards.answer:
Three instruments use the pitot-static system:

Airspeed Indicator:
• Uses both pitot (ram air) and static pressure
• Measures difference between pressures
• Displays airspeed in knots or mph

Altimeter:
• Uses only static pressure
• Aneroid wafers expand/contract with pressure changes
• Set to local altimeter setting for altitude above MSL
• Set to 29.92 above 18,000 feet (flight levels)

Vertical Speed Indicator (VSI):
• Uses only static pressure
• Shows rate of climb or descent in feet per minute
• Has 6-9 second lag (trend instrument)

Blockages:
• Pitot tube blocked (drain open): Airspeed reads zero
• Pitot tube blocked (drain blocked): Airspeed acts like altimeter
• Static port blocked: All three instruments freeze
• Alternate static source: Lower pressure in cockpit may cause slightly high readings

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Gyroscopic flight instruments
cards.answer:
Three primary gyroscopic instruments:

Attitude Indicator (Artificial Horizon):
• Uses gyroscope with vertical spin axis
• Displays pitch and bank attitude relative to horizon
• Powered by vacuum system or electricity
• Primary pitch and bank reference during instrument flight

Heading Indicator (Directional Gyro):
• Uses gyroscope with horizontal spin axis
• More stable than magnetic compass
• Must be set to magnetic compass and rechecked every 15 minutes (precession)
• Powered by vacuum system or electricity

Turn Coordinator/Turn and Slip Indicator:
• Uses gyroscope tilted 30° from horizontal
• Shows rate of turn and coordination (ball/slip indicator)
• Usually electrically powered (backup for vacuum failure)

Vacuum System Failure:
• Attitude indicator and heading indicator fail
• Turn coordinator (if electric) still works
• Rely on magnetic compass, airspeed, altimeter, VSI for control

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Magnetic compass errors
cards.answer:
The magnetic compass is subject to several errors:

Variation: Difference between true and magnetic north. Varies by location. Applied using isogonic lines on charts. 'East is least, West is best.'

Deviation: Error caused by aircraft's magnetic fields. Varies with heading. Deviation card shows corrections.

Magnetic Dip: Compass needle tilts toward magnetic pole. Causes errors during turns and acceleration.

Acceleration Errors (ANDS):
• Accelerate: Compass shows turn to North
• Decelerate: Compass shows turn to South
• Only significant on East/West headings

Northerly Turning Error (UNOS):
• Undershoot North: When turning to north, compass leads; roll out early
• Overshoot South: When turning to south, compass lags; roll out late
• Most pronounced at high latitudes

Oscillation Error: Erratic needle movement during turbulence.

cards.question: AIM 1-1-3 - VOR navigation principles
cards.answer:
VOR (VHF Omnidirectional Range):
• Ground-based radio navigation system
• Operates on frequencies 108.0-117.95 MHz
• Provides 360 magnetic courses (radials) TO or FROM the station

Using VOR:
• Tune frequency and identify station (Morse code or voice)
• Rotate OBS until FROM flag appears with CDI centered
• Number at top of OBS is radial you are on

CDI (Course Deviation Indicator):
• Full-scale deflection = 10° off course
• Each dot represents 2° deviation

TO/FROM Flag:
• Shows whether selected course takes you TO or FROM station
• OFF or NAV flag indicates unreliable signal

VOR Service Volumes:
• Terminal (T): 25 NM, 1,000-12,000 feet AGL
• Low (L): 40 NM, 1,000-18,000 feet AGL
• High (H): 40-130 NM depending on altitude

VOR Check Required: Within 30 days for IFR operations.

cards.question: AIM 1-1-17 - GPS navigation
cards.answer:
GPS (Global Positioning System):
• Satellite-based navigation system
• 24+ satellites in constellation
• Requires signals from minimum 4 satellites for 3D fix

RAIM (Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring):
• Monitors GPS signal integrity
• Alerts pilot if accuracy insufficient
• Required for IFR GPS operations
• Check RAIM availability before IFR flight

WAAS (Wide Area Augmentation System):
• Improves GPS accuracy (7 meters or better)
• Enables precision GPS approaches (LPV)
• WAAS-equipped GPS doesn't require separate RAIM check

GPS Use:
• VFR: May use as primary navigation if properly installed
• IFR: Must be TSO-approved and installed per regulations
• Database must be current for IFR operations
• Pilot must be proficient in GPS operation
• Always have backup navigation capability

cards.question: AIM 8-1-2 - Hypoxia
cards.answer:
Hypoxia is a state of oxygen deficiency in the body sufficient to impair functions of the brain and other organs.

Types of Hypoxia:
• Hypoxic: Insufficient oxygen available (high altitude)
• Hypemic: Blood cannot carry adequate oxygen (carbon monoxide, blood loss)
• Stagnant: Oxygen-rich blood cannot circulate (heart problems, G-forces)
• Histotoxic: Cells cannot use oxygen (alcohol, drugs)

Symptoms (vary by individual):
• Impaired judgment (often first symptom)
• Euphoria (false sense of well-being)
• Visual impairment
• Headache, dizziness
• Tingling sensations
• Cyanosis (blue fingernails, lips)

Time of Useful Consciousness (without supplemental O2):
• 30,000 feet: 1-2 minutes
• 25,000 feet: 3-5 minutes
• 22,000 feet: 5-10 minutes

Treatment: Use supplemental oxygen and descend immediately.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Spatial disorientation illusions
cards.answer:
The Leans: Most common illusion. Abrupt return to level flight from gradual turn causes sensation of turning in opposite direction. Pilot may lean toward original turn.

Coriolis Illusion: During prolonged turn, head movement causes sense of rotation in different plane. Can be severe and disorienting.

Graveyard Spiral: Prolonged turn leads to unnoticed altitude loss. Pilot recovers from turn, feels like turning opposite way, returns to original turn while descending.

Somatogravic Illusion: Rapid acceleration creates sense of nose-up pitch. Pilot may push nose down, especially dangerous on takeoff.

Inversion Illusion: Abrupt change from climb to level flight creates sense of tumbling backward. Pilot may push aircraft into dive.

Elevator Illusion: Abrupt upward vertical acceleration creates illusion of climb. Pilot may push nose down.

False Horizon: Sloping clouds, Aurora Borealis, or lights mistaken for horizon.

Prevention: Trust instruments over sensations. Avoid head movements during instrument flight. Maintain instrument scan.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Hazardous attitudes and antidotes
cards.answer:
Five Hazardous Attitudes in Aeronautical Decision Making:

1. Anti-Authority: 'Don't tell me what to do.'
Antidote: 'Follow the rules. They are usually right.'

2. Impulsivity: 'Do something quickly! Don't waste time.'
Antidote: 'Not so fast. Think first.'

3. Invulnerability: 'It won't happen to me.'
Antidote: 'It could happen to me.'

4. Macho: 'I can do it. I'll show them.'
Antidote: 'Taking chances is foolish.'

5. Resignation: 'What's the use? I can't make a difference.'
Antidote: 'I'm not helpless. I can make a difference.'

Recognizing hazardous attitudes in yourself is the first step toward mitigating their effects on decision making. Apply the appropriate antidote when you recognize the attitude.

cards.question: AIM 8-1-2 - Flying after scuba diving
cards.answer:
Flying after scuba diving can cause decompression sickness at cabin altitudes far lower than would normally cause problems.

Recommended Wait Times Before Flight:

• Non-decompression diving (no controlled ascent required): Wait at least 12 hours before flight to cabin altitude up to 8,000 feet

• Decompression diving (controlled ascent required): Wait at least 24 hours before flight to cabin altitude up to 8,000 feet

• For altitude above 8,000 feet: Allow additional time

Decompression Sickness Symptoms:
• Joint pain ('the bends')
• Skin rashes/itching
• Fatigue
• Confusion
• Difficulty breathing
• Paralysis (severe cases)

Reduced atmospheric pressure at altitude allows nitrogen absorbed during diving to form bubbles in tissues.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Night vision and adaptation
cards.answer:
Night Vision Adaptation:

The eye uses two types of photoreceptors:
• Cones: Concentrated in fovea (center). Provide color and detail vision. Work in bright light. Adapt in 5-10 minutes.
• Rods: Located in periphery. Provide peripheral and night vision. Sensitive to movement. Take 30 minutes to fully adapt.

Night Adaptation Techniques:
• Allow 30 minutes in darkness for full rod adaptation
• Use red cockpit lighting (least disruptive to rod sensitivity)
• Avoid bright lights before flight
• Use off-center viewing (look 10-15° to side of object)
• Scan slowly (rods detect movement)

Factors Reducing Night Vision:
• Bright lights
• Smoking (carbon monoxide)
• Alcohol
• Fatigue
• Hypoxia (night vision affected above 5,000 feet)
• Age (older eyes adapt more slowly)

Supplemental oxygen at night may help maintain visual acuity.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Density altitude effects on performance
cards.answer:
Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature. High density altitude = low air density = reduced aircraft performance.

Factors Increasing Density Altitude:
• High elevation (pressure altitude)
• High temperature
• High humidity

Mnemonic: 'High, Hot, and Humid = High Density Altitude'

Performance Effects of High Density Altitude:
• Longer takeoff roll (less lift, less thrust)
• Reduced rate of climb
• Longer landing roll
• Higher true airspeed for given indicated airspeed
• Engine produces less power
• Propeller less efficient

Density Altitude Calculation:
• Start with pressure altitude (set altimeter to 29.92)
• Add 120 feet for each 1°C above standard temperature
• Or use flight computer/calculator

Standard Temperature: 15°C at sea level, decreasing 2°C per 1,000 feet

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Effects of weight on aircraft performance
cards.answer:
Increased aircraft weight negatively affects all aspects of performance:

• Longer takeoff distance required
• Reduced rate of climb
• Reduced maximum altitude (service ceiling)
• Reduced range and endurance
• Higher stall speed (stall speed ∝ √weight)
• Reduced cruise speed for given power
• Longer landing distance required
• Reduced maneuverability
• Higher fuel consumption

Weight Change Effects on Stall Speed:
New stall speed = Old stall speed × √(New weight / Old weight)

Example: If stall speed is 50 knots at 2,000 lbs, at 2,400 lbs:
New stall speed = 50 × √(2,400/2,000) = 50 × 1.095 = 54.8 knots

Importance:
• Always calculate W&B before flight
• Stay within CG envelope
• Performance charts assume maximum gross weight unless specified

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Effects of wind on takeoff and landing
cards.answer:
Headwind Effects:
• Shorter takeoff ground roll
• Steeper climb angle over obstacles
• Shorter landing ground roll
• Steeper approach angle

Tailwind Effects:
• Longer takeoff ground roll
• Shallower climb angle over obstacles
• Longer landing ground roll
• Shallower approach angle

Rules of Thumb:
• 10% headwind decreases takeoff/landing distance by approximately 10%
• 10% tailwind increases takeoff/landing distance by approximately 20%
• Never use more than 50% of reported headwind for performance calculations (wind may decrease)
• Always use 150% of reported tailwind component for planning

Crosswind:
• Does not directly affect takeoff/landing distance
• Requires crab or sideslip technique
• Maximum demonstrated crosswind component in POH
• Strong crosswinds increase pilot workload

cards.question: AIM 3-4 - Special use airspace types
cards.answer:
Prohibited Area (P):
• Flight prohibited for security/national welfare
• Examples: White House (P-56), Camp David (P-40)
• Never enter without specific authorization

Restricted Area (R):
• Contains hazardous activities (artillery, missiles, aerial gunnery)
• Flight prohibited when active
• May enter when not active (check NOTAMs) or with controlling agency permission

Warning Area (W):
• Contains same hazards as Restricted Area
• Located over international waters (3+ NM from coast)
• Flight not prohibited but exercise extreme caution

Military Operations Area (MOA):
• Military training activities
• VFR flight permitted but exercise caution
• IFR flight requires ATC clearance

Alert Area (A):
• High volume of pilot training or unusual aerial activity
• Flight not restricted
• All pilots equally responsible for collision avoidance

Controlled Firing Area (CFA):
• Activities suspended when aircraft spotted
• Not charted because no hazard to aircraft

cards.question: AIM 3-5-3 - Temporary Flight Restrictions (TFRs)
cards.answer:
TFRs are temporary airspace restrictions issued for specific reasons:

§91.137 - Disaster/Hazard Areas:
• Protect persons/property on surface
• Provide safe environment for disaster relief
• Prevent unsafe congestion of sightseeing aircraft

§91.138 - National Disaster Areas:
• Declared by President
• Restrict flight over disaster areas

§91.141 - Presidential and VIP TFRs:
• Protect President and other dignitaries
• Usually 10-30 NM radius, surface to various altitudes
• Inner ring typically prohibited, outer ring restricted

§91.143 - Space Operations:
• Protect space operations (launches, recoveries)

§91.145 - Special Events:
• Major sporting events (Super Bowl, World Series)
• Other events as designated

Checking TFRs:
• 1-800-WX-BRIEF
• TFR.FAA.gov
• NOTAMs
• Flight planning apps

Violating TFRs can result in certificate action, fines, or worse (especially VIP TFRs).

cards.question: §61.51 - Pilot logbook requirements
cards.answer:
Logging Requirements:

Must Log:
• Date
• Total flight or lesson time
• Location (departure and arrival)
• Type and identification of aircraft
• Name of safety pilot (if required)

For Training:
• Name and signature of instructor
• Type of training given

PIC Time (§61.51(e)): May log when:
• Sole manipulator of controls of aircraft for which rated
• Acting as required PIC when more than one pilot required
• When sport pilot is sole occupant and PIC

SIC Time (§61.51(f)): May log when:
• Type certification requires more than one pilot
• Regulations require more than one pilot

Instrument Time: Must log:
• Location and type of approach
• Name of safety pilot if in VFR conditions

Night Time: Log between end of evening civil twilight and beginning of morning civil twilight.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Cross-country flight planning basics
cards.answer:
Pre-Flight Planning Steps:

1. Route Selection:
• Plot course on sectional chart
• Identify checkpoints every 10-15 NM
• Note terrain, obstacles, airspace

2. Navigation Calculations:
• Measure true course
• Determine wind correction angle
• Calculate magnetic heading (TC ± WCA = TH; TH ± VAR = MH)
• Estimate groundspeed and time between checkpoints

3. Fuel Planning:
• Calculate fuel burn
• Ensure legal fuel reserves (30 min day/45 min night)
• Plan fuel stops if needed

4. Weather:
• Obtain standard briefing (1-800-WX-BRIEF or online)
• Review METARs, TAFs, AIRMETs, SIGMETs
• Check NOTAMs
• Assess go/no-go decision

5. Performance:
• Calculate takeoff/landing distances
• Determine climb performance
• Consider density altitude

6. Weight & Balance:
• Calculate W&B for departure and landing
• Verify within limits

7. File Flight Plan (recommended for VFR)

cards.question: AIM 6-2-4 - Lost procedures (The Four C's)
cards.answer:
If you become lost or disoriented, follow the Four C's:

1. CLIMB:
• Gain altitude for better visibility
• Improve radio/radar coverage
• See more landmarks
• Conserve fuel by slowing down

2. COMMUNICATE:
• Contact ATC on current frequency
• If unknown, use 121.5 MHz (emergency)
• Provide: Aircraft ID, type, position (last known), altitude, fuel remaining, souls on board

3. CONFESS:
• Admit you are lost or uncertain of position
• ATC cannot help if they don't know you need help
• No penalty for asking for help

4. COMPLY:
• Follow ATC instructions
• Squawk 7700 if emergency
• Squawk assigned code if given
• ATC can provide radar vectors, DF steers

Additional Actions:
• Circle prominent landmark if found
• Fly toward populated area or coastline
• Look for major highways, railroad tracks, rivers
• Conserve fuel

cards.question: AIM 6-1-2 - Emergency transponder codes
cards.answer:
Emergency Transponder Codes:

7500 - Hijack (unlawful interference):
• Squawk if aircraft is being hijacked
• ATC will not acknowledge verbally (to avoid alerting hijacker)
• May ask to 'verify squawk' - respond appropriately
• Mnemonic: '75 - Taken alive'

7600 - Lost Communications (radio failure):
• Squawk when unable to communicate by radio
• Continue flight per §91.185 procedures
• Mnemonic: '76 - Radio tricks (technical problems)'

7700 - General Emergency:
• Any other emergency situation
• Alerts ATC to emergency status
• Priority handling
• Mnemonic: '77 - Going to heaven'

Squawking 7700 will trigger alert at ATC facilities and all available assistance will be provided. Do not hesitate to declare an emergency when warranted - it's better to have help available and not need it than to need it and not have it.

cards.question: §91.111 - Operating near other aircraft
cards.answer:
(a) No person may operate an aircraft so close to another aircraft as to create a collision hazard.

(b) No person may operate an aircraft in formation flight except by arrangement with the pilot in command of each aircraft in the formation.

(c) No person may operate an aircraft, carrying passengers for hire, in formation flight.

Formation flight requires prior arrangement with all participating pilots. 'Formation flight' means aircraft operating together intentionally. Simply flying in the same direction or at the same altitude is not formation flight.

This regulation emphasizes the pilot's responsibility to maintain safe separation from other aircraft at all times.

cards.question: §91.15 - Dropping objects from aircraft
cards.answer:
No pilot in command of a civil aircraft may allow any object to be dropped from that aircraft in flight that creates a hazard to persons or property.

However, this section does not prohibit the dropping of any object if reasonable precautions are taken to avoid injury or damage to persons or property.

Examples of permitted drops (with precautions):
• Crop dusting operations
• Aerial firefighting
• Parachute operations
• Search and rescue supply drops
• Authorized experimental drops

Key consideration: The pilot must take reasonable precautions to avoid injury or damage. Intent matters less than whether reasonable precautions were taken.

cards.question: §91.107 - Use of safety belts and shoulder harnesses
cards.answer:
PIC Responsibilities:

(a)(1) Before takeoff, notify passengers how to fasten and unfasten safety belts and shoulder harnesses.

(a)(2) Before movement on surface, takeoff, and landing, notify passengers to fasten safety belts and shoulder harnesses (if installed).

(a)(3) During takeoff and landing, each person must occupy seat or berth with safety belt and shoulder harness (if installed) properly secured.

Exceptions:
• Children under 2 may be held by an adult
• Crew performing duties requiring mobility (flight attendants)
• Use of approved child restraint system

Shoulder Harness:
• Required in front seats of small civil airplanes manufactured after July 18, 1978
• Pilot and copilot must use during takeoff and landing
• Passengers may decline use during cruise

(b) Crewmembers must use safety belts during takeoff and landing.

cards.question: 14 CFR §1.1 - Definitions of Night and Twilight
cards.answer:
Night: The time between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight, as published in the Air Almanac, converted to local time.

Civil Twilight:
• Morning civil twilight begins when the geometric center of the sun is 6° below the horizon and ends at sunrise
• Evening civil twilight begins at sunset and ends when the geometric center of the sun is 6° below the horizon
• Usually 30-40 minutes before sunrise / after sunset (varies by latitude and season)

Important Distinctions:
• Night currency (§61.57): 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise
• Position lights required (§91.209): Sunset to sunrise
• Night time logging: End of evening civil twilight to beginning of morning civil twilight

The differences matter for logging, currency, and equipment requirements.

cards.question: §91.209 - Aircraft lights
cards.answer:
Position Lights and Anti-Collision Lights:

No person may operate an aircraft during the period from sunset to sunrise unless the aircraft has:

(a) Lighted position lights:
• Red light on left wingtip
• Green light on right wingtip
• White light on tail

(b) Anti-collision lights (if the aircraft is so equipped):
• White strobe or rotating beacon
• Required on aircraft certificated after March 11, 1996

Exceptions for Anti-Collision Lights:
• Pilot determines in interest of safety to turn off
• Examples: In clouds (disorienting), ground operations (blinding ground crew)

Landing Lights:
• Required for aircraft operated for hire
• Recommended for all night operations
• Use for enhanced visibility during takeoff, landing, and when in the vicinity of other aircraft

cards.question: §61.89 - General limitations on student pilots
cards.answer:
A student pilot may not act as pilot in command of an aircraft:

(a)(1) That is carrying a passenger

(a)(2) That is carrying property for compensation or hire

(a)(3) For compensation or hire

(a)(4) In furtherance of a business

(a)(5) On an international flight (except to/from Canada with CFI endorsement and approval of both countries)

(a)(6) With flight or surface visibility less than 3 SM during day or 5 SM at night

(a)(7) When flight cannot be made with visual reference to the surface

(a)(8) In a manner contrary to any limitations placed in the pilot's logbook by an authorized instructor

Additional endorsement requirements apply for:
• Class B airspace operations (§61.95)
• Solo cross-country flights (§61.93)
• Flights to airports within Class B or at specific high-traffic airports

cards.question: AIM 7-1-30 - METAR aviation routine weather report
cards.answer:
METAR is an aviation routine weather report issued hourly (or SPECI for significant changes).

Format:
• Type (METAR/SPECI)
• Station identifier (4-letter ICAO)
• Date/Time (day/time in Zulu)
• Wind (direction/speed in knots, gusts)
• Visibility (statute miles)
• Weather phenomena (rain, snow, fog, etc.)
• Sky condition (CLR, FEW, SCT, BKN, OVC with height)
• Temperature/Dewpoint (Celsius)
• Altimeter setting (inches Hg)
• Remarks (RMK)

Example:
METAR KLAX 121853Z 25012G20KT 10SM FEW025 BKN150 22/12 A3002 RMK AO2

Translation: Los Angeles, 12th day at 1853Z, wind 250° at 12 knots gusting 20, 10 statute miles visibility, few clouds at 2,500 feet, broken at 15,000 feet, temp 22°C dewpoint 12°C, altimeter 30.02.

cards.question: AIM 7-1-31 - TAF terminal aerodrome forecast
cards.answer:
TAF is a terminal aerodrome forecast valid for 24-30 hours.

Format:
• TAF identifier
• Station identifier
• Issue date/time
• Valid period
• Forecast wind, visibility, weather, sky condition
• Change groups (FM, TEMPO, PROB)

Change Indicators:
• FM (From): Significant change expected at specified time
• TEMPO: Temporary fluctuations (less than 1 hour, less than half the period)
• PROB: Probability of occurrence (PROB30 = 30% chance, PROB40 = 40% chance)
• BECMG: Gradual change during specified period

Example:
TAF KLAX 121730Z 1218/1324 25010KT P6SM SCT025 FM122000 28015G25KT P6SM BKN040

Translation: Valid 12th at 18Z to 13th at 24Z. Wind 250° at 10 knots, greater than 6 SM visibility, scattered at 2,500. From 12th at 2000Z, wind 280° at 15 gusting 25, broken at 4,000.

cards.question: AIM 7-1-6 - AIRMETs and SIGMETs
cards.answer:
AIRMETs (Airman's Meteorological Information):
Hazardous to small aircraft, VFR pilots. Valid for 6 hours.

• AIRMET Sierra: IFR conditions, mountain obscuration
• AIRMET Tango: Moderate turbulence, sustained surface winds ≥30 knots, low-level wind shear
• AIRMET Zulu: Moderate icing, freezing levels

SIGMETs (Significant Meteorological Information):
Hazardous to ALL aircraft. Valid for 4 hours (6 for hurricanes).

• Severe icing not associated with thunderstorms
• Severe or extreme turbulence not associated with thunderstorms
• Dust storms, sandstorms reducing visibility to <3 SM
• Volcanic ash

Convective SIGMETs:
Valid for 2 hours. Issued for:
• Severe thunderstorms with surface winds ≥50 knots
• Hail ≥3/4 inch diameter
• Tornadoes
• Embedded thunderstorms
• Line of thunderstorms
• Thunderstorms affecting 40%+ of area

Convective SIGMET implies severe or greater turbulence, severe icing, and low-level wind shear.

cards.question: §61.93 - Solo cross-country requirements for student pilots
cards.answer:
Before conducting solo cross-country flight, a student pilot must:

(c)(1) Receive ground and flight training covering:
• Use of aeronautical charts and navigation systems
• Pilotage and dead reckoning
• Use of radios for VFR navigation and two-way communication
• Cross-country flight planning
• Recognition of critical weather situations and avoidance
• Emergency procedures

(c)(2) Receive an endorsement certifying that student has:
• Received cross-country training
• Been found proficient for cross-country requirements

(c)(3) For each cross-country flight, receive an endorsement certifying instructor:
• Reviewed flight planning and weather
• Determined student prepared for the flight

Long Cross-Country for Private (§61.109(a)(5)(ii)):
• 150 NM total with full-stop landings at 3 points
• One segment straight-line distance >50 NM between takeoff and landing locations

cards.question: §91.407 - Operation after maintenance
cards.answer:
No person may operate an aircraft that has undergone maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, or alteration unless:

(a) It has been approved for return to service by a person authorized under §43.7

(b) The maintenance record entry has been made in accordance with §43.9 or §43.11

Test Flight Requirements (§91.407(b)):
No person may carry any person (other than crew) in an aircraft that has been maintained, rebuilt, or altered in a manner that may have appreciably changed its flight characteristics or substantially affected its operation in flight until an appropriately rated pilot with at least a private pilot certificate:
• Flies the aircraft
• Makes an operational check of maintenance performed
• Logs the flight in aircraft records

This test flight protects passengers by ensuring flight characteristics are verified before carrying passengers.

cards.question: §91.303 - Aerobatic flight restrictions
cards.answer:
No person may operate an aircraft in aerobatic flight:

(a) Over any congested area of a city, town, or settlement

(b) Over an open air assembly of persons

(c) Within the lateral boundaries of Class B, Class C, Class D, or Class E surface airspace designated for an airport

(d) Within 4 nautical miles of the center line of any Federal airway

(e) Below an altitude of 1,500 feet above the surface

(f) When flight visibility is less than 3 statute miles

Aerobatic flight means an intentional maneuver involving an abrupt change in an aircraft's attitude, an abnormal attitude, or abnormal acceleration, not necessary for normal flight.

Parachute requirements (§91.307): When exceeding 60° bank or 30° nose up/down pitch relative to horizon (with non-crew passengers), parachutes are required for each occupant.

cards.question: §91.9 - Operating limitations
cards.answer:
No person may operate a civil aircraft without complying with the operating limitations:

(a) Specified in the approved Airplane or Rotorcraft Flight Manual, markings, and placards

(b) For an aircraft of U.S. registry, required to have a flight manual, the approved flight manual must be in the aircraft

Operating limitations include:
• V-speeds (VNE, VNO, VA, VFE, etc.)
• Weight and balance limits
• Maneuvering limits (bank angles, G-loads)
• System limitations
• Approved operations (VFR/IFR, day/night)
• Prohibited maneuvers
• Minimum crew

Markings and Placards:
• Must be visible to pilot during normal operation
• Airspeed indicator markings (colored arcs and lines)
• Engine instrument limitations
• Required equipment placards

Violating operating limitations can result in structural damage or failure.

cards.question: §91.126 & §91.127 - Traffic pattern operations at non-towered airports
cards.answer:
§91.126 - Operations at airports within Class G airspace:

(a) Each person operating to or from an airport within Class G airspace:
(1) In the case of a turbine-powered airplane, make all turns to the left unless the airport has visual markings indicating right turns should be made
(2) In the case of an airplane approaching to land, make all turns to the left unless the airport displays approved light signals or markings indicating right turns should be made

(b) Each person operating must comply with traffic patterns established for that airport in Part 93

§91.127 - Operating on or in the vicinity of an airport in Class E airspace:
Same traffic pattern requirements as Class G.

Traffic Pattern Indicators:
• Segmented circle shows traffic pattern direction
• L-shaped markers indicate right traffic if placed to the right of the runway
• Wind indicators (windsock, tetrahedron) show wind direction

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Fuel contamination prevention
cards.answer:
Fuel Contamination Types:

1. Water:
• Most common contaminant
• Heavier than avgas, settles to bottom
• Check fuel sumps during preflight
• Sources: condensation, rain entry, defective caps

2. Sediment and Particles:
• Filter through fuel strainers
• May clog injectors or carburetor
• Drain sumps until clear

3. Wrong Fuel Grade:
• Lower octane can cause detonation
• Check fuel color and grade
• 100LL is blue, Jet-A is clear/straw

4. Microbial Growth:
• Bacteria/fungi at water-fuel interface
• More common in warm, humid conditions
• Can clog filters

Prevention:
• Drain sumps before EVERY flight
• Wait after refueling for water to settle
• Keep tanks full when parked (reduces condensation)
• Use proper fuel grade
• Maintain fuel caps and seals

cards.question: §91.409 - Inspection intervals and requirements
cards.answer:
Annual Inspection (§91.409(a)):
• Required every 12 calendar months
• Must be performed by IA (Inspection Authorization) or manufacturer's maintenance facility
• Must be approved for return to service

100-Hour Inspection (§91.409(b)):
• Required for aircraft carrying passengers for hire
• Required for flight instruction for hire
• May exceed 100 hours by up to 10 hours to reach place of inspection
• Excess hours must be included in next 100 hours
• May be performed by A&P mechanic

Progressive Inspection (§91.409(d)):
• Alternative to annual/100-hour system
• Spreads inspections over time
• Approved by FAA

Calendar Month Calculation:
• 12 calendar months from date of inspection
• Example: Annual on June 15, 2024 expires end of June 2025

Airworthiness: Aircraft is NOT airworthy if inspections are overdue.
glance: Annual: every 12 calendar months (IA)
100-hour: carrying passengers for hire or flight instruction for hire (A&P)
May exceed by up to 10 hr to reach the inspection place

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.65(a) - Instrument Rating Eligibility
cards.answer: A person who applies for an instrument rating must: (1) Hold at least a current private pilot certificate, or be concurrently applying for a private pilot certificate, with an airplane, helicopter, or powered-lift rating appropriate to the instrument rating sought; (2) Be able to read, speak, write, and understand the English language.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.65(d) - Aeronautical Experience for Instrument-Airplane
cards.answer: A person who applies for an instrument-airplane rating must have logged: (1) 50 hours of cross-country flight time as pilot in command, of which 10 hours must have been in an airplane; and (2) 40 hours of actual or simulated instrument time in the areas of operation listed under 61.65(c), of which 15 hours must have been received from an authorized instructor who holds an instrument-airplane rating.
glance: 50 hours cross-country PIC (10 in airplanes)
40 hours actual or simulated instrument
15 of the 40 from a CFII (instrument-airplane)

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.65(d)(2)(ii) - Instrument Cross-Country Flight
cards.answer: The aeronautical experience for an instrument rating must include: One cross-country flight of at least 250 nautical miles along airways or by directed routing from an air traffic control facility, with an instrument approach at each airport, and three different kinds of approaches with the use of navigation systems.
glance: One XC of at least 250 NM along airways or ATC-directed routing
An instrument approach at each airport
3 different kinds of approaches

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.65(i) - Use of Full Flight Simulator or Flight Training Device
cards.answer: A maximum of 20 hours of instrument time received in a full flight simulator or flight training device may be credited toward the 40 hours of instrument time required. A maximum of 10 hours of instrument time received in a basic aviation training device may be credited toward the 40 hours.
glance: Max 20 hours in a full flight simulator or FTD
Max 10 hours in a basic aviation training device (BATD)
Counts toward the 40 hours of instrument time

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.57(c)(1) - Instrument Experience Requirements
cards.answer: No person may act as pilot in command under IFR or in weather conditions less than the minimums prescribed for VFR, unless within the 6 calendar months preceding the month of the flight, that person has performed and logged under actual or simulated instrument conditions: (i) Six instrument approaches; (ii) Holding procedures and tasks; and (iii) Intercepting and tracking courses through the use of navigational electronic systems.
glance: Within the preceding 6 calendar months
6 instrument approaches
Holding procedures and tasks
Intercepting and tracking courses

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.57(c)(2) - Grace Period for Instrument Currency
cards.answer: A person who does not meet the instrument experience requirements within the prescribed time may not serve as pilot in command under IFR or in weather conditions less than the minimums prescribed for VFR until that person passes an instrument proficiency check.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.57(d) - Instrument Proficiency Check
cards.answer: An instrument proficiency check consists of a representative number of tasks required by the instrument rating practical test. The instrument proficiency check must be conducted by an examiner, an authorized instructor, or a person approved by the Administrator to conduct instrument practical tests.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.51(g)(1) - Logging Instrument Flight Time
cards.answer: A person may log instrument time only for that flight time when the person operates the aircraft solely by reference to instruments under actual or simulated instrument conditions.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.51(g)(2) - Instructor Logging Instrument Time
cards.answer: An authorized instructor may log instrument time when conducting instrument flight instruction in actual instrument flight conditions.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.51(g)(4) - Logging Instrument Approaches
cards.answer: A person can log an instrument approach when the person conducts the approach under actual or simulated instrument conditions and the approach is conducted in compliance with an instrument approach procedure under part 91.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.109(c) - Safety Pilot Requirements
cards.answer: No person may operate a civil aircraft in simulated instrument flight unless: (1) The other control seat is occupied by a safety pilot who possesses at least: (i) A private pilot certificate with category and class ratings appropriate to the aircraft being flown; (ii) Adequate vision forward and to each side of the aircraft, or a competent observer in the aircraft who adequately supplements the vision of the safety pilot; and (iii) Except in the case of lighter-than-air aircraft, an appropriate current medical certificate.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.109(c)(2) - Dual Controls for Simulated IMC
cards.answer: No person may operate a civil aircraft in simulated instrument flight unless the aircraft is equipped with fully functioning dual controls.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.167 - Fuel Requirements for IFR Flight
cards.answer: No person may operate a civil aircraft in IFR conditions unless it carries enough fuel (considering weather reports and forecasts and weather conditions) to: (1) Complete the flight to the first airport of intended landing; (2) Fly from that airport to the alternate airport; and (3) Fly after that for 45 minutes at normal cruising speed.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.167(b) - When Alternate Not Required
cards.answer: No alternate airport is required if: (1) Part 97 of this chapter prescribes a standard instrument approach procedure for the first airport of intended landing; and (2) For at least 1 hour before and for 1 hour after the estimated time of arrival, the ceiling will be at least 2,000 feet above the airport elevation and the visibility will be at least 3 statute miles.
glance: No alternate if: instrument approach at destination, AND
1 hr before to 1 hr after ETA: ceiling ≥ 2,000 ft and visibility ≥ 3 SM (1-2-3 rule)

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.169(c) - Alternate Airport Weather Minimums
cards.answer: Unless otherwise authorized by the Administrator, no person may include an alternate airport in an IFR flight plan unless appropriate weather reports or forecasts indicate that, at the estimated time of arrival at the alternate airport, the ceiling and visibility will be at or above the following weather minimums: (1) If an instrument approach procedure has been published for that airport: (i) For a precision approach procedure, 600-foot ceiling and 2 statute miles visibility; (ii) For a nonprecision approach procedure, 800-foot ceiling and 2 statute miles visibility.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.171(a) - VOR Check Required for IFR
cards.answer: No person may operate a civil aircraft under IFR using the VOR system of radio navigation unless the VOR equipment of that aircraft has been operationally checked within the preceding 30 days, and was found to be within the limits of the permissible indicated bearing error.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.171(b) - VOR Test Facility (VOT) Check
cards.answer: When using a VOT check, the maximum permissible indicated bearing error is plus or minus 4 degrees.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.171(c) - VOR Ground Checkpoint
cards.answer: When using a FAA certified ground checkpoint, the maximum permissible indicated bearing error is plus or minus 4 degrees.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.171(c)(3) - VOR Airborne Checkpoint
cards.answer: When using an approved airborne checkpoint, the maximum permissible indicated bearing error is plus or minus 6 degrees.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.171(d) - VOR Check Log Requirements
cards.answer: Each person making a VOR operational check shall enter the date, place, bearing error, and sign the aircraft log or other record.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.173 - ATC Clearance and Flight Plan Required
cards.answer: No person may operate an aircraft in controlled airspace under IFR unless that person has: (a) Filed an IFR flight plan; and (b) Received an appropriate ATC clearance.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.175(c) - Operation Below DA/DH or MDA
cards.answer: No pilot may operate an aircraft below the prescribed MDA or continue an approach below the authorized DA/DH unless: (1) The aircraft is continuously in a position from which a descent to a landing on the intended runway can be made at a normal rate of descent using normal maneuvers; (2) The flight visibility is not less than the visibility prescribed in the standard instrument approach procedure; and (3) At least one of the specified visual references for the runway is distinctly visible and identifiable.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.175(c)(3) - Required Visual References
cards.answer: The pilot must have distinctly visible at least one of the following: (i) The approach light system; (ii) The threshold; (iii) The threshold markings; (iv) The threshold lights; (v) The runway end identifier lights; (vi) The visual glideslope indicator; (vii) The touchdown zone or touchdown zone markings; (viii) The touchdown zone lights; (ix) The runway or runway markings; (x) The runway lights.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i) - Approach Lights Only
cards.answer: If the pilot uses approach lights as a reference, the pilot may not descend below 100 feet above the touchdown zone elevation unless the red terminating bars or the red side row bars are also distinctly visible and identifiable.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.175(d) - Landing Requirement
cards.answer: A pilot may not land if the flight visibility is less than the visibility prescribed in the standard instrument approach procedure being used.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.177 - Minimum IFR Altitudes
cards.answer: Except when necessary for takeoff or landing, no person may operate an aircraft under IFR below: (1) The applicable minimum altitudes prescribed in parts 95 and 97; or (2) If no applicable minimum altitude is prescribed: (i) In mountainous terrain, an altitude of 2,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal distance of 4 nautical miles from the course to be flown; or (ii) Other than mountainous terrain, an altitude of 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal distance of 4 nautical miles from the course to be flown.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.179 - IFR Cruising Altitude or Flight Level
cards.answer: In controlled airspace, pilots shall maintain the altitude or flight level assigned by ATC. In uncontrolled airspace, IFR altitude requirements are: Below 18,000 feet MSL - On a magnetic course of 0 through 179 degrees, any odd thousand foot MSL altitude; On a magnetic course of 180 through 359 degrees, any even thousand foot MSL altitude.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.181 - Course to be Flown
cards.answer: Unless otherwise authorized by ATC, no person may operate an aircraft within controlled airspace under IFR except as follows: (a) On an ATS route, along the centerline of that airway; (b) On any other route, along the direct course between the navigational aids or fixes defining that route.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.183 - IFR Communications
cards.answer: Unless otherwise authorized by ATC, the pilot in command of each aircraft operated under IFR in controlled airspace must report: (1) The time and altitude of passing each designated reporting point; (2) Any unforecast weather conditions encountered; (3) Any other information relating to the safety of flight.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.187 - Operation Under IFR: Malfunction Reports
cards.answer: The pilot in command of each aircraft operated in controlled airspace under IFR shall report as soon as practical to ATC any malfunctions of navigational, approach, or communication equipment occurring in flight. The report shall include: (1) Aircraft identification; (2) Equipment affected; (3) Degree to which the capability of the pilot to operate under IFR is impaired; (4) Nature and extent of assistance desired from ATC.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.185(b) - VFR Conditions
cards.answer: If the failure occurs in VFR conditions, or if VFR conditions are encountered after the failure, each pilot shall continue the flight under VFR and land as soon as practicable.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.185(c)(1) - Route to Fly
cards.answer: If the failure occurs in IFR conditions, the pilot shall continue along the route: Assigned in the last ATC clearance received; If being radar vectored, by the direct route from the point of radio failure to the fix, route, or airway specified in the vector clearance; In the absence of an assigned route, by the route that ATC has advised may be expected in a further clearance; In the absence of an assigned route or a route that ATC has advised may be expected, by the route filed in the flight plan.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.185(c)(2) - Altitude to Fly
cards.answer: If the failure occurs in IFR conditions, at the highest of the following altitudes for the route segment being flown: The altitude or flight level assigned in the last ATC clearance received; The minimum altitude for IFR operations; or The altitude or flight level ATC has advised may be expected in a further clearance.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.185(c)(3) - Leave Clearance Limit
cards.answer: If the clearance limit is a fix from which an approach begins, commence descent or descent and approach as close as possible to the expect-further-clearance time if one has been received, or if one has not been received, as close as possible to the estimated time of arrival as calculated from the filed or amended (with ATC) estimated time en route.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.205(d) - Instrument Flight Rules Equipment
cards.answer: For IFR flight, the required instruments and equipment are: (1) Two-way radio communication and navigation equipment suitable for the route; (2) Gyroscopic rate-of-turn indicator; (3) Slip-skid indicator; (4) Sensitive altimeter adjustable for barometric pressure; (5) A clock displaying hours, minutes, and seconds with a sweep-second pointer or digital presentation; (6) Generator or alternator of adequate capacity; (7) Gyroscopic pitch and bank indicator (artificial horizon); (8) Gyroscopic direction indicator (directional gyro or equivalent).

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.211(a) - Supplemental Oxygen Requirements
cards.answer: No person may operate a civil aircraft of U.S. registry: (1) At cabin pressure altitudes above 12,500 feet MSL up to and including 14,000 feet MSL unless the required minimum flight crew is provided with and uses supplemental oxygen for that part of the flight at those altitudes that is of more than 30 minutes duration; (2) At cabin pressure altitudes above 14,000 feet MSL unless the required minimum flight crew is provided with and uses supplemental oxygen during the entire flight time at those altitudes; and (3) At cabin pressure altitudes above 15,000 feet MSL unless each occupant of the aircraft is provided with supplemental oxygen.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.211(b)(1) - Pressurized Cabin Above FL250
cards.answer: Above flight level 250, at least a 10-minute supply of supplemental oxygen, in addition to any oxygen required for emergencies, is available for each occupant of the aircraft for use in the event that a descent is necessitated by loss of cabin pressurization.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.215 - ATC Transponder and Altitude Reporting Equipment
cards.answer: All airspace: All aircraft. For operations not conducted under part 121 or 135, ATC transponder equipment must meet the performance and environmental requirements of TSO-C74b or TSO-C74c.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.215(b)(5)(ii) - Class B and C Airspace
cards.answer: A transponder with automatic altitude reporting capability is required: In Class B and Class C airspace areas, and in all airspace within 30 nautical miles of an airport listed in appendix D, section 1 of this part from the surface upward to 10,000 feet MSL.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.121 - Altimeter Settings
cards.answer: Each person operating an aircraft shall maintain the cruising altitude or flight level by reference to an altimeter that is set, when operating below 18,000 feet MSL, to the current reported altimeter setting of a station along the route and within 100 nautical miles of the aircraft. When operating at or above 18,000 feet MSL, to 29.92 inches of mercury.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.411 - Altimeter System and Altitude Reporting Equipment Tests
cards.answer: No person may operate an airplane in controlled airspace under IFR unless within the preceding 24 calendar months, each static pressure system, each altimeter instrument, and each automatic pressure altitude reporting system has been tested and inspected and found to comply with appendices E and F of part 43.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.413 - ATC Transponder Tests and Inspections
cards.answer: No person may use an ATC transponder unless, within the preceding 24 calendar months, the ATC transponder has been tested and inspected and found to comply with appendix F of part 43.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.157(a) - Special VFR Weather Minimums
cards.answer: Special VFR operations may be conducted under the weather minimums and requirements of this section, instead of those contained in 91.155, below 10,000 feet MSL within the airspace contained by the upward extension of the lateral boundaries of the controlled airspace designated to the surface for an airport.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.157(b)(4) - Night Special VFR
cards.answer: No person may take off or land an aircraft under special VFR between sunset and sunrise unless the person is instrument rated and the aircraft is instrument equipped, and unless the flight visibility is at least 1 statute mile.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.135 - Operations in Class A Airspace
cards.answer: Unless otherwise authorized by ATC, each person operating an aircraft in Class A airspace must operate that aircraft under instrument flight rules (IFR). Each pilot must be instrument rated. Operations must be conducted in compliance with an ATC clearance received prior to entering the airspace.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.17(a) - Alcohol Prohibition
cards.answer: No person may act or attempt to act as a crewmember of a civil aircraft: (1) Within 8 hours after the consumption of any alcoholic beverage; (2) While under the influence of alcohol; (3) While using any drug that affects the person's faculties in any way contrary to safety; or (4) While having an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater in a blood or breath specimen.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.103 - Preflight Action
cards.answer: Each pilot in command shall, before beginning a flight, become familiar with all available information concerning that flight. This information must include: (a) For a flight under IFR or a flight not in the vicinity of an airport, weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, alternatives available if the planned flight cannot be completed, and any known traffic delays of which the pilot in command has been advised by ATC.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.103(b) - Runway Length
cards.answer: For any flight, runway lengths at airports of intended use, and aircraft takeoff and landing distance data.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.213(d) - Operations Without MEL
cards.answer: An aircraft with inoperative instruments or equipment without an MEL may be operated under certain conditions: The aircraft is not listed in 91.205 or required by ATC; The inoperative equipment is not required by an airworthiness directive; The equipment is removed or deactivated and placarded 'Inoperative'; A determination is made by a pilot that the inoperative equipment does not constitute a hazard to the aircraft.

cards.question: AIM 5-4-5 - Instrument Approach Procedure Charts
cards.answer: Approach procedure charts are designed to provide an IFR descent path for aircraft to an airport under normal or adverse weather conditions. When operating on an IFR flight plan, pilots are expected to remain on the centerline of the published route unless otherwise instructed by ATC.

cards.question: AIM 5-4-5 - Precision vs Non-Precision Approaches
cards.answer: A precision approach provides both horizontal and vertical guidance to a decision altitude/decision height (DA/DH). A non-precision approach provides horizontal guidance only, to a minimum descent altitude (MDA). Approaches with vertical guidance (APV) provide vertical guidance but not precision approach standards.

cards.question: AIM 5-4-5 - Visual Descent Point (VDP)
cards.answer: The VDP is a defined point on the final approach course of a nonprecision straight-in approach procedure from which normal descent from the MDA to the runway touchdown point may be commenced, provided visual reference is established.

cards.question: AIM 5-4-9 - Procedure Turn
cards.answer: A procedure turn is a maneuver prescribed when it is necessary to reverse direction to establish the aircraft on the intermediate or final approach course. The outbound course, direction of turn, distance within which the turn must be completed, and minimum altitude are specified in the procedure. The maximum speed is 200 knots IAS. Remain within the distance specified in the profile view.

cards.question: AIM 5-4-9 - When Procedure Turn Not Required
cards.answer: A procedure turn is not required when: an approach can be made directly from a specified intermediate fix to the final approach fix; when radar vectors are provided to the final approach course; when conducting a timed approach from a holding fix; when 'NoPT' is shown on the approach chart; when the procedure specifies a hold-in-lieu-of procedure turn.

cards.question: AIM 5-3-8 - Holding Pattern Airspeeds
cards.answer: Maximum holding airspeeds: MHA through 6,000 feet: 200 knots IAS; Above 6,000 feet through 14,000 feet: 230 knots IAS; Above 14,000 feet: 265 knots IAS. All turns are to be made at 3 degrees per second or 30 degrees bank angle, or 25 degrees bank provided a flight director system is used, whichever requires the lesser bank.

cards.question: AIM 5-3-8 - Holding Pattern Leg Timing
cards.answer: Timing for outbound leg begins over/abeam the fix, whichever occurs later. If the abeam position cannot be determined, start timing when turn to outbound is completed. Outbound timing is adjusted so that the inbound leg is: 1 minute at or below 14,000 feet MSL; 1-1/2 minutes above 14,000 feet MSL.

cards.question: AIM 5-3-8 - Holding Pattern Entry
cards.answer: Standard holding pattern entries: (a) Parallel - on a heading parallel to the outbound course for one minute, turn in the direction of the holding pattern to intercept the holding course; (b) Teardrop - turn to a heading 30 degrees from the outbound course for one minute, then turn in the direction of holding to intercept the inbound course; (c) Direct - turn to follow the holding pattern.

cards.question: AIM 5-2-9 - Instrument Departure Procedures
cards.answer: Departure Procedures (DPs) are established to provide obstacle clearance protection to aircraft in instrument meteorological conditions (IMC). They are also used to reduce pilot/controller workload. DPs provide obstacle clearance provided the aircraft crosses the departure end of the runway at least 35 feet above the departure end of runway elevation, and maintains a climb gradient of at least 200 feet per nautical mile, unless a higher climb gradient is specified.

cards.question: AIM 5-2-9 - Obstacle Departure Procedure (ODP)
cards.answer: ODPs provide obstruction clearance via the least onerous route from the terminal area to the appropriate en route structure. ODPs are recommended for obstruction clearance and may be flown without ATC clearance unless an alternate departure procedure (SID) has been specifically assigned by ATC.

cards.question: AIM 5-2-9 - Standard Instrument Departure (SID)
cards.answer: A SID is an ATC coded departure procedure that has been established at certain airports to simplify clearance delivery procedures. SIDs provide obstacle clearance and a transition from the terminal area to the appropriate en route structure. Pilots may be assigned SIDs without pilot request. Pilots should notify ATC if they do not wish to fly a SID by stating 'NO SID' in the remarks section of the flight plan.

cards.question: AIM 5-4-1 - Standard Terminal Arrival (STAR)
cards.answer: A STAR is an ATC coded IFR arrival route established for application to arriving IFR aircraft destined for certain airports. STARs simplify clearance delivery procedures and facilitate transition between en route and instrument approach procedures. Pilots may be assigned STARs without pilot request. Pilots should notify ATC if they do not wish to fly a STAR.

cards.question: AIM 5-4-1 - Descend Via Clearance
cards.answer: A 'descend via' clearance authorizes pilots to: (1) Vertically and laterally navigate on a STAR; (2) Descend at pilot's discretion to meet published altitude restrictions and speeds; and (3) Descend to the altitude specified in the clearance. Pilots should not descend below the last assigned altitude until receiving a clearance.

cards.question: AIM 1-1-9 - ILS Localizer
cards.answer: The localizer transmitter, operating on one of 40 ILS channels within the frequency range of 108.10 to 111.95 MHz, provides course guidance to the runway centerline. The localizer course width is between 3 and 6 degrees, with the standard course width being 5 degrees. Full scale deflection of the CDI represents 2.5 degrees each side of center.

cards.question: AIM 1-1-9 - ILS Glide Slope
cards.answer: The glide slope transmitter, operating on one of 40 paired ILS channels within the frequency range 329.15 MHz to 335.00 MHz, provides vertical course guidance. The glide slope projection angle is normally adjusted to 3 degrees above horizontal. The glide slope course width is normally 1.4 degrees (0.7 degrees above and below the center of the glide slope beam).

cards.question: AIM 1-1-9 - Marker Beacons
cards.answer: Marker beacons operate at 75 MHz and identify specific points along an ILS. The Outer Marker (OM) is located 4-7 miles from the runway, transmits dashes at 2 per second and displays a blue light. The Middle Marker (MM) is located approximately 3,500 feet from the runway, transmits alternating dots and dashes and displays an amber light.

cards.question: AIM 1-1-17 - GPS
cards.answer: The Global Positioning System (GPS) is a satellite-based radio navigation system. GPS provides highly accurate position and velocity information, and precise time, on a continuous global basis to users with appropriate receiving equipment. A minimum of four satellites must be in view of a GPS receiver for 3D position (latitude, longitude, and altitude) determination.

cards.question: AIM 1-1-17 - RAIM
cards.answer: Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring (RAIM) is a technique whereby a GPS receiver/processor determines the integrity of the GPS navigation signals using redundant signals. RAIM requires a minimum of five satellites, or four satellites and barometric altimeter input (baro-aiding), to detect an integrity anomaly. For receivers capable of isolating the corrupt satellite, six satellites or five satellites and baro-aiding are needed.

cards.question: AIM 1-1-18 - WAAS
cards.answer: The Wide Area Augmentation System (WAAS) provides a means to navigate from takeoff through approach. WAAS improves the accuracy of basic GPS signals and provides integrity monitoring. WAAS enables LPV approaches, which provide vertical guidance to minima as low as 200 feet above the runway threshold with visibility minimums as low as 1/2 mile.

cards.question: AIM 5-4-5 - RNAV Approach Types
cards.answer: RNAV approaches are classified by the equipment required: LNAV - lateral navigation only, requires basic GPS; LNAV/VNAV - lateral navigation with vertical guidance to a DA, requires WAAS or approved baro-VNAV; LPV - localizer performance with vertical guidance to a DA, requires WAAS; LP - localizer performance to an MDA, requires WAAS.

cards.question: AIM 7-1-6 - SIGMET
cards.answer: SIGMETs advise of non-convective weather that is potentially hazardous to all aircraft. SIGMETs are issued for: (1) Severe icing not associated with thunderstorms; (2) Severe or extreme turbulence or clear air turbulence (CAT) not associated with thunderstorms; (3) Dust storms or sandstorms lowering surface visibilities to below 3 miles. SIGMETs are valid for 4 hours.

cards.question: AIM 7-1-6 - Convective SIGMET
cards.answer: Convective SIGMETs are issued for convective hazards including: tornadoes, lines of thunderstorms, embedded thunderstorms, areas of thunderstorms greater than or equal to VIP level 4 (heavy precipitation) affecting 40 percent or more of an area at least 3,000 square miles, and hail greater than or equal to 3/4 inch in diameter and/or wind gusts to 50 knots or greater. Convective SIGMETs are valid for 2 hours.

cards.question: AIM 7-1-6 - AIRMET
cards.answer: AIRMETs are advisories of significant weather phenomena that describe conditions at intensities lower than those which require the issuance of SIGMETs. AIRMETs are intended for dissemination to all pilots. AIRMET TANGO - Turbulence; AIRMET ZULU - Icing and freezing levels; AIRMET SIERRA - IFR conditions and mountain obscuration. AIRMETs are valid for 6 hours.

cards.question: AIM 5-3-3 - Position Reporting
cards.answer: Position reports should include: (1) Identification; (2) Position; (3) Time; (4) Altitude or flight level; (5) Type of flight plan (not required in IFR position reports made to ARTCCs or approach control); (6) ETA and name of next reporting point; (7) The name only of the next succeeding reporting point along the route of flight; (8) Pertinent remarks.

cards.question: AIM 5-3-3 - Additional Reports
cards.answer: Pilots shall report: Leaving an assigned altitude; When unable to climb/descend at a rate of at least 500 feet per minute; Change in average true airspeed exceeding 5 percent or 10 knots; Time and altitude/flight level reaching a holding fix; Leaving any assigned holding fix or point; Missed approach; Any unforecast weather conditions encountered.

cards.question: AIM 5-4-24 - Visual Approach
cards.answer: A visual approach is an IFR approach conducted under IFR in visual conditions where part or all of an instrument approach procedure is not completed, and the approach is made visually to the airport. The pilot must have either the airport or the preceding aircraft in sight. At least 1,000 foot ceiling and 3 statute miles flight visibility is required.

cards.question: AIM 5-4-25 - Contact Approach
cards.answer: A contact approach is an approach wherein an aircraft on an IFR flight plan, having an ATC authorization, operating clear of clouds with at least 1 statute mile flight visibility and having the ground in sight, may deviate from the instrument approach procedure and proceed to the destination airport by visual reference to the surface. A contact approach must be requested by the pilot; it cannot be initiated by ATC.

cards.question: AIM 5-4-21 - Missed Approach
cards.answer: A pilot must execute a missed approach when: (1) Arrival at the missed approach point and the runway environment is not in sight; (2) Anytime a pilot determines that a safe landing is not possible; (3) When instructed by ATC. Upon executing a missed approach, pilots should notify ATC and comply with the missed approach instructions for the procedure being executed.

cards.question: AIM 5-2-5 - IFR Clearance
cards.answer: An IFR clearance authorizes a pilot to conduct flight under instrument flight rules. The clearance contains: Clearance limit, route of flight, altitude, departure control frequency, transponder code. Pilots should record the clearance (CRAFT: Clearance limit, Route, Altitude, Frequency, Transponder).

cards.question: AIM 5-2-6 - Abbreviated IFR Clearance
cards.answer: An abbreviated clearance may be issued using terms such as 'Cleared as filed.' This clearance includes the route of flight shown in the flight plan. If a SID is assigned without pilot request, the pilot must receive a complete description of the SID with the clearance, unless they have indicated they possess the SID.

cards.question: AIM 6-2-2 - Emergency Transponder Codes
cards.answer: When an aircraft is in distress or has an emergency, the pilot should squawk transponder code 7700. If experiencing radio communication failure, squawk code 7600. If the aircraft is being subjected to unlawful interference (hijack), squawk code 7500.

cards.question: AIM 2-1-1 - Approach Light Systems
cards.answer: Approach Light Systems provide the basic means to transition from instrument flight to visual flight for landing. High intensity lights are used primarily on precision approach runways where low visibility conditions are common. Medium intensity lights are typically used for non-precision approaches or where lower visibility minima are not required.

cards.question: AIM 2-1-2 - PAPI
cards.answer: Precision Approach Path Indicator (PAPI) uses light units installed on the left side of the runway. Each PAPI has four light units. The visual glide path is normally 3 degrees. Interpretation: All red - too low; three red one white - slightly low; two red two white - on glide path; one red three white - slightly high; all white - too high.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.56 - Flight Review
cards.answer: No person may act as pilot in command of an aircraft unless, since the beginning of the 24th calendar month before the month in which that pilot acts as PIC, that person has accomplished a flight review consisting of: (1) A minimum of 1 hour of flight training and 1 hour of ground training that includes a review of current general operating and flight rules of part 91; (2) A review of those maneuvers and procedures necessary for the pilot to demonstrate safe exercise of the privileges of the pilot certificate.
glance: Every 24 calendar months
Minimum 1 hr ground + 1 hr flight

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.57(a) - Recent Experience: Pilot in Command
cards.answer: No person may act as pilot in command of an aircraft carrying passengers unless that person has made, within the preceding 90 days, three takeoffs and three landings as the sole manipulator of the flight controls in an aircraft of the same category, class, and type (if a type rating is required).
glance: Carrying passengers: 3 takeoffs & 3 landings in the preceding 90 days
Sole manipulator · same category, class, and type

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.57(b) - Night Takeoff and Landing Experience
cards.answer: No person may act as pilot in command of an aircraft carrying passengers during the period beginning 1 hour after sunset and ending 1 hour before sunrise, unless within the preceding 90 days that person has made at least three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop during that period in an aircraft of the same category, class, and type.
glance: Night passengers: 3 takeoffs & 3 full-stop landings in the preceding 90 days
Between 1 hr after sunset and 1 hr before sunrise

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.117 - Aircraft Speed
cards.answer: Unless otherwise authorized by the Administrator, no person may operate an aircraft: (a) Below 10,000 feet MSL, at an indicated airspeed of more than 250 knots; (b) Beneath the lateral limits of Class B airspace, or in a VFR corridor through Class B airspace, at an indicated airspeed of more than 200 knots; (c) At or below 2,500 feet above the surface within 4 nautical miles of a Class C or Class D airspace primary airport, at an indicated airspeed of more than 200 knots.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.113(c) - In Distress
cards.answer: An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other air traffic.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.303 - Aerobatic Flight
cards.answer: No person may operate an aircraft in aerobatic flight: (a) Over any congested area of a city, town, or settlement; (b) Over an open air assembly of persons; (c) Within the lateral boundaries of Class B, Class C, Class D, or Class E surface area airspace designated for an airport; (d) Within 4 nautical miles of the centerline of any Federal airway; (e) Below an altitude of 1,500 feet above the surface; or (f) When flight visibility is less than 3 statute miles.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.111 - Operating Near Other Aircraft
cards.answer: No person may operate an aircraft so close to another aircraft as to create a collision hazard. No person may operate an aircraft in formation flight except by arrangement with the pilot in command of each aircraft in the formation. No person may operate an aircraft, carrying passengers for hire, in formation flight.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.3 - Responsibility and Authority of the Pilot in Command
cards.answer: (a) The pilot in command of an aircraft is directly responsible for, and is the final authority as to, the operation of that aircraft. (b) In an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action, the pilot in command may deviate from any rule of this part to the extent required to meet that emergency. (c) Each pilot in command who deviates from a rule under paragraph (b) shall, upon the request of the Administrator, send a written report of that deviation to the Administrator.

cards.question: AIM 5-3-8 - Maximum Holding Airspeeds
cards.answer:
Maximum holding airspeeds for civil aircraft:

• MHA through 6,000 feet: 200 KIAS
• 6,001 feet through 14,000 feet: 230 KIAS
• 14,001 feet and above: 265 KIAS

Speed reduction should be initiated at least 3 minutes before arriving at the holding fix.

cards.question: AIM 5-3-8 - Holding Pattern Leg Timing
cards.answer:
Standard holding pattern leg timing:

• At or below 14,000 feet MSL: 1 minute inbound leg
• Above 14,000 feet MSL: 1.5 minute inbound leg

Timing begins over or abeam the fix, whichever occurs later. If the abeam position cannot be determined, start timing when the turn to outbound is completed.

cards.question: AIM 5-3-8 - Standard Holding Pattern Entry Procedures
cards.answer:
Three standard entry procedures based on heading to the holding fix:

1. DIRECT ENTRY (70° sector): Upon reaching the fix, turn to follow the holding pattern.

2. TEARDROP ENTRY (120° sector): Upon reaching the fix, turn to a heading for a 30° teardrop entry within the pattern for a period of one minute, then turn in the direction of the holding pattern to intercept the inbound course.

3. PARALLEL ENTRY (110° sector): Upon reaching the fix, turn to a heading to parallel the holding course outbound for one minute, turn in the direction of the holding pattern through more than 180° to return to the holding fix or intercept the holding course inbound.

cards.question: AIM 5-3-8 - Standard Holding Pattern Turns
cards.answer:
All turns during entry and while holding shall be made:

• At 3 degrees per second, or
• At 30 degrees bank angle, or
• At 25 degrees bank angle if using flight director

Whichever requires the least bank angle.

cards.question: AIM 5-2-9 - Obstacle Departure Procedures (ODP)
cards.answer:
Obstacle Departure Procedures (ODPs) are preplanned departure procedures designed to provide obstruction clearance via the least onerous route from the terminal area to the appropriate en route structure.

ODPs provide obstacle clearance if the pilot:
• Crosses the departure end of runway at least 35 feet above the departure end of runway elevation
• Climbs to 400 feet above the departure end of runway elevation before making the initial turn
• Maintains a minimum climb gradient of 200 feet per nautical mile, unless a higher gradient is specified

cards.question: AIM 5-2-9 - Standard Instrument Departures (SIDs)
cards.answer:
Standard Instrument Departures (SIDs) are preplanned IFR departure procedures published for pilot use in graphic and textual form. SIDs provide transition from the terminal to the appropriate en route structure.

SIDs are designed to:
• Increase capacity
• Reduce pilot/controller workload
• Expedite traffic flow

Pilots may accept a SID or request 'NO SIDs' in the remarks section of the flight plan. If unable to accept a SID, pilots should advise ATC.

cards.question: AIM 5-2-9 - Climb Gradient Requirements
cards.answer:
Standard climb gradient is 200 feet per nautical mile (FPNM).

To convert climb gradient to feet per minute:
FPM = Groundspeed × Climb Gradient (FPNM) ÷ 60

Example: At 120 knots groundspeed with 200 FPNM gradient:
FPM = 120 × 200 ÷ 60 = 400 feet per minute

Higher climb gradients may be required when specified in the departure procedure.

cards.question: AIM 5-4-1 - Standard Terminal Arrival Routes (STARs)
cards.answer:
A Standard Terminal Arrival Route (STAR) is a preplanned IFR arrival procedure published for pilot use in graphic and textual form.

STARs:
• Provide transition from the en route structure to an approach fix or point in the terminal area
• Reduce pilot/controller workload
• Simplify clearance delivery

Pilots may accept a STAR or indicate 'NO STARs' in the remarks section of the flight plan.

cards.question: AIM 5-4-1 - Descend Via Clearance
cards.answer:
A 'Descend Via' clearance authorizes pilots to:

• Descend at pilot's discretion to meet published restrictions
• Laterally navigate on a STAR
• When cleared to a waypoint depicted on a STAR, descend from a previously assigned altitude to the altitude depicted at that waypoint

Pilots must meet all published or assigned altitude and speed restrictions.

cards.question: AIM 5-4-5 - Types of Instrument Approach Procedures
cards.answer:
Instrument approach procedures are classified as:

Precision Approach (PA): Provides lateral and vertical guidance with a Decision Altitude (DA). Includes: ILS, PAR, GLS.

Approach with Vertical Guidance (APV): Provides lateral and vertical guidance with a Decision Altitude. Includes: LNAV/VNAV, LPV, Baro-VNAV.

Non-Precision Approach (NPA): Provides lateral guidance only with a Minimum Descent Altitude (MDA). Includes: VOR, NDB, LOC, LNAV, ASR.

cards.question: AIM 5-4-9 - Procedure Turn Requirements
cards.answer:
A procedure turn is the maneuver prescribed when it is necessary to reverse direction to establish an aircraft on the intermediate approach segment or final approach course.

Procedure turn requirements:
• Must remain within the distance specified (normally 10 NM)
• Maximum speed: 200 KIAS
• Only the turn direction is mandatory unless a specific pattern is depicted

A procedure turn is NOT required when:
• Receiving radar vectors to final approach course
• The procedure specifies 'NoPT'
• Conducting a timed approach from a holding fix
• Holding in lieu of procedure turn is published

cards.question: AIM 5-4-21 - Missed Approach Procedures
cards.answer:
A missed approach procedure is executed when:

• The required visual references are not established at DA/DH or MDA
• At any time during the approach when it becomes apparent that a safe approach and landing cannot be completed
• When directed by ATC

The missed approach point (MAP) is the point prescribed in each approach at which a missed approach procedure shall be executed if the required visual reference does not exist.

cards.question: AIM 5-5-3 - Contact Approach
cards.answer:
A contact approach may be authorized when:

• The pilot requests it (ATC cannot initiate)
• The airport has a published instrument approach procedure
• The reported ground visibility at the destination airport is at least 1 statute mile
• The pilot can operate clear of clouds with at least 1 statute mile flight visibility

The pilot assumes responsibility for obstruction clearance.

cards.question: AIM 5-5-11 - Visual Approach
cards.answer:
A visual approach may be authorized when:
