• The ceiling is at or above 1,000 feet and visibility is at least 3 statute miles
• The pilot has the airport or preceding aircraft in sight
• ATC or the pilot may initiate the request

The pilot is responsible for:
• Wake turbulence separation from preceding aircraft
• Terrain and obstruction clearance
• Separation from aircraft to follow if accepted

cards.question: 14 CFR 97.3 - Aircraft Approach Categories
cards.answer:
Aircraft approach category means a grouping of aircraft based on a speed of 1.3 Vso at the maximum certificated landing weight:

• Category A: Speed less than 91 knots
• Category B: Speed 91 knots or more but less than 121 knots
• Category C: Speed 121 knots or more but less than 141 knots
• Category D: Speed 141 knots or more but less than 166 knots
• Category E: Speed 166 knots or more

If the aircraft speed is increased above the upper limit for the category, the minimums for the next higher category apply.

cards.question: AIM 1-1-9 - ILS Localizer
cards.answer:
The localizer transmitter provides lateral course guidance.

Localizer characteristics:
• Frequency range: 108.10 to 111.95 MHz (odd tenths only)
• Course width: 3° to 6° (typically 5° total, 2.5° either side of centerline)
• Accuracy: One dot deflection equals 1/4 of course width
• Range: 18 NM within 10° of course centerline

The localizer is approximately 4 times more sensitive than a VOR.

cards.question: AIM 1-1-9 - ILS Glide Slope
cards.answer:
The glide slope transmitter provides vertical guidance.

Glide slope characteristics:
• Frequency range: 329.15 to 335.00 MHz (UHF)
• Automatically paired with localizer frequency
• Standard angle: 3° (may range from 2.5° to 3.5°)
• Course width: 1.4° (0.7° full-scale deflection)

A false glide slope exists at a higher angle (typically 6°). Pilots should intercept the glide slope from below.

cards.question: AIM 1-1-9 - ILS Marker Beacons
cards.answer:
Marker beacons identify specific points along the approach:

Outer Marker (OM):
• Blue light, low-pitched tone, dashes
• Identifies glide slope intercept at intermediate altitude
• Located 4-7 miles from runway

Middle Marker (MM):
• Amber light, medium-pitched tone, alternating dots and dashes
• Indicates approximately 3,500 feet from runway threshold
• Visual descent point for Category I approach

Inner Marker (IM):
• White light, high-pitched tone, dots
• Used for Category II approaches
• Indicates decision height point

cards.question: AIM 1-1-17 - RAIM Requirements
cards.answer:
Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring (RAIM) is a form of ABAS that monitors the integrity of GPS satellite signals.

RAIM requirements:
• RAIM availability must be confirmed for IFR flight using GPS
• Fault detection: Minimum 5 satellites or 4 satellites plus baro-aiding
• Fault detection and exclusion: 6 satellites or 5 satellites plus baro-aiding

If RAIM is not available, the pilot must use an alternate means of navigation.

cards.question: AIM 1-1-18 - WAAS Description
cards.answer:
The Wide Area Augmentation System (WAAS) is a satellite-based augmentation system (SBAS) that provides:

• Enhanced GPS accuracy (typically 7 meters or better)
• Integrity monitoring
• Availability alerting

WAAS enables approaches with vertical guidance:
• LPV (Localizer Performance with Vertical guidance): Similar to ILS precision
• LNAV/VNAV: Lateral and vertical navigation to DA
• LP: Lateral navigation only to MDA (when vertical guidance unavailable)
• LNAV: Lateral navigation only to MDA

cards.question: AIM 1-2-2 - Required Navigation Performance (RNP)
cards.answer:
RNP is RNAV with on-board performance monitoring and alerting capability.

RNP values represent the accuracy required 95% of flight time:

• RNP 2.0: Oceanic and remote continental
• RNP 1.0: Terminal area operations
• RNP 0.3: Approach operations
• RNP AR: Authorization Required approaches (values from 0.3 to 0.1)

RNP AR approaches require special crew and aircraft authorization.

cards.question: AIM 7-1-3 - SIGMET (WS)
cards.answer:
A SIGMET advises of non-convective weather that is potentially hazardous to ALL aircraft.

SIGMETs are issued for:
• Severe icing not associated with thunderstorms
• Severe or extreme turbulence not associated with thunderstorms
• Dust storms, sandstorms, or volcanic ash lowering visibility below 3 miles

SIGMETs are valid for 4 hours (6 hours for volcanic ash and tropical cyclones).

cards.question: AIM 7-1-6 - Convective SIGMET (WST)
cards.answer:
Convective SIGMETs are issued for the following conditions:

• Severe thunderstorm (surface winds ≥50 knots or hail ≥3/4 inch diameter)
• Tornadoes
• Embedded thunderstorms
• Lines of thunderstorms
• Thunderstorms producing precipitation with VIP levels ≥4 affecting 40% or more of an area at least 3,000 square miles

Convective SIGMETs are issued hourly and are valid for 2 hours. They imply severe or greater turbulence, severe icing, and low-level wind shear.

cards.question: AIM 7-1-5 - AIRMET (WA)
cards.answer:
AIRMETs advise of weather that may be hazardous to single-engine, light aircraft and VFR pilots.

Three types of AIRMETs:

• AIRMET Sierra: IFR conditions and/or extensive mountain obscurations
• AIRMET Tango: Moderate turbulence, sustained surface winds of 30 knots or greater, and/or non-convective low-level wind shear
• AIRMET Zulu: Moderate icing and provides freezing level heights

AIRMETs are valid for 6 hours.

cards.question: AIM 7-1-4 - PIREPs (UA/UUA)
cards.answer:
Pilot Weather Reports (PIREPs) provide observations of actual flight conditions.

PIREP types:
• Routine (UA): General conditions
• Urgent (UUA): Hazardous conditions

Required elements:
• Location
• Time
• Flight level
• Aircraft type

Optional elements:
• Sky cover
• Weather and visibility
• Temperature
• Wind
• Turbulence
• Icing
• Remarks

Pilots are encouraged to report actual weather conditions, especially when encountering sky cover, turbulence, icing, wind shear, or volcanic ash.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-15 - Gyroscopic Principles
cards.answer:
Two fundamental properties of gyroscopes:

1. RIGIDITY IN SPACE: A spinning gyroscope tends to remain in a fixed position in the plane in which it is spinning. Used by the attitude indicator and heading indicator.

2. PRECESSION: When a force is applied to a spinning gyroscope, the resulting motion occurs 90° in the direction of rotation from where the force was applied. Used by the turn coordinator/turn-and-slip indicator.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-15 - Attitude Indicator Operation
cards.answer:
The attitude indicator uses a gyroscope with a vertical spin axis (rigidity in space) to display the aircraft's pitch and bank attitude relative to the horizon.

Limitations:
• May tumble at extreme attitudes (some older models)
• Requires approximately 5 minutes to stabilize after engine start

Errors:
• Acceleration error: Shows slight climb during acceleration, slight descent during deceleration
• Turning error: May show slight turn in opposite direction following a 180° turn

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-15 - Heading Indicator Operation
cards.answer:
The heading indicator (directional gyro) uses rigidity in space to provide a stable heading reference.

Characteristics:
• Does not seek magnetic north (must be set to magnetic compass)
• Should be realigned with magnetic compass every 15 minutes
• Subject to precession error (drift)
• May be slaved to a magnetic flux valve for automatic correction

The heading indicator provides a more stable heading reference than the magnetic compass, which is subject to turning and acceleration errors.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-15 - Turn Coordinator/Turn-and-Slip Indicator
cards.answer:
These instruments use precession to measure rate of turn.

Turn Coordinator:
• Gyro tilted approximately 30° from horizontal
• Displays rate of turn AND rate of roll
• Miniature aircraft indicates turn direction and rate

Turn-and-Slip Indicator:
• Gyro horizontal
• Shows rate of turn only (not rate of roll)
• Needle indicates turn direction and rate

Both include an inclinometer (ball) to indicate coordination. Standard rate turn: 3° per second (360° in 2 minutes).

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-15 - Magnetic Compass Errors
cards.answer:
Magnetic compass errors:

VARIATION: Difference between true and magnetic north. Apply isogonic lines.

DEVIATION: Error caused by aircraft magnetic fields. Use deviation card.

DIP ERRORS:

• Northerly Turning Error: In Northern Hemisphere, compass leads when turning through north (undershoot), lags when turning through south (overshoot). Mnemonic: UNOS (Undershoot North, Overshoot South).

• Acceleration Error: In Northern Hemisphere, accelerating shows apparent turn to north, decelerating shows apparent turn to south. Mnemonic: ANDS (Accelerate North, Decelerate South).

OSCILLATION: Erratic movement during turbulence.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-15 - Pitot-Static System Instruments
cards.answer:
Three instruments use the pitot-static system:

1. AIRSPEED INDICATOR: Uses both pitot (ram air) and static pressure. Displays difference as airspeed.

2. ALTIMETER: Uses static pressure only. Aneroid wafers expand/contract with pressure changes to display altitude.

3. VERTICAL SPEED INDICATOR: Uses static pressure only. Measures rate of change of static pressure to display climb or descent rate.

The pitot tube provides impact (ram) air pressure. The static port provides ambient atmospheric pressure.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-15 - Blocked Pitot Tube Effects
cards.answer:
Effects of a blocked pitot tube:

• Airspeed indicator is the ONLY affected instrument

Pitot tube blocked, drain hole open:
• Airspeed drops to zero

Pitot tube and drain hole blocked (complete blockage):
• Airspeed indicator acts as an altimeter
• Airspeed increases during climb, decreases during descent
• Air trapped in pitot system expands/contracts with altitude changes

Pitot heat should be used to prevent or clear ice blockage.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-15 - Blocked Static Port Effects
cards.answer:
Effects of a blocked static port:

ALL THREE pitot-static instruments are affected:

• ALTIMETER: Freezes at altitude where blockage occurred

• VERTICAL SPEED INDICATOR: Freezes at zero

• AIRSPEED INDICATOR: Operates, but indicates incorrectly. At higher altitudes than blockage: indicates lower than actual. At lower altitudes: indicates higher than actual.

Alternate Static Source: If used, cockpit static pressure (slightly lower than outside) causes:
• Altimeter to read slightly high
• Airspeed to read slightly high
• VSI to momentarily show a climb

cards.question: AIM 8-1-2 - Types of Hypoxia
cards.answer:
Hypoxia is a state of oxygen deficiency sufficient to impair functions of the brain and other organs.

Four types of hypoxia:

1. HYPOXIC: Insufficient oxygen available to the body (high altitude, reduced atmospheric pressure)

2. HYPEMIC: Blood cannot carry adequate oxygen (carbon monoxide poisoning, blood loss, anemia)

3. STAGNANT: Oxygen-rich blood cannot circulate adequately (heart failure, shock, excessive G-forces)

4. HISTOTOXIC: Body cells cannot effectively use oxygen (alcohol, drugs, certain poisons)

cards.question: AIM 8-1-5 - Spatial Disorientation
cards.answer:
Spatial disorientation is the inability to correctly determine body position or motion relative to the surface of the Earth.

Common illusions:

• THE LEANS: Abrupt recovery from a gradual turn causes sensation of turning in opposite direction

• CORIOLIS ILLUSION: Head movement during prolonged turn causes false sensation of rotation

• GRAVEYARD SPIRAL: Prolonged turn causes loss of sensation of turn, leading to gradual descent

• SOMATOGRAVIC ILLUSION: Rapid acceleration creates illusion of nose-up attitude; rapid deceleration creates nose-down sensation

• INVERSION ILLUSION: Abrupt change from climb to level flight creates sensation of tumbling backward

Prevention: Trust and rely on flight instruments.

cards.question: AIM 8-1-2 - Scuba Diving and Flying
cards.answer:
Flying after scuba diving requires a surface interval to allow nitrogen absorbed during diving to be eliminated.

Recommended waiting times before flight:

• Nondecompression Stop Diving (no controlled ascent required):
  - Wait at least 12 hours before flight up to 8,000 feet cabin altitude

• Decompression Stop Diving (controlled ascent required) or flights above 8,000 feet:
  - Wait at least 24 hours

Flying too soon after diving may result in decompression sickness.

cards.question: AC 00-6 - Types of Structural Icing
cards.answer:
Structural icing forms when supercooled water freezes on aircraft surfaces.

Clear Ice:
• Glossy, transparent ice
• Forms from large supercooled water droplets that spread before freezing
• Most hazardous type - heavy, hard to remove, can change airfoil shape
• Typically forms at temperatures 0°C to -10°C

Rime Ice:
• Rough, milky, opaque ice
• Forms from small supercooled droplets that freeze on contact
• Lighter than clear ice, easier to remove
• Typically forms at temperatures -10°C to -20°C

Mixed Ice:
• Combination of clear and rime ice
• Forms when droplet sizes vary or temperature fluctuates

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Carburetor Icing
cards.answer:
Carburetor icing can occur at ambient temperatures between 20°F and 70°F (-7°C to 21°C) when there is visible moisture or high humidity.

Cause: Fuel vaporization and air expansion in the carburetor venturi cause a temperature drop of 60-70°F, freezing moisture on the throttle valve.

Indications:
• Fixed-pitch propeller: RPM decrease
• Constant-speed propeller: Manifold pressure decrease
• Rough engine operation

Procedure:
• Apply full carburetor heat
• Expect initial power decrease (warm air less dense)
• Engine may run rough as ice melts and passes through
• Power should increase as ice clears

cards.question: AC 00-6 - Three Stages of Thunderstorm Development
cards.answer:
1. CUMULUS (Building) Stage:
• Characterized by continuous updrafts
• Updrafts may reach 3,000 feet per minute or more
• Duration: 10-15 minutes
• Little or no precipitation at surface

2. MATURE Stage:
• Characterized by both updrafts AND downdrafts
• Precipitation begins to fall
• Most hazardous stage - all weather hazards at maximum intensity
• Updrafts may exceed 6,000 feet per minute
• Lasts 15-30 minutes

3. DISSIPATING Stage:
• Characterized by downdrafts throughout the cell
• Precipitation decreases
• Cell dissipates as downdrafts cut off updraft supply

cards.question: AIM 7-1-26 - Microbursts
cards.answer:
A microburst is a small-scale intense downdraft which, upon reaching the surface, spreads outward in all directions from the downdraft center.

Characteristics:
• Size: Less than 2.5 miles in diameter
• Duration: Peak intensity lasts 2-4 minutes (max 15 minutes)
• Downdraft speeds: May exceed 6,000 feet per minute
• Horizontal winds: May exceed 45 knots, with differential of 90 knots

Hazard sequence for landing aircraft:
• Initial headwind (increased performance)
• Strong downdraft (rapid altitude loss)
• Tailwind (decreased performance)

Recovery: Maximum thrust, maintain or increase pitch attitude. Do not retract flaps or gear.

cards.question: AIM 6-2-2 - Emergency Transponder Codes
cards.answer:
Emergency transponder codes:

7500 - Hijacking (unlawful interference)
• ATC will not acknowledge overtly to avoid alerting hijacker
• May ask to verify squawk as confirmation

7600 - Lost Communications (radio failure)
• Continue flight per 14 CFR 91.185 procedures
• ATC will monitor flight progress

7700 - General Emergency
• Any emergency requiring immediate assistance
• Alerts all ATC facilities
• Priority handling provided

Mnemonic: 75 - Taken Alive, 76 - Technical Difficulty, 77 - Going to Heaven

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.117 - Aircraft Speed Limits
cards.answer:
No person may operate an aircraft:

(a) Below 10,000 feet MSL: Maximum 250 knots indicated airspeed

(b) Beneath the lateral limits of Class B airspace, or in a VFR corridor through Class B: Maximum 200 knots indicated airspeed

(c) Within 4 nautical miles of the primary airport of Class C or D airspace, at or below 2,500 feet AGL: Maximum 200 knots indicated airspeed

Exceptions:
• Aircraft cannot be operated safely at specified speeds due to design or flight characteristics
• ATC issues a specific speed authorization or assignment

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.157 - Special VFR Weather Minimums
cards.answer:
Special VFR operations in the traffic pattern of an airport in Class B, C, D, or E surface area airspace:

• May be authorized by ATC if the pilot requests
• Requires clear of clouds
• Requires at least 1 statute mile flight visibility
• Ground visibility at the airport must be at least 1 statute mile (if reported)

Night Special VFR (14 CFR 91.157(b)):
Pilot must be instrument rated and aircraft must be instrument equipped.

Special VFR is not authorized at some airports (listed in 14 CFR Part 91 Appendix D).

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.169 - IFR Alternate Airport Selection
cards.answer:
An alternate airport is NOT required if:

1. For at least 1 hour before and 1 hour after the estimated time of arrival:
   • Ceiling will be at least 2,000 feet above the airport elevation
   • Visibility will be at least 3 statute miles

2. The first airport of intended landing has a standard instrument approach procedure

Alternate Airport Weather Minimums:
If an alternate is required, weather must forecast at the estimated time of arrival:
• Precision approach: 600-foot ceiling and 2 statute miles visibility
• Nonprecision approach: 800-foot ceiling and 2 statute miles visibility
• No instrument approach: Descent from MEA, approach, and landing under basic VFR
glance: No alternate: 1 hr before to 1 hr after ETA, ceiling ≥ 2,000 ft & vis ≥ 3 SM, with an instrument approach
Alternate minimums — precision: 600 ft & 2 SM
Alternate minimums — nonprecision: 800 ft & 2 SM
No approach at alternate: descend from MEA and land under basic VFR

cards.question: AIM 2-1-1 - Approach Light Systems
cards.answer:
Major approach light systems:

ALSF-1/ALSF-2:
• High intensity, 2,400-3,000 feet long
• Used for precision approaches (Category I and II)
• Includes sequenced flashing lights ('the rabbit')

MALSR/MALSF:
• Medium intensity, 2,400 feet long
• MALSR has Runway Alignment Indicator Lights (RAIL)
• MALSF has sequenced flashers

ODALS:
• Omnidirectional, 1,500 feet long
• Flashing lights visible from all directions

REIL:
• Runway End Identifier Lights
• Synchronized flashing lights at runway threshold

cards.question: AIM 2-1-2 - Visual Glideslope Indicators
cards.answer:
VASI (Visual Approach Slope Indicator):
• 2-bar VASI provides visual glidepath (typically 3°)
• Indications:
  - Both bars white: Too high
  - Far bar red, near bar white: On glidepath
  - Both bars red: Too low

PAPI (Precision Approach Path Indicator):
• 4-light single row system
• Indications:
  - 4 white: Too high (>3.5°)
  - 3 white/1 red: Slightly high
  - 2 white/2 red: On glidepath (3°)
  - 1 white/3 red: Slightly low
  - 4 red: Too low (<2.5°)

Mnemonic: 'Red over white, you're alright. Red over red, you're dead.'

cards.question: AIM 5-2-6 - IFR Clearance Components (CRAFT)
cards.answer:
IFR clearance contains the following elements:

C - Clearance limit (usually the destination airport)

R - Route (airways, direct, or as filed)

A - Altitude (initial altitude or 'climb and maintain')

F - Frequency (departure control frequency)

T - Transponder code (squawk code)

Additional elements may include:
• Departure procedure or SID
• Expect further clearance (EFC) time
• Void time (for release from non-towered airports)
• Hold for release instructions

cards.question: AIM 5-2-6 - Clearance Void Time
cards.answer:
A clearance void time is the time after which the IFR clearance is void and aircraft cannot depart IFR.

Requirements:
• Used primarily at non-towered airports
• Pilot must depart BEFORE the void time
• If unable to depart by void time, pilot must advise ATC

If not airborne by void time:
• The pilot must advise ATC as soon as possible but no later than 30 minutes after void time
• Failure to notify ATC may result in search and rescue being initiated

cards.question: AIM 4-4-10 - Cruise Clearance
cards.answer:
A 'cruise' clearance authorizes the pilot to:

• Conduct flight at any altitude from the minimum IFR altitude up to and including the altitude specified in the clearance
• Climb and descend within that block of airspace
• Proceed to and execute an approach at the destination

Important:
• Once the pilot reports leaving an altitude during descent, that altitude may not be returned to without additional clearance
• Descent below the minimum IFR altitude is NOT authorized until the pilot is established on a segment of a published approach procedure

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.183 - IFR Required Reports
cards.answer:
The pilot in command shall report immediately to ATC:

• Leaving any assigned altitude or flight level
• Altitude or flight level changes when operating on a VFR-on-top clearance
• Inability to climb or descend at a rate of at least 500 feet per minute
• Change in True Airspeed of 5% or 10 knots (whichever is greater) from filed flight plan
• Time and altitude upon reaching a holding fix or clearance limit
• Leaving any assigned holding fix or point
• Unforecast weather conditions encountered
• Any other information relating to the safety of flight

cards.question: AIM 5-3-3 - Non-Radar Position Reports
cards.answer:
When operating in a non-radar environment, position reports are required over:

• Compulsory reporting points (solid triangles on charts)
• All IFR intersections and fixes used in the flight plan

Position report elements:
• Aircraft identification
• Position (fix name)
• Time over the fix
• Altitude or flight level
• Type of flight plan (not required with approach control or ARTCC)
• ETA and name of next reporting point
• Name only of succeeding reporting point
• Remarks (pertinent information)

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-2 - IM SAFE Checklist
cards.answer:
The IM SAFE checklist is a personal fitness assessment before flight:

I - Illness: Am I suffering from any illness or symptoms?

M - Medication: Am I taking any medications that could impair judgment or performance?

S - Stress: Am I under unusual psychological stress from home, work, or other factors?

A - Alcohol: Have I consumed alcohol within the last 8 hours? Do I have a blood alcohol level above 0.04%?

F - Fatigue: Am I adequately rested? Have I had sufficient sleep?

E - Eating/Emotion: Have I eaten properly? Am I emotionally ready to fly?

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-2 - PAVE Checklist
cards.answer:
The PAVE checklist identifies risk factors before flight:

P - Pilot:
• Experience, currency, and proficiency
• Physical and emotional condition
• Situational awareness capability

A - Aircraft:
• Airworthiness and equipment
• Performance capability for the flight
• Familiarity with aircraft systems

V - enVironment:
• Weather conditions
• Terrain
• Airports and airspace
• Night or day operations

E - External Pressures:
• Meetings or appointments
• Passengers expecting on-time arrival
• Self-induced pressure to complete flight

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-15 - Rate of Descent for 3° Glidepath
cards.answer:
To maintain a standard 3° glidepath:

Rate of Descent (FPM) = Groundspeed × 5

OR

Rate of Descent (FPM) = Groundspeed ÷ 2 × 10

Examples:
• 90 knots groundspeed: 90 × 5 = 450 FPM
• 120 knots groundspeed: 120 × 5 = 600 FPM
• 150 knots groundspeed: 150 × 5 = 750 FPM

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-15 - Top of Descent Calculation
cards.answer:
To calculate distance from destination to begin descent:

Top of Descent (NM) = Altitude to lose (feet) ÷ 300

This formula provides approximately a 3° descent path.

Examples:
• Descend from 10,000 to 2,000 (8,000 feet): 8,000 ÷ 300 = 26.7 NM
• Descend from FL350 to FL240 (11,000 feet): 11,000 ÷ 300 = 36.7 NM

For approach:
Visual Descent Point = MDA height above TDZE ÷ 300

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-15 - Standard Rate Turn Bank Angle
cards.answer:
To calculate bank angle for a standard rate turn (3° per second):

Bank Angle = (TAS ÷ 10) + 7

OR approximately:

Bank Angle = TAS ÷ 10 × 1.5

Examples:
• 100 KTAS: (100 ÷ 10) + 7 = 17° bank
• 120 KTAS: (120 ÷ 10) + 7 = 19° bank
• 150 KTAS: (150 ÷ 10) + 7 = 22° bank

Note: Maximum 30° bank angle (25° with flight director) for instrument flight.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.123 - Eligibility Requirements: General
cards.answer: To be eligible for a commercial pilot certificate, a person must: (1) Be at least 18 years of age; (2) Be able to read, speak, write, and understand the English language; (3) Hold at least a private pilot certificate; (4) Receive a logbook endorsement certifying preparation for the knowledge test; (5) Pass the required knowledge test; (6) Receive training and a logbook endorsement for the practical test; (7) Pass the required practical test; (8) Meet the aeronautical experience requirements.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.129(a)(1) - Total Time Required
cards.answer: For an airplane category rating with a single-engine class rating: 250 hours of flight time as a pilot that consists of at least: (i) 100 hours in powered aircraft, of which 50 hours must be in airplanes; (ii) 100 hours of pilot-in-command flight time, which includes at least 50 hours in airplanes and 50 hours in cross-country flight of which at least 10 hours must be in airplanes.
glance: 250 hours total flight time
100 hours in powered aircraft (50 in airplanes)
100 hours PIC (50 in airplanes)
50 hours cross-country PIC (10 in airplanes)

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.129(a)(3) - Training Requirements
cards.answer: 20 hours of training on the areas of operation listed in 61.127(b)(1) including: (i) Ten hours of instrument training using a view-limiting device; (ii) 10 hours of training in a complex airplane or technically advanced airplane, or any combination thereof; (iii) One 2-hour cross-country flight in a single engine airplane in daytime conditions with a total straight-line distance of more than 100 nautical miles; (iv) One 2-hour cross-country flight in a single engine airplane in nighttime conditions with a total straight-line distance of more than 100 nautical miles; (v) Three hours in a single-engine airplane within 2 calendar months preceding the practical test.
glance: 20 hours of training, including:
10 hr instrument training (view-limiting device)
10 hr in a complex or technically advanced airplane (or combination)
One 2-hr day XC, over 100 NM straight-line
One 2-hr night XC, over 100 NM straight-line
3 hr checkride prep within 2 calendar months

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.129(a)(4) - Solo/PIC Requirements
cards.answer: 10 hours of solo flight time in a single engine airplane or 10 hours of flight time performing the duties of pilot in command in a single engine airplane with an authorized instructor, on the areas of operation listed in 61.127(b)(1) that includes: (i) One cross-country flight of not less than 300 nautical miles total distance, with landings at a minimum of 3 points, one of which is a straight-line distance of at least 250 nautical miles from the original departure point; (ii) 5 hours in night VFR conditions with 10 takeoffs and 10 landings at an airport with an operating control tower.
glance: 10 hours solo (or performing PIC duties with an instructor)
One XC of at least 300 NM total, 3 landing points, one at least 250 NM straight-line from departure
5 hr night VFR with 10 takeoffs & 10 landings at a towered airport

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.133(a) - Privileges
cards.answer: A person who holds a commercial pilot certificate may act as pilot in command of an aircraft: (1) Carrying persons or property for compensation or hire, provided the person is qualified in accordance with this part and with the applicable parts of this chapter that apply to the operation; and (2) For compensation or hire, provided the person is qualified in accordance with this part and with the applicable parts of this chapter that apply to the operation.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.133(b) - Limitations
cards.answer: A person who holds a commercial pilot certificate has the following limitations: (1) Except as provided in paragraph (b)(2), a commercial pilot may not act as pilot in command of an aircraft that is carrying passengers or property for compensation or hire, or operate for compensation or hire, unless that person holds an instrument rating in the same category and class of aircraft that is being flown, when operating: (i) At night, or (ii) On cross-country flights in excess of 50 nautical miles.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.31(e) - Additional Training: Complex Airplanes
cards.answer: No person may act as pilot in command of a complex airplane (an airplane that has a retractable landing gear, flaps, and a controllable pitch propeller; or, in the case of a seaplane, flaps and a controllable pitch propeller) unless the person has received and logged ground and flight training from an authorized instructor in a complex airplane, and has received a logbook endorsement.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.31(f) - Additional Training: High-Performance Airplanes
cards.answer: No person may act as pilot in command of a high-performance airplane (an airplane with an engine of more than 200 horsepower) unless that person has received and logged ground and flight training from an authorized instructor in a high-performance airplane, and has received a logbook endorsement that the person is proficient to operate a high-performance airplane.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.31(g) - Additional Training: Pressurized Aircraft
cards.answer: No person may act as pilot in command of a pressurized aircraft capable of operating at high altitudes (aircraft that has a service ceiling or maximum operating altitude, whichever is lower, above 25,000 feet MSL) unless that person has received and logged ground training covering: (i) High-altitude aerodynamics and meteorology; (ii) Respiration; (iii) Effects, symptoms, and causes of hypoxia and any other high-altitude sickness; (iv) Duration of consciousness without supplemental oxygen; (v) Effects of prolonged usage of supplemental oxygen; (vi) Causes and effects of gas expansion and gas bubble formation; (vii) Preventive measures for decompression; (viii) Physical phenomena and incidents of decompression.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.31(i) - Additional Training: Tailwheel Airplanes
cards.answer: No person may act as pilot in command of a tailwheel airplane unless that person has received and logged flight training from an authorized instructor in a tailwheel airplane and received a logbook endorsement that the person is proficient in the operation of a tailwheel airplane. The flight training must include at least the following maneuvers and procedures: (1) Normal and crosswind takeoffs and landings; (2) Wheel landings (unless the manufacturer has recommended against such landings); and (3) Go-around procedures.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.1 - Technically Advanced Airplane (TAA)
cards.answer: Technically advanced airplane (TAA) means an airplane equipped with an electronically advanced avionics system that includes the following installed components: (1) An electronic Primary Flight Display (PFD) that includes, at a minimum, an airspeed indicator, turn coordinator, attitude indicator, heading indicator, altimeter, and vertical speed indicator; (2) An electronic Multifunction Display (MFD) that includes, at a minimum, a moving map using Global Positioning System (GPS) navigation with the aircraft position displayed; (3) A two axis autopilot integrated with the navigation and heading guidance system.

cards.question: 14 CFR 119.1(e) - Operations Not Requiring Certificate
cards.answer: The following operations are not required to have an air carrier or operating certificate: (1) Student instruction; (2) Nonstop Commercial Air Tours conducted within a 25 statute mile radius of the airport of takeoff, that begin and end at the same airport; (3) Ferry or training flights; (4) Aerial work operations, including: (i) Crop dusting, seeding, spraying, and bird chasing; (ii) Banner towing; (iii) Aerial photography or survey; (iv) Fire fighting; (v) Helicopter operations in construction or repair work; (vi) Powerline or pipeline patrol.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.23(a)(1) - First-Class Medical Certificate
cards.answer: Operations requiring a first-class medical certificate: (i) When exercising the pilot-in-command privileges of an airline transport pilot certificate; (ii) When exercising the second-in-command privileges of an airline transport pilot certificate in a flag or supplemental operation in part 121; (iii) When serving as a required pilot flightcrew member in an operation conducted under part 121 if the pilot has reached his or her 60th birthday.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.23(a)(2) - Second-Class Medical Certificate
cards.answer: Operations requiring a second-class medical certificate: (i) When exercising commercial pilot privileges; (ii) When exercising flight instructor certificate privileges; (iii) When taking a practical test in an aircraft for an airline transport pilot certificate, or for a type rating.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.23(d) - Duration of Medical Certificates
cards.answer: First-class medical certificate: Under age 40, valid for 12 calendar months; age 40 or older, valid for 6 calendar months for operations requiring first-class. Second-class medical certificate: Valid for 12 calendar months. Third-class medical certificate: Under age 40, valid for 60 calendar months; age 40 or older, valid for 24 calendar months.

cards.question: 14 CFR 68.3 - BasicMed Medical Education Course
cards.answer: A person must complete the aeromedical factors course required by 61.23(c)(2)(iv) covering: (1) Pilot health; (2) Medical issues relevant to pilot performance; (3) Aeromedical factors affecting pilot fitness; (4) Self-assessment and reporting requirements.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.113(i) - BasicMed Operating Limitations
cards.answer: A person operating under BasicMed: (1) May not act as pilot in command or serve as a required flightcrew member for compensation or hire; (2) May operate only aircraft authorized to carry not more than 6 occupants; (3) May operate aircraft with maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 6,000 pounds; (4) May not operate at an indicated airspeed exceeding 250 knots; (5) May not operate above 18,000 feet MSL; (6) May not operate for compensation or hire.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.17 - Alcohol or Drugs
cards.answer: No person may act or attempt to act as a crewmember of a civil aircraft: (1) Within 8 hours after the consumption of any alcoholic beverage; (2) While under the influence of alcohol; (3) While using any drug that affects the person's faculties in any way contrary to safety; or (4) While having an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater in a blood or breath specimen.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.103 - Preflight Action
cards.answer: Each pilot in command shall, before beginning a flight, become familiar with all available information concerning that flight. This information must include: (a) For a flight under IFR or a flight not in the vicinity of an airport, weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, alternatives available if the planned flight cannot be completed, and any known traffic delays; (b) For any flight, runway lengths at airports of intended use, and the following takeoff and landing distance information.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.205(b) - Visual Flight Rules (Day)
cards.answer: For VFR flight during the day, the required instruments and equipment are: (1) Airspeed indicator; (2) Altimeter; (3) Magnetic direction indicator; (4) Tachometer for each engine; (5) Oil pressure gauge for each engine; (6) Temperature gauge for each liquid-cooled engine; (7) Oil temperature gauge for each air-cooled engine; (8) Manifold pressure gauge for each altitude engine; (9) Fuel gauge indicating the quantity of fuel in each tank; (10) Landing gear position indicator, if the aircraft has a retractable landing gear; (11) An approved aviation red or aviation white anticollision light system; (12) If operated for hire over water and beyond power-off gliding distance from shore, flotation gear; (13) An approved safety belt for each occupant; (14) For small civil airplanes, an emergency locator transmitter.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.205(c) - Visual Flight Rules (Night)
cards.answer: For VFR flight at night, in addition to the instruments and equipment specified in paragraph (b), the following instruments and equipment are required: (1) Approved position lights; (2) An approved aviation red or aviation white anticollision light system; (3) If the aircraft is operated for hire, one electric landing light; (4) An adequate source of electrical energy for all installed electrical and radio equipment; and (5) One spare set of fuses, or three spare fuses of each kind required.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.205(d) - Instrument Flight Rules
cards.answer: For IFR flight, the required instruments and equipment are: (1) Two-way radio communication and navigation equipment suitable for the route; (2) Gyroscopic rate-of-turn indicator; (3) Slip-skid indicator; (4) Sensitive altimeter adjustable for barometric pressure; (5) A clock displaying hours, minutes, and seconds with a sweep-second pointer or digital presentation; (6) Generator or alternator of adequate capacity; (7) Gyroscopic pitch and bank indicator (artificial horizon); (8) Gyroscopic direction indicator (directional gyro or equivalent).

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.213(d) - Operations Without MEL
cards.answer: A person may takeoff an aircraft in operations not conducted under part 121, 125, 129, or 135 of this chapter with inoperative instruments and equipment without an MEL provided: (1) The flight operation is conducted in a rotorcraft, non-turbine-powered airplane, glider, lighter-than-air aircraft, powered parachute, or weight-shift-control aircraft; (2) The inoperative instruments and equipment are not: (i) Part of the VFR-day type certification instruments and equipment; (ii) Indicated as required on the aircraft's equipment list or Kinds of Operations Equipment List; (iii) Required by 91.205 or any other rule; (iv) Required by an airworthiness directive; (3) The inoperative instruments and equipment are removed from the aircraft, the cockpit control placarded, and the maintenance recorded in accordance with 43.9; or the inoperative instruments and equipment are deactivated and placarded 'Inoperative.'

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.409(a) - Annual Inspection
cards.answer: No person may operate an aircraft unless, within the preceding 12 calendar months, it has had an annual inspection in accordance with part 43 and has been approved for return to service by a person authorized to approve aircraft for return to service.
glance: Annual inspection within the preceding 12 calendar months

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.409(b) - 100-Hour Inspection
cards.answer: No person may operate an aircraft carrying any person (other than a crewmember) for hire, and no person may give flight instruction for hire in an aircraft which that person provides, unless within the preceding 100 hours of time in service the aircraft has received an annual or 100-hour inspection and been approved for return to service.
glance: 100-hour inspection required when carrying people for hire
…or giving flight instruction for hire in an aircraft you provide

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.411 - Altimeter System and Altitude Reporting Equipment Tests
cards.answer: No person may operate an airplane, or helicopter, in controlled airspace under IFR unless, within the preceding 24 calendar months, each static pressure system, each altimeter instrument, and each automatic pressure altitude reporting system has been tested and inspected and found to comply with appendices E and F of part 43.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.413 - ATC Transponder Tests and Inspections
cards.answer: No person may use an ATC transponder that is specified in 91.215(a), 91.## 17(b), or 91.225 unless, within the preceding 24 calendar months, the ATC transponder has been tested and inspected and found to comply with appendix F of part 43.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.171 - VOR Equipment Check for IFR Operations
cards.answer: No person may operate a civil aircraft under IFR using the VOR system of radio navigation unless the VOR equipment of that aircraft has been operationally checked within the preceding 30 days, and was found to be within the limits of the permissible indicated bearing error.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.207 - Emergency Locator Transmitters
cards.answer: No person may operate a U.S.-registered civil airplane unless there is attached to the airplane an approved automatic type emergency locator transmitter. Each ELT must be inspected within 12 calendar months after the last inspection for proper operation and battery corrosion. The ELT batteries must be replaced when the transmitter has been in use for more than 1 cumulative hour, or when 50 percent of their useful life has expired.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.171(b)(c) - VOR Check Tolerances
cards.answer: VOR check tolerance limits: (1) VOT check (FAA VOR test facility): Plus or minus 4 degrees; (2) Ground checkpoint: Plus or minus 4 degrees; (3) Airborne checkpoint: Plus or minus 6 degrees; (4) Dual VOR check (comparing two independent VOR receivers): Within 4 degrees of each other; (5) Over a prominent ground point at a distance of not more than 20 nautical miles from the VOR at a reasonably low altitude: Plus or minus 6 degrees.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.203 - Civil Aircraft: Certifications Required
cards.answer: No person may operate a civil aircraft unless it has within it: (1) An appropriate and current airworthiness certificate; (2) An effective U.S. registration certificate issued to its owner or, for operation within the United States, the second copy of the Aircraft Registration Application.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.9 - Civil Aircraft Flight Manual, Marking, and Placard Requirements
cards.answer: No person may operate a civil aircraft without complying with the operating limitations specified in the approved Airplane or Rotorcraft Flight Manual, markings, and placards. No person may operate a U.S.-registered civil aircraft for which an Airplane or Rotorcraft Flight Manual is required unless there is available in the aircraft a current, approved Airplane or Rotorcraft Flight Manual or the manual provided for in 121.141(b).

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.119 - Minimum Safe Altitudes: General
cards.answer: Except when necessary for takeoff or landing, no person may operate an aircraft below the following altitudes: (a) Anywhere: An altitude allowing, if a power unit fails, an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property on the surface; (b) Over congested areas: An altitude of 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal radius of 2,000 feet of the aircraft; (c) Over other than congested areas: An altitude of 500 feet above the surface, except over open water or sparsely populated areas. In those cases, the aircraft may not be operated closer than 500 feet to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.117 - Aircraft Speed
cards.answer: Unless otherwise authorized by the Administrator, no person may operate an aircraft: (a) Below 10,000 feet MSL, at an indicated airspeed of more than 250 knots (288 m.p.h.); (b) Beneath the lateral limits of Class B airspace, or in a VFR corridor through such Class B airspace, at an indicated airspeed of more than 200 knots (230 m.p.h.); (c) At or below 2,500 feet above the surface within 4 nautical miles of the primary airport of a Class C or Class D airspace area, at an indicated airspeed of more than 200 knots (230 m.p.h.).

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.113(b) - General Right-of-Way
cards.answer: When weather conditions permit, regardless of whether an operation is conducted under instrument flight rules or visual flight rules, vigilance shall be maintained by each person operating an aircraft so as to see and avoid other aircraft. When a rule of this section gives another aircraft the right-of-way, the pilot shall give way to that aircraft and may not pass over, under, or ahead of it unless well clear.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.113(c) - In Distress
cards.answer: An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other air traffic.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.113(d) - Converging
cards.answer: When aircraft of the same category are converging at approximately the same altitude (except head-on, or nearly so), the aircraft to the other's right has the right-of-way. If the aircraft are of different categories: (1) A balloon has the right-of-way over any other category of aircraft; (2) A glider has the right-of-way over an airship, powered parachute, weight-shift-control aircraft, airplane, or rotorcraft; (3) An airship has the right-of-way over a powered parachute, weight-shift-control aircraft, airplane, or rotorcraft.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.113(e)(f) - Approaching Head-On and Overtaking
cards.answer: (e) Approaching head-on: When aircraft are approaching each other head-on, or nearly so, each pilot of each aircraft shall alter course to the right. (f) Overtaking: Each aircraft that is being overtaken has the right-of-way and each pilot of an overtaking aircraft shall alter course to the right to pass well clear.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.113(g) - Landing
cards.answer: Aircraft, while on final approach to land or while landing, have the right-of-way over other aircraft in flight or operating on the surface, except that they shall not take advantage of this rule to force an aircraft off the runway surface which has already landed and is attempting to make way for an aircraft on final approach. When two or more aircraft are approaching an airport for the purpose of landing, the aircraft at the lower altitude has the right-of-way, but it shall not take advantage of this rule to cut in front of another which is on final approach to land or to overtake that aircraft.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.111 - Operating Near Other Aircraft
cards.answer: (a) No person may operate an aircraft so close to another aircraft as to create a collision hazard. (b) No person may operate an aircraft in formation flight except by arrangement with the pilot in command of each aircraft in the formation. (c) No person may operate an aircraft, carrying passengers for hire, in formation flight.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.211(a) - Supplemental Oxygen Requirements
cards.answer: No person may operate a civil aircraft of U.S. registry: (1) At cabin pressure altitudes above 12,500 feet MSL up to and including 14,000 feet MSL unless the required minimum flight crew is provided with and uses supplemental oxygen for that part of the flight at those altitudes that is of more than 30 minutes duration; (2) At cabin pressure altitudes above 14,000 feet MSL unless the required minimum flight crew is provided with and uses supplemental oxygen during the entire flight time at those altitudes; (3) At cabin pressure altitudes above 15,000 feet MSL unless each occupant of the aircraft is provided with supplemental oxygen.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.215(b) - ATC Transponder Required
cards.answer: All airspace: No person may operate an aircraft in the airspace described in paragraphs (b)(1) through (b)(5) unless that aircraft is equipped with an operable coded radar beacon transponder: (1) All aircraft in Class A, Class B, and Class C airspace; (2) All aircraft in all airspace within 30 nautical miles of an airport listed in appendix D, section 1 of this part from the surface upward to 10,000 feet MSL; (3) All aircraft in all airspace of the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia at and above 10,000 feet MSL, excluding the airspace at and below 2,500 feet above the surface.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.225 - Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) Out Equipment
cards.answer: After January 1, 2020, no person may operate an aircraft in the following airspace unless the aircraft has ADS-B Out equipment: (1) Class A, B, and C airspace; (2) Class E airspace within the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia at and above 10,000 feet MSL, excluding the airspace at and below 2,500 feet AGL; (3) Class E airspace at and above 3,000 feet MSL over the Gulf of Mexico from the coastline of the United States out to 12 nautical miles; (4) Class B and C airspace areas, and those Class E surface areas within 30 nautical miles of a Class B primary airport.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.125 - ATC Light Signals
cards.answer: ATC light signals and their meanings: Movement of vehicles/equipment/personnel on airport: (1) Steady green - Cleared to cross, proceed or go; (2) Flashing green - Not applicable; (3) Steady red - Stop; (4) Flashing red - Clear the taxiway/runway; (5) Flashing white - Return to starting point on airport; (6) Alternating red and green - Exercise extreme caution. Aircraft on surface: Steady green - Cleared for takeoff; Flashing green - Cleared to taxi; Steady red - Stop; Flashing red - Taxi clear of runway in use; Flashing white - Return to starting point. Aircraft in flight: Steady green - Cleared to land; Flashing green - Return for landing; Steady red - Give way to other aircraft and continue circling; Flashing red - Airport unsafe, do not land; Alternating red and green - Exercise extreme caution.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.167 - Fuel Requirements for Flight in IFR Conditions
cards.answer: No person may operate a civil aircraft in IFR conditions unless it carries enough fuel (considering weather reports and forecasts and weather conditions) to: (1) Complete the flight to the first airport of intended landing; (2) Except as provided in paragraph (b), fly from that airport to the alternate airport; and (3) Fly after that for 45 minutes at normal cruising speed or, for helicopters, fly after that for 30 minutes at normal cruising speed.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.169(b) - No Alternate Required (1-2-3 Rule)
cards.answer: No alternate airport is required if: (1) Part 97 of this chapter prescribes a standard instrument approach procedure for the first airport of intended landing; and (2) Appropriate weather reports or weather forecasts, or a combination of them, indicate that: (i) For at least 1 hour before and for 1 hour after the estimated time of arrival at the airport, the ceiling will be at least 2,000 feet above the airport elevation and the visibility will be at least 3 statute miles.
glance: No alternate if: instrument approach at destination, AND
1 hr before to 1 hr after ETA: ceiling ≥ 2,000 ft and visibility ≥ 3 SM (1-2-3 rule)

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.169(c) - Alternate Airport Weather Minimums
cards.answer: No person may include an alternate airport in an IFR flight plan unless appropriate weather reports or forecasts indicate that, at the estimated time of arrival at the alternate airport, the ceiling and visibility at that airport will be at or above the following weather minimums: (1) If an instrument approach procedure has been published for that airport: (i) For a precision approach, 600-foot ceiling and 2 statute miles visibility; (ii) For a nonprecision approach, 800-foot ceiling and 2 statute miles visibility.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.183 - IFR Communications
cards.answer: Unless otherwise authorized by ATC, the pilot in command of each aircraft operated under IFR in controlled airspace must ensure that a continuous watch is maintained on the appropriate frequency and must report: (1) The time and altitude of passing each designated reporting point; (2) Any unforecast weather conditions encountered; (3) Any other information relating to the safety of flight.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.187 - Operation Under IFR: Malfunction Reports
cards.answer: The pilot in command of each aircraft operated in controlled airspace under IFR shall report as soon as practical to ATC any malfunctions of navigational, approach, or communication equipment occurring in flight. In each report the pilot in command shall include: (1) Aircraft identification; (2) Equipment affected; (3) Degree to which the capability of the pilot to operate under IFR is impaired; (4) Nature and extent of assistance desired from ATC.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.3 - Responsibility and Authority of the Pilot in Command
cards.answer: (a) The pilot in command of an aircraft is directly responsible for, and is the final authority as to, the operation of that aircraft. (b) In an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action, the pilot in command may deviate from any rule of this part to the extent required to meet that emergency. (c) Each pilot in command who deviates from a rule under paragraph (b) of this section shall, upon the request of the Administrator, send a written report of that deviation to the Administrator.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.407 - Operation After Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, Rebuilding, or Alteration
cards.answer: (a) No person may operate any aircraft that has undergone maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, or alteration unless: (1) It has been approved for return to service by a person authorized to approve aircraft for return to service; and (2) The maintenance record entry required by 43.9 or 43.11, as applicable, has been made. (b) No person may carry any person (other than crewmembers) in an aircraft that has been maintained, rebuilt, or altered in a manner that may have appreciably changed its flight characteristics or substantially affected its operation in flight until an appropriately rated pilot with at least a private pilot certificate flies the aircraft, makes an operational check of the maintenance performed or alteration made, and logs the flight in the aircraft records.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.157 - Special VFR Weather Minimums
cards.answer: (a) Special VFR operations may be conducted under the weather minimums and requirements of this section, instead of those contained in 91.155, below 10,000 feet MSL within the airspace contained by the upward extension of the lateral boundaries of the controlled airspace designated to the surface for an airport. (b) No person may operate an aircraft in special VFR conditions unless: (1) Flight visibility is at least 1 statute mile; (2) The aircraft is operated clear of clouds.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.157(b)(4) - Night Special VFR Requirements
cards.answer: No person may take off or land an aircraft under special VFR: (i) Unless that person is instrument rated and the aircraft is instrument equipped; (ii) Between sunset and sunrise, unless the flight visibility is at least 1 statute mile.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.303 - Aerobatic Flight
cards.answer: No person may operate an aircraft in aerobatic flight: (a) Over any congested area of a city, town, or settlement; (b) Over an open air assembly of persons; (c) Within the lateral boundaries of the surface areas of Class B, Class C, Class D, or Class E airspace designated for an airport; (d) Within 4 nautical miles of the center line of any Federal airway; (e) Below an altitude of 1,500 feet above the surface; or (f) When flight visibility is less than 3 statute miles.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.307 - Parachutes and Parachuting
cards.answer: (a) No pilot of a civil aircraft may allow a parachute that is available for emergency use to be carried in that aircraft unless it is an approved type and: (1) If a chair type, has been packed by a certificated and appropriately rated parachute rigger within the preceding 180 days; or (2) If a back, seat, chest, or lap belt type, has been packed by a certificated and appropriately rated parachute rigger within the preceding 180 days.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.155(a) - Class B Airspace
cards.answer: VFR weather minimums for Class B airspace: Flight visibility 3 statute miles; Clear of clouds.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.155(a) - Class C, D, E Airspace Below 10,000 MSL
cards.answer: VFR weather minimums for Class C, D, and E airspace less than 10,000 feet MSL: Flight visibility 3 statute miles; 500 feet below clouds; 1,000 feet above clouds; 2,000 feet horizontal distance from clouds.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.155(a) - Class E Airspace At or Above 10,000 MSL
cards.answer: VFR weather minimums for Class E airspace at or above 10,000 feet MSL: Flight visibility 5 statute miles; 1,000 feet below clouds; 1,000 feet above clouds; 1 statute mile horizontal distance from clouds.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.155(a) - Class G Airspace 1,200 feet or Less AGL, Day
cards.answer: VFR weather minimums for Class G airspace 1,200 feet or less above the surface (regardless of MSL altitude), during the day: Flight visibility 1 statute mile; Clear of clouds.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.155(a) - Class G Airspace 1,200 feet or Less AGL, Night
cards.answer: VFR weather minimums for Class G airspace 1,200 feet or less above the surface (regardless of MSL altitude), at night: Flight visibility 3 statute miles; 500 feet below clouds; 1,000 feet above clouds; 2,000 feet horizontal distance from clouds (except for helicopters flying at 1/2 mile or less from runway at an airport, 1 statute mile visibility and clear of clouds).

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.56 - Flight Review
cards.answer: No person may act as pilot in command of an aircraft unless, since the beginning of the 24th calendar month before the month in which that pilot acts as pilot in command, that pilot has: (1) Accomplished a flight review given in an aircraft for which that pilot is rated by an authorized instructor; and (2) A logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor who gave the review certifying that the person has satisfactorily completed the review. The review must consist of: (1) A minimum of 1 hour of flight training and 1 hour of ground training; (2) A review of current general operating and flight rules of part 91; (3) A review of those maneuvers and procedures necessary to demonstrate safe exercise of privileges.
glance: Every 24 calendar months
Minimum 1 hr ground + 1 hr flight
Logbook endorsement from the instructor

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.57(a) - Recent Experience: Pilot in Command
cards.answer: No person may act as pilot in command of an aircraft carrying passengers or of an aircraft certificated for more than one pilot flight crewmember unless that person has made at least three takeoffs and three landings within the preceding 90 days, and: (1) The person acted as the sole manipulator of the flight controls; and (2) The required takeoffs and landings were performed in an aircraft of the same category, class, and type (if a type rating is required).
glance: Carrying passengers: 3 takeoffs & 3 landings in the preceding 90 days
Sole manipulator · same category, class, and type

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.57(b) - Night Takeoff and Landing Experience
cards.answer: No person may act as pilot in command of an aircraft carrying passengers during the period beginning 1 hour after sunset and ending 1 hour before sunrise, unless within the preceding 90 days that person has made at least three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop during the period beginning 1 hour after sunset and ending 1 hour before sunrise, and: (1) That person acted as sole manipulator of the flight controls; and (2) The required takeoffs and landings were performed in an aircraft of the same category, class, and type (if a type rating is required).
glance: Night passengers: 3 takeoffs & 3 full-stop landings in the preceding 90 days
Between 1 hr after sunset and 1 hr before sunrise

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.57(c) - Instrument Experience Requirements
cards.answer: No person may act as pilot in command under IFR or in weather conditions less than the minimums prescribed for VFR, unless within the 6 calendar months preceding the month of the flight, that person has: (1) Performed and logged under actual or simulated instrument conditions: (i) At least six instrument approaches; (ii) Holding procedures and tasks; and (iii) Intercepting and tracking courses through the use of navigational electronic systems.
glance: Within the preceding 6 calendar months
6 instrument approaches
Holding procedures and tasks
Intercepting and tracking courses

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.51(e) - Logging Pilot-in-Command Flight Time
cards.answer: A sport, recreational, private, commercial, or airline transport pilot may log pilot in command flight time for flights when that person: (i) Is the sole manipulator of the controls of an aircraft for which the pilot is rated, or has sport pilot privileges for that category and class of aircraft; (ii) Is the sole occupant in the aircraft; (iii) Except for a holder of a sport or recreational pilot certificate, is acting as pilot in command of an aircraft for which more than one pilot is required under the type certification of the aircraft or the regulations under which the flight is conducted; or (iv) Is performing the duties of pilot in command while under the supervision of a qualified pilot in command provided the person is a required pilot flightcrew member.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.113(c) - Cost Sharing
cards.answer: A private pilot may not pay less than the pro rata share of the operating expenses of a flight with passengers, provided the expenses involve only fuel, oil, airport expenditures, or rental fees.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.125 - Aeronautical Knowledge
cards.answer: A person who applies for a commercial pilot certificate must receive and log ground training from an authorized instructor, or complete a home-study course, on the aeronautical knowledge areas that apply to the aircraft category and class rating sought: (1) Federal Aviation Regulations relating to commercial pilot privileges, limitations, and flight operations; (2) Accident reporting requirements of NTSB; (3) Basic aerodynamics and principles of flight; (4) Meteorology; (5) Safe and efficient operation of aircraft; (6) Weight and balance; (7) Aircraft performance; (8) Aircraft systems; (9) Maneuver recognition; (10) Aeronautical decision making; (11) Crew resource management.

cards.question: AIM 7-1-6 - SIGMET
cards.answer: SIGMETs (Significant Meteorological Information) advise of non-convective weather that is potentially hazardous to all aircraft. SIGMETs are issued for: (1) Severe icing not associated with thunderstorms; (2) Severe or extreme turbulence or clear air turbulence (CAT) not associated with thunderstorms; (3) Dust storms or sandstorms lowering surface visibilities to below 3 miles; (4) Volcanic ash. SIGMETs are valid for 4 hours (6 hours for volcanic ash).

cards.question: AIM 7-1-6 - Convective SIGMET
cards.answer: Convective SIGMETs are issued for convective hazards: (1) Tornadoes; (2) Lines of thunderstorms; (3) Embedded thunderstorms; (4) Areas of thunderstorms greater than or equal to VIP level 4 affecting 40 percent or more of an area at least 3,000 square miles; (5) Hail greater than or equal to 3/4 inch in diameter; (6) Wind gusts to 50 knots or greater. Convective SIGMETs are valid for 2 hours.

cards.question: AIM 7-1-6 - AIRMET
cards.answer: AIRMETs (Airman's Meteorological Information) are advisories of significant weather phenomena that describe conditions at intensities lower than those which require the issuance of SIGMETs. AIRMETs are intended for dissemination to all pilots. Types: AIRMET SIERRA - Describes IFR conditions and/or extensive mountain obscuration; AIRMET TANGO - Describes moderate turbulence, sustained surface winds of 30 knots or greater, and/or nonconvective low-level wind shear; AIRMET ZULU - Describes moderate icing and provides freezing level heights. AIRMETs are valid for 6 hours.

cards.question: AIM 7-1-27 - Thunderstorm Hazards
cards.answer: Thunderstorms produce hazardous weather including: (1) Lightning; (2) Tornadoes; (3) Turbulence; (4) Icing; (5) Hail; (6) Wind shear; (7) Microbursts. The mature stage of a thunderstorm is characterized by the presence of both updrafts and downdrafts within the cell. The danger from microbursts is that an airplane may experience a sudden loss of airspeed (tailwind component) and altitude that can lead to an accident.

cards.question: AIM 7-1-21 - Types of Aircraft Icing
cards.answer: Clear ice forms when, after initial impact, the remaining liquid portion of the drop flows out over the aircraft surface, gradually freezing as a smooth sheet of solid ice. Rime ice forms when the water drops are small, such as those in stratiform clouds or light drizzle. The liquid portion remaining after initial impact freezes rapidly before the drop has time to spread over the aircraft surface, creating a rough, milky, opaque ice. Mixed ice forms when drops vary in size or when liquid drops are intermingled with snow or ice particles.

cards.question: AIM 4-3-3 - Traffic Patterns
cards.answer: Components of a traffic pattern: (1) Upwind leg - A flight path parallel to the landing runway in the direction of landing; (2) Crosswind leg - A flight path at right angles to the landing runway off its upwind end; (3) Downwind leg - A flight path parallel to the landing runway in the opposite direction of landing; (4) Base leg - A flight path at right angles to the landing runway off its approach end; (5) Final approach - A flight path in the direction of landing along the extended runway centerline. Standard traffic pattern altitude is 1,000 feet AGL unless otherwise established. Left-hand traffic is standard unless otherwise indicated.

cards.question: AIM 2-3-3 - Displaced Threshold
cards.answer: A displaced threshold is a threshold located at a point on the runway other than the designated beginning of the runway. The portion of runway behind a displaced threshold is available for takeoffs in either direction and landings from the opposite direction. A ten-foot-wide white threshold bar is used to denote the beginning of the runway that is available for landing when a threshold has been relocated or displaced. White arrows are located on the centerline in the area between the beginning of the runway and displaced threshold.

cards.question: AIM 2-3-3 - Blast Pad/Stopway
cards.answer: Blast pads or stopways are areas beyond the takeoff runway end that appear to be usable runway but are not intended for aircraft use. Yellow chevrons mark these areas. This area is not suitable for taxiing, takeoff, or landing of aircraft.

cards.question: AIM 2-3-5 - Holding Position Markings
cards.answer: Runway holding position markings consist of four yellow lines, two solid and two dashed, spaced six or twelve inches apart, and extending across the width of the taxiway or runway. The solid lines are always on the side where the aircraft must hold. The dashed lines face the runway. An aircraft exiting a runway is not clear of the runway until all parts of the aircraft have crossed the applicable holding position marking.

cards.question: AIM 2-1-1 - Approach Light Systems (ALS)
cards.answer: Approach Light Systems provide the basic means to transition from instrument flight to visual flight for landing. The ALS configuration provides the pilot with a visible means of going from the approach minimum altitude to the runway threshold. High intensity lights are used primarily on precision approach runways where low visibility conditions are common. Pilots should not mistake the approach lights for the runway.

cards.question: AIM 2-1-2 - Precision Approach Path Indicator (PAPI)
cards.answer: PAPI uses light units installed in a single row of either two or four light units on the left side of the runway. PAPI has an effective visual range of about 5 miles during the day and up to 20 miles at night. The visual glide path is normally set at 3 degrees. Interpretation: All white - high (more than 3.5 degrees); Three white one red - slightly high; Two white two red - on glide path (3 degrees); One white three red - slightly low; All red - low (less than 2.5 degrees).

cards.question: AIM 7-4-3 - Wake Turbulence Avoidance
cards.answer: All aircraft generate wake turbulence, with the greatest vortex strength occurring when the generating aircraft is heavy, clean, and slow. Vortices from large aircraft sink at a rate of several hundred feet per minute. Pilots should land beyond the touchdown point of a preceding large aircraft or rotate prior to the rotation point of a preceding large aircraft. When departing behind a larger aircraft, note its rotation point, rotate prior to that point, and climb above its climb path.

cards.question: AIM 5-3-8 - Holding
cards.answer: Holding patterns are racetrack patterns based on a holding fix. Standard pattern turns are to the right; nonstandard pattern turns are to the left. Maximum holding airspeeds: MHA-6,000 feet: 200 KIAS; 6,001-14,000 feet: 230 KIAS; 14,001 feet and above: 265 KIAS. Timing for the outbound leg begins over/abeam the fix, whichever occurs later. Outbound leg timing: 1 minute at or below 14,000 feet MSL; 1.5 minutes above 14,000 feet MSL.

cards.question: FAA-S-ACS-7B - Chandelles
cards.answer: A chandelle is a maximum performance climbing turn, beginning from straight-and-level flight, and ending at the completion of a 180 degree turn in a wings-level, nose-high attitude at the minimum controllable airspeed. The chandelle demonstrates the ability to smoothly combine the maximum performance capability of the airplane in a coordinated manner. Objective: Complete at 180 degrees of turn in a nose-high attitude, just above stall speed, at or before reaching the specified heading within +/- 10 degrees. Altitude gained should be appropriate for conditions.

cards.question: FAA-S-ACS-7B - Lazy Eights
cards.answer: A lazy eight is a maneuver designed to develop the proper coordination of the flight controls across a wide range of airspeeds and attitudes. At no time during the lazy eight is the flight path straight. It consists of two symmetrical looping patterns followed by a 90-degree turn. At the 45-degree points the nose should be at the highest pitch attitude and the bank angle increasing. At the 90-degree point the aircraft should be in a level, maximum bank attitude at minimum airspeed. Standards: +/- 100 feet at 180-degree point; +/- 10 knots at 180-degree point; bank approximately 30 degrees at steepest point; +/- 10 degrees at 180-degree point.

cards.question: FAA-S-ACS-7B - Steep Spirals
cards.answer: A steep spiral is a constant gliding turn, during which a constant radius around a point on the ground is maintained similar to the turn around a point maneuver. The objective is to improve pilot techniques for power-off accuracy landings by demonstrating the ability to maintain a radius around a selected ground reference point while maintaining adequate glide performance and airspeed. Standards: Maintain specified airspeed +/- 10 knots; complete maneuver no lower than 1,500 feet AGL; maximum bank angle 60 degrees; complete 3 turns.

cards.question: FAA-S-ACS-7B - Eights on Pylons
cards.answer: Eights on pylons is a ground reference maneuver wherein the extended lateral axis of the aircraft is made to appear as if pivoting on a selected point on the ground. The pilot flies the airplane so that its wingtip appears to be on the pylon throughout the turn. Pivotal altitude varies with groundspeed and can be calculated as groundspeed squared divided by 11.3 (for feet), plus the elevation of the pylon. As groundspeed increases, pivotal altitude increases; as groundspeed decreases, pivotal altitude decreases. Standards: Bank not to exceed 40 degrees; maintain pivotal altitude so line-of-sight reference remains on pylon.

cards.question: AIM 8-1-5 - Spatial Disorientation and Illusions
cards.answer: The Leans: A banking illusion caused by sudden return to level flight following gradual and prolonged turn that went unnoticed. Coriolis Illusion: An extreme tumbling sensation caused by turning or tilting the head during a prolonged constant-rate turn. Graveyard Spiral: The illusion of being in a level turn when actually in a descending turn. Somatogravic Illusion: A rapid acceleration during takeoff creates the illusion of being in a nose-up attitude. Inversion Illusion: An abrupt change from climb to straight-and-level flight can create the illusion of tumbling backward. Prevention: Rely on flight instruments.

cards.question: AIM 8-1-2 - Effects of Altitude
cards.answer: Hypoxia is a state of oxygen deficiency in the body sufficient to impair functions of the brain and other organs. Types include: Hypoxic hypoxia - insufficient oxygen available to the body as a whole; Hypemic hypoxia - blood not able to take up and transport sufficient oxygen; Stagnant hypoxia - oxygen-rich blood in lungs is not moving; Histotoxic hypoxia - inability of cells to effectively use oxygen. Treatment: Use supplemental oxygen; descend immediately to lower altitude.

cards.question: AIM 8-1-2 - Hyperventilation
cards.answer: Hyperventilation is an abnormal increase in the volume of air breathed in and out of the lungs. This results in a significant decrease in the carbon dioxide content of the blood. Symptoms are similar to those of hypoxia. The cure for hyperventilation involves restoring the proper carbon dioxide level in the body. This can be done by talking, singing, or slowing the breathing rate, or by breathing into a paper bag.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Effects of Weight
cards.answer: An increase in weight causes: Higher takeoff speed required; longer takeoff run; reduced rate and angle of climb; lower maximum altitude; shorter range; reduced cruising speed; reduced maneuverability; higher stalling speed; higher approach and landing speed; longer landing roll.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Effects of CG Position
cards.answer: Forward CG: More stable; higher stall speed; more elevator pressure required; longer takeoff distance; better cruise performance. Aft CG: Less stable; lower stall speed; lighter control forces; may be difficult or impossible to recover from stalls; if beyond aft limit, aircraft may be uncontrollable. The CG must remain within the envelope throughout the entire flight.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Density Altitude Effects
cards.answer: High density altitude (high, hot, humid conditions) reduces aircraft performance: Reduced engine power output; reduced propeller efficiency; reduced lift production; increased takeoff distance; reduced rate of climb; increased true airspeed for a given indicated airspeed. Performance decreases approximately 3.5% for each 1,000 feet of density altitude increase.

cards.question: 14 CFR 1.1 - Definition of Night
cards.answer:
Night means the time between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight, as published in the Air Almanac, converted to local time.

Civil Twilight:
• Morning civil twilight begins when the geometric center of the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon and ends at sunrise
• Evening civil twilight begins at sunset and ends when the geometric center of the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon

Note: For night landing currency purposes (§61.57), the period is 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.209 - Aircraft Lights
cards.answer:
No person may operate an aircraft during the period from sunset to sunrise unless it has lighted position lights. In addition, the aircraft must have an anticollision light system if the aircraft was originally certificated with one.

Position lights:
• Red on left wingtip
• Green on right wingtip
• White on tail

The pilot in command may turn off the anticollision lights if, in the pilot's judgment, it would be in the interest of safety to do so (such as in clouds where the flashing could be disorienting).

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Stall Characteristics
cards.answer:
A stall is a rapid decrease in lift caused by the separation of airflow from the wing's surface, brought on by exceeding the critical angle of attack.

Key principles:
• A stall can occur at ANY pitch attitude or airspeed
• The wing always stalls at the same critical angle of attack
• Stall speed increases with increased load factor
• Stall speed increases with weight
• Stall speed increases in turns (proportional to square root of load factor)

Recovery: Reduce angle of attack by lowering the nose, add power as needed, level wings, return to desired flight path.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Aircraft Stability Types
cards.answer:
Static Stability: The initial tendency to return to equilibrium after being disturbed.
• Positive Static Stability: Tends to return to original condition
• Neutral Static Stability: Remains in new condition
• Negative Static Stability: Continues away from original condition

Dynamic Stability: The motion of the aircraft over time after being disturbed.
• Positive Dynamic Stability: Oscillations decrease over time
• Neutral Dynamic Stability: Oscillations continue unchanged
• Negative Dynamic Stability: Oscillations increase over time

An aircraft can have positive static stability but negative dynamic stability (phugoid oscillation).

cards.question: 14 CFR 119.1 - Applicability of Part 119
cards.answer:
Part 119 establishes certification requirements for air carriers and commercial operators.

Operations NOT requiring an operating certificate (§119.1(e)):
• Student instruction
• Nonstop commercial air tours conducted within 25 statute miles of departure airport (if beginning and ending at same airport)
• Ferry or training flights
• Aerial work including: crop dusting, seeding, spraying, bird chasing, banner towing, aerial photography or survey, firefighting, powerline or pipeline patrol
• Helicopter external-load operations
• Sightseeing flights over national parks

cards.question: AC 120-12A - Common Carriage vs Private Carriage
cards.answer:
Common Carriage consists of four elements:
1. A holding out of a willingness to
2. Transport persons or property
3. From place to place
4. For compensation

'Holding out' includes advertising, soliciting, or making known that transportation is available. If all four elements are present, an operating certificate is required.

Private Carriage: Carriage for hire that does NOT involve 'holding out.' Example: A pilot contracted by one specific company for exclusive use does not need an operating certificate.

The test is whether the public has access to the transportation offered.

cards.question: AC 61-142 - Definition of Compensation
cards.answer:
Compensation is anything of value that is given in exchange for the flight. It includes:

• Money (direct payment)
• Sharing of expenses (in some situations)
• Good will or future economic benefit
• Accruing flight time (when offered as incentive)
• Reimbursement of expenses
• Exchange of services

Flight time can be considered compensation when a pilot would not otherwise have made the flight but for the opportunity to build time.

Key: If you would not have made the flight 'but for' the compensation received, it is likely compensated carriage.

cards.question: 14 CFR Part 121 - Domestic and Flag Operations
cards.answer:
Part 121 governs scheduled domestic and flag air carrier operations (airlines).

Applies to operations using:
• Airplanes with more than 30 passenger seats
• Airplanes with payload capacity greater than 7,500 pounds (for passenger operations)
• Scheduled passenger operations

Requires the highest level of regulatory compliance including:
• Comprehensive training programs
• Maintenance programs
• Operations specifications
• Crew scheduling and duty time limitations
• Dispatcher oversight

cards.question: 14 CFR Part 135 - Commuter and On-Demand Operations
cards.answer:
Part 135 governs commuter and on-demand (charter) operations.
