On-Demand Operations:
• Unscheduled passenger or cargo operations
• Aircraft with 30 or fewer seats
• Payload capacity of 7,500 pounds or less

Commuter Operations:
• Scheduled passenger operations
• Aircraft with 9 or fewer passenger seats

Pilot Qualifications (§135.243):
• Commercial pilot certificate with appropriate ratings
• Instrument rating (for operations at night or beyond 50 NM)
• Meet experience and recency requirements
• Pass Part 135 competency check

cards.question: AC 00-6 - Stable vs Unstable Air
cards.answer:
Stable Atmosphere:
• Resists vertical motion
• Smooth flying conditions
• Stratiform (layered) clouds
• Continuous precipitation
• Poor visibility in haze, fog, smoke
• Temperature decreases slowly with altitude

Unstable Atmosphere:
• Promotes vertical motion
• Turbulent flying conditions
• Cumuliform (puffy, towering) clouds
• Showery precipitation
• Good visibility (except in precipitation)
• Temperature decreases rapidly with altitude

Stability is determined by comparing the temperature of rising air to the surrounding environment.

cards.question: AC 00-6 - Cold Front Characteristics
cards.answer:
A cold front forms when a cold air mass advances and replaces a warmer air mass.

Characteristics:
• Fast-moving (20-35 knots typically)
• Steep frontal slope
• Cumuliform clouds (due to rapid lifting)
• Heavy, showery precipitation in narrow band
• Good visibility after passage
• Turbulence
• Possible thunderstorms and wind shear
• Rapid temperature drop after passage
• Wind shift (veering - clockwise in Northern Hemisphere)
• Pressure rises after passage

Fast-moving cold fronts produce the most severe weather.

cards.question: AC 00-6 - Warm Front Characteristics
cards.answer:
A warm front forms when a warm air mass advances and overrides a cooler air mass.

Characteristics:
• Slow-moving (10-15 knots typically)
• Shallow frontal slope
• Stratiform clouds extending far ahead of front
• Steady, widespread precipitation
• Poor visibility (fog, mist, haze)
• Possible embedded thunderstorms in summer
• Gradual temperature rise after passage
• Wind shift (veering - clockwise in Northern Hemisphere)
• Pressure falls, then steadies after passage

Weather may begin 500+ miles ahead of surface front.

cards.question: AC 00-6 - Types of Fog
cards.answer:
Radiation Fog: Forms on clear, calm nights when ground cools by radiation. Requires light winds (under 5 knots) and moist air. Burns off after sunrise.

Advection Fog: Forms when warm, moist air moves over cooler surface. Requires wind for formation. Common along coastlines.

Upslope Fog: Forms when moist, stable air is forced up sloping terrain, cooling to dewpoint. Common on eastern slopes of mountains.

Steam Fog (Arctic Sea Smoke): Forms when cold, dry air moves over warm water. Water evaporates, saturating cold air.

Precipitation-Induced Fog: Forms when warm rain falls through cold air, evaporating and saturating the air. Common with warm fronts.

cards.question: AC 00-6 - Three Stages of Thunderstorm Development
cards.answer:
Three ingredients required: Moisture, lifting action, and unstable air.

1. Cumulus (Building) Stage:
• Characterized by updrafts throughout cell
• Warm, moist air rises and condenses
• Duration: 10-15 minutes
• Little or no precipitation at surface

2. Mature Stage:
• Characterized by BOTH updrafts AND downdrafts
• Most hazardous stage - all hazards at maximum intensity
• Heavy precipitation, hail, lightning, turbulence, wind shear
• Downdrafts spread out upon reaching surface (gust front)
• Duration: 15-30 minutes

3. Dissipating Stage:
• Characterized by downdrafts throughout cell
• Precipitation decreases
• Downdrafts cut off updraft supply

cards.question: AIM 7-1-26 - Microbursts
cards.answer:
A microburst is a small-scale intense downdraft which, upon reaching the surface, spreads outward in all directions.

Characteristics:
• Less than 2.5 miles in diameter
• Peak intensity lasts 2-4 minutes (maximum 15 minutes)
• Downdraft speeds may exceed 6,000 feet per minute
• Horizontal winds may exceed 45 knots, with differential of 90 knots

Hazard sequence for landing aircraft:
1. Initial headwind (increased performance - false sense of security)
2. Strong downdraft (rapid altitude loss)
3. Tailwind (decreased performance - critical)

Recovery: Maximum thrust, maintain or increase pitch attitude. Do NOT retract flaps or gear until clear.

cards.question: AIM 8-1-2 - Scuba Diving and Flying
cards.answer:
Flying after scuba diving requires a surface interval to allow nitrogen absorbed during diving to be eliminated.

Recommended waiting times before flight:

• Nondecompression Stop Diving (no controlled ascent required):
  - Wait at least 12 hours before flight to cabin altitude up to 8,000 feet

• Decompression Stop Diving (controlled ascent required):
  - Wait at least 24 hours before flight

• Flights above 8,000 feet cabin altitude:
  - Wait at least 24 hours

Reason: Reduced pressure at altitude allows residual nitrogen to form bubbles in tissues (decompression sickness).

cards.question: AIM 8-1-2 - Middle Ear and Sinus Problems
cards.answer:
The middle ear and sinuses contain air that must equalize with atmospheric pressure.

Ear Block:
• During descent, increasing pressure may cause pain if Eustachian tube is blocked
• Most severe during descent
• Can rupture eardrum in severe cases

Relief - Valsalva Maneuver:
• Pinch nostrils, close mouth, gently try to blow
• Forces air through Eustachian tube
• May not work with cold or congestion

Sinus Block:
• Similar mechanism in sinus cavities
• Causes sharp pain in forehead or cheek area

Prevention: Avoid flying with head cold, sinus infection, or upper respiratory infection.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.113(e) - Approaching Head-On
cards.answer: When aircraft are approaching each other head-on, or nearly so, each pilot of each aircraft shall alter course to the right.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.113(f) - Overtaking
cards.answer:
Each aircraft that is being overtaken has the right-of-way and each pilot of an overtaking aircraft shall alter course to the right to pass well clear.

An aircraft is considered to be overtaking if it approaches another from a direction within an angle of 70 degrees from directly behind.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.113(g) - Landing
cards.answer:
Aircraft, while on final approach to land or while landing, have the right-of-way over other aircraft in flight or operating on the surface, except that they shall not take advantage of this rule to force an aircraft off the runway surface which has already landed and is attempting to make way for an aircraft on final approach.

When two or more aircraft are approaching an airport for the purpose of landing, the aircraft at the lower altitude has the right-of-way, but it shall not take advantage of this rule to cut in front of another which is on final approach to land or to overtake that aircraft.

cards.question: AIM 4-3-3 - Traffic Patterns
cards.answer:
Standard traffic pattern:
• All turns are to the LEFT unless otherwise indicated
• Pattern altitude: Typically 1,000 feet AGL for single-engine aircraft, 1,500 feet AGL for large or turbine aircraft

Pattern legs:
1. Departure (Upwind) - parallel to runway in direction of takeoff
2. Crosswind - perpendicular turn after departure
3. Downwind - parallel to runway, opposite direction of landing
4. Base - turn toward runway
5. Final - aligned with runway centerline

Standard entry: Enter at 45° angle to midpoint of downwind leg at pattern altitude.

Right traffic indicated by: visual markings, chart notation, or ATC instruction.

cards.question: AIM 2-3-3 - Displaced Threshold
cards.answer:
A displaced threshold is a threshold located at a point on the runway other than the designated beginning of the runway.

Marking: White arrows on runway centerline pointing toward the displaced threshold.

Use of area preceding displaced threshold:
• Available for takeoffs in either direction
• Available for landing rollout from opposite direction
• Available for taxiing

NOT available for:
• Landing from the approach direction (must land at or beyond the displaced threshold)

Reason: Provides obstacle clearance for aircraft on approach.

cards.question: AIM 2-3-3 - Blast Pad/Stopway
cards.answer:
Blast pads and stopways are areas beyond the takeoff runway end that appear to be usable runway but are not intended for aircraft use.

Marking: Yellow chevrons

NOT available for:
• Takeoff
• Landing
• Taxiing

Purpose:
• Blast pad: Prevents erosion from jet blast during takeoff
• Stopway: Provides overrun area in case of rejected takeoff

May be used for emergency overrun only.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.111 - Operating Near Other Aircraft
cards.answer:
No person may operate an aircraft so close to another aircraft as to create a collision hazard.

No person may operate an aircraft in formation flight except by arrangement with the pilot in command of each aircraft in the formation.

No person may operate an aircraft, carrying passengers for hire, in formation flight.

Formation flight is defined as flight in which aircraft maintain close proximity to each other, generally within 1 nautical mile laterally and 100 feet vertically.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.51(e) - Logging PIC Time
14 CFR 61.51 - Required Logging
cards.answer:
A person must document and record the following flight time when used to meet requirements for a certificate, rating, or currency:

• Date
• Total flight or lesson time
• Location (departure and arrival)
• Type and identification of aircraft or training device
• Name of safety pilot, if required

For training received:
• Type of training
• Name of instructor

A pilot must be able to present logbook records to show currency and recent experience requirements are met.

cards.question: FAA-S-ACS-7B - Power-Off 180° Accuracy Approach
cards.answer:
The power-off 180° accuracy approach and landing demonstrates the pilot's ability to establish and maintain a stabilized descent and approach from a point 1,000 feet AGL on downwind, complete a 180° turn, and land at a specified touchdown point.

Objective: Simulate engine failure during the traffic pattern.

Standards:
• Maintain positive aircraft control throughout
• Establish proper configuration (gear down, flaps as needed)
• Touch down at or within 200 feet beyond the specified point
• Complete approach without excessive maneuvering
• Maintain coordination

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Constant-Speed Propeller
cards.answer:
A constant-speed propeller automatically adjusts blade pitch to maintain a selected RPM regardless of aircraft speed or power changes.

Operation:
• Governor senses RPM and adjusts blade pitch
• Higher pitch (coarse) = cruise efficiency, lower RPM
• Lower pitch (fine) = takeoff power, higher RPM

Pilot controls:
• Throttle: Controls manifold pressure (power)
• Propeller control: Sets desired RPM

Power settings:
• Avoid high manifold pressure with low RPM (over-square operation may stress engine)
• Reduce manifold pressure before reducing RPM when reducing power
• Increase RPM before increasing manifold pressure when increasing power

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Fuel Mixture Leaning
cards.answer:
The fuel-air mixture must be adjusted (leaned) at higher altitudes because air density decreases.

Why lean:
• At altitude, less oxygen available per unit volume
• Fixed fuel flow + less air = overly rich mixture
• Rich mixture causes reduced power, fouled spark plugs, excessive fuel consumption

How to lean:
• Slowly reduce mixture until engine RPM peaks (fixed-pitch) or EGT peaks then reduce slightly (if equipped)
• Follow POH procedures

When to lean:
• During cruise at any altitude when less than 75% power
• During ground operations at high elevation airports
• Do NOT lean during takeoff or climb unless specified in POH

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-25 - Dual Ignition System
cards.answer:
Most aircraft piston engines have two separate magneto ignition systems for safety and efficiency.

Safety benefits:
• Redundancy - engine continues if one magneto fails
• Each cylinder has two spark plugs
• Magnetos operate independently of aircraft electrical system

Efficiency benefits:
• Two spark plugs create two flame fronts
• More complete and even combustion
• Increased power output
• Smoother engine operation

Magneto check during runup:
• Typical acceptable drop: 50-175 RPM each magneto
• Maximum differential between magnetos: 50 RPM
• If excessive drop or no drop, do not fly (indicates problem)

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - GUMPS Pre-Landing Checklist
cards.answer:
GUMPS is a pre-landing checklist for complex aircraft:

G - Gas (Fuel selector on proper tank, fuel pump on if required)

U - Undercarriage (Landing gear DOWN and locked, verify 3 green lights)

M - Mixture (Full rich or as required for landing)

P - Propeller (Full forward/high RPM for go-around capability)

S - Switches/Seatbelts (Landing light on, seatbelts/harnesses secured)

Perform on downwind leg and verify on final approach.

Gear-up landings often result from distraction or interrupted checklists.

cards.question: 14 CFR 1.2 - VMC Definition
cards.answer: VMC means minimum control speed with the critical engine inoperative. VMC is indicated by a red radial line on the airspeed indicator. VMC is the calibrated airspeed at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, it is possible to maintain control of the airplane with that engine still inoperative and maintain straight flight with an angle of bank of not more than 5 degrees.

cards.question: 14 CFR 23.149 - VMC Test Conditions
cards.answer: VMC is determined under the following conditions: (1) Maximum available takeoff power on the operating engine(s); (2) The most unfavorable center of gravity; (3) The airplane trimmed for takeoff; (4) In the most critical takeoff configuration; (5) Flaps in takeoff position; (6) Landing gear retracted; (7) Propeller of the inoperative engine in the position it achieves without pilot action, assuming the engine fails while at maximum power.

cards.question: 14 CFR 1.2 - VYSE Definition
cards.answer: VYSE means best rate-of-climb speed with one engine inoperative. VYSE is indicated by a blue radial line on the airspeed indicator (commonly called 'blue line'). This is the speed that provides the best climb performance when operating with one engine inoperative.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - VXSE and VSSE Definitions
cards.answer: VXSE is the best angle-of-climb speed with one engine inoperative. It provides the greatest altitude gain over a given distance during single-engine operations. VSSE is the minimum intentional one-engine-inoperative speed. This is the minimum speed at which intentional engine cuts may be safely performed during training. The purpose of VSSE is to reduce the risk of loss of control due to simulated engine failures during training.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Factors Affecting VMC
cards.answer: VMC increases with: (1) Decrease in weight (lighter aircraft has less inertia to resist yaw); (2) Rearward CG position (reduces rudder effectiveness); (3) Increase in altitude (up to critical density altitude where VMC equals stall speed, then decreases); (4) Increase in power on operative engine; (5) Windmilling propeller on inoperative engine (more drag than feathered); (6) Extended landing gear; (7) Flaps retracted.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Effect of Weight on VMC
cards.answer: VMC increases as weight decreases. A lighter aircraft has less inertia to resist the yawing moment caused by asymmetric thrust. The published VMC is determined at the lightest weight because this represents the most critical condition. At heavier weights, the actual VMC would be lower than published, providing additional safety margin.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Effect of CG on VMC
cards.answer: VMC increases with rearward (aft) center of gravity. An aft CG reduces the moment arm between the rudder and the aircraft CG, reducing rudder effectiveness. More rudder deflection is required to counteract the yawing moment from asymmetric thrust. The published VMC is determined at the most aft CG limit because this represents the most critical condition.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Effect of Altitude on VMC
cards.answer: VMC generally decreases with altitude because engine power decreases with altitude, producing less asymmetric thrust to overcome. However, at some altitude (critical density altitude), VMC equals the stall speed. Above this altitude, the aircraft will stall before reaching VMC. Below this altitude, VMC occurs before stall. This relationship is critical for safety because loss of directional control may occur with little warning.

cards.question: 14 CFR 1.1 - Critical Engine Definition
cards.answer: Critical engine means the engine whose failure would most adversely affect the performance or handling qualities of an aircraft. In most conventional multi-engine aircraft with clockwise-rotating propellers (as viewed from the pilot's seat), the left engine is the critical engine because loss of the left engine results in the greatest adverse effect on aircraft control.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - P-Factor Effect on Critical Engine
cards.answer: P-factor (asymmetric propeller loading) is one of four factors that determine the critical engine. The descending propeller blade has a higher angle of attack and produces more thrust than the ascending blade. On the right engine, this thrust is produced farther from the aircraft centerline, creating a larger yawing moment. When the left engine fails, the right engine's P-factor creates greater yaw than if the right engine failed.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Counter-Rotating Propellers
cards.answer: Aircraft with counter-rotating propellers do not have a critical engine. Counter-rotating propellers rotate in opposite directions (typically left engine clockwise, right engine counterclockwise as viewed from behind). This cancels out the asymmetric effects of P-factor, accelerated slipstream, and spiraling slipstream, making the loss of either engine equally manageable.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Four Factors Affecting Critical Engine
cards.answer: Four aerodynamic factors determine the critical engine: (1) P-factor (asymmetric thrust) - descending blade produces more thrust; (2) Accelerated slipstream - propeller wash accelerates over wing, affecting lift distribution; (3) Spiraling slipstream - propeller wash rotates and impacts vertical stabilizer; (4) Torque reaction - propeller rotation creates rolling tendency opposite to rotation direction.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Zero-Sideslip Technique
cards.answer: Zero-sideslip is the condition where the fuselage is aligned with the relative wind during single-engine operations. This provides optimal single-engine performance by minimizing drag. Zero-sideslip is achieved by banking approximately 2-3 degrees toward the operating engine, with the slip/skid ball displaced approximately one-half ball width toward the operating engine. This technique is sometimes called 'raise the dead' because the wing on the side of the inoperative engine is raised.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Bank and Ball Position
cards.answer: For best single-engine performance with zero-sideslip: Bank 2-3 degrees toward the operating engine; slip/skid ball positioned approximately one-half ball width toward the operating engine. Wings-level single-engine flight results in sideslip toward the operative engine, increasing drag and reducing climb performance. The small bank reduces the sideslip and associated drag.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Identifying the Failed Engine
cards.answer: The failed engine is identified using the 'dead foot, dead engine' technique. When an engine fails, asymmetric thrust causes the aircraft to yaw toward the inoperative engine. The pilot applies rudder pressure toward the operative engine to maintain directional control. The foot that is not applying pressure (dead foot) is on the side of the failed engine.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Verifying the Failed Engine
cards.answer: After identifying the suspected failed engine using 'dead foot, dead engine,' verify the failed engine before feathering: (1) Slowly retard the throttle on the suspected engine; (2) If there is no change in performance, the engine is confirmed inoperative; (3) If performance decreases, the wrong engine was identified - immediately restore power; (4) Only after positive verification should the propeller be feathered and the engine secured.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Immediate Actions After Engine Failure
cards.answer: Immediate actions when an engine fails (memory items): (1) Maintain directional control - apply rudder toward operating engine; (2) Maintain airspeed - pitch for VYSE (blue line); (3) Identify failed engine - 'dead foot, dead engine'; (4) Verify failed engine - throttle check; (5) Feather propeller on failed engine; (6) Bank 2-3 degrees toward operating engine for zero-sideslip; (7) Complete engine securing checklist.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Engine Securing Checklist
cards.answer: After feathering the failed engine propeller: (1) Mixture - idle cutoff; (2) Propeller - feathered (verify); (3) Throttle - closed; (4) Fuel selector - off; (5) Fuel boost pump - off; (6) Magnetos/ignition - off; (7) Alternator/generator - off; (8) Cowl flaps - closed. This sequence reduces fire risk and conserves fuel for the operating engine.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Single-Engine Performance Loss
cards.answer: Loss of one engine in a twin-engine aircraft results in approximately 80 percent loss of climb performance, not 50 percent. The operating engine must: (1) Produce all thrust; (2) Overcome all drag including that from the failed engine; (3) Overcome the adverse yaw from asymmetric thrust. Additionally, drag from windmilling propeller, extended gear, and flaps significantly reduces remaining performance.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Single-Engine Service Ceiling
cards.answer: Single-engine service ceiling is the maximum altitude at which the aircraft can maintain a 50 feet per minute rate of climb with the critical engine feathered, operating engine at maximum continuous power, at best single-engine rate-of-climb speed (VYSE), and at maximum certificated weight. Above this altitude, the aircraft cannot maintain altitude on one engine.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Drag Penalties
cards.answer: Configuration changes significantly affect single-engine climb performance. Typical drag penalties: Windmilling propeller: approximately 200 feet per minute loss; Extended landing gear: approximately 250 feet per minute loss; Full flaps extended: approximately 275 feet per minute loss. These penalties can exceed available single-engine climb performance, making prompt configuration changes critical.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Purpose of Propeller Feathering
cards.answer: Propeller feathering rotates the propeller blades to approximately 90 degrees (edge-on to the relative wind), stopping propeller rotation and minimizing drag. A windmilling propeller produces significant drag (approximately 200 feet per minute climb penalty). Feathering is essential for single-engine performance and is accomplished by moving the propeller control to the feather position or activating the feather button.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Windmilling vs Feathered Propeller
cards.answer: Windmilling propeller: Blades at low pitch angle; propeller continues rotating from airflow; creates significant drag; reduces climb performance by approximately 200 feet per minute. Feathered propeller: Blades rotated to high pitch (edge-on to wind); propeller stopped or slowly rotating; minimal drag; preserves climb performance. Always feather inoperative engine propeller to minimize drag.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Minimum Rotation Speed
cards.answer: The minimum rotation speed (VR) for multi-engine aircraft should be at least VMC plus 5 knots if not published in the POH/AFM. This provides adequate directional control margin if an engine fails at or immediately after rotation. Below this speed, an engine failure during takeoff roll should result in rejected takeoff.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Engine Failure Before VR
cards.answer: If an engine fails before reaching rotation speed (VR), the takeoff must be rejected: (1) Close both throttles immediately; (2) Maintain directional control with rudder and brakes; (3) Bring aircraft to a stop on remaining runway. At speeds below VR, there is insufficient airspeed for directional control in flight with one engine inoperative.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Engine Failure After Liftoff
cards.answer: If an engine fails shortly after liftoff: (1) If gear is not retracted and runway remains, land immediately; (2) If gear is retracted but aircraft cannot climb, maintain control and land on best available surface; (3) If aircraft can climb, maintain VYSE, identify and verify failed engine, feather propeller, establish zero-sideslip bank, and proceed with emergency procedures. The go/no-go decision depends on aircraft performance capability.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Best Single-Engine Climb Speed
cards.answer: After engine failure, maintain VYSE (blue line) for best rate-of-climb performance. VYSE provides the maximum altitude gain per unit of time during single-engine operations. Use VXSE (best angle-of-climb speed) only when obstacle clearance is required, as it provides minimal margin above VMC and higher pilot workload. Once obstacles are cleared, accelerate to VYSE.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Critical Density Altitude
cards.answer: Critical density altitude is the altitude where VMC equals the stall speed. At this altitude and above, the aircraft will stall before reaching VMC. Below critical density altitude, VMC occurs before stall speed, presenting risk of loss of directional control. The relationship between VMC and stall speed varies with altitude due to the effect of air density on both engine power and aerodynamic forces.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Single-Engine Approach Technique
cards.answer: During single-engine approach: (1) Maintain VYSE or higher until landing is assured; (2) Delay gear extension until within gliding distance of runway; (3) Delay flap extension until landing is assured; (4) Maintain a normal approach angle (3 degrees); (5) Anticipate increased rudder pressure changes during flare as power is reduced. Each configuration change reduces climb capability - once committed to land, complete the landing.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Single-Engine Go-Around
cards.answer: A single-engine go-around is extremely hazardous and should be avoided: (1) With gear and flaps extended, climb performance is severely degraded; (2) Drag from extended configuration may exceed available thrust; (3) Directional control becomes difficult at low speeds and high power; (4) Risk of VMC loss at low altitude is high. Once configured for landing on final approach with gear and flaps extended, commit to landing.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.45(d)(3) - Engine Failure Training Limitations
cards.answer: During practical tests or training, engine failure simulation must be performed in accordance with safe practices. In multi-engine airplanes: (1) Simulated engine failures below 3,000 feet AGL should be performed by reducing power only (zero-thrust), not by feathering; (2) No engine failure should be simulated below VSSE; (3) Feathering may only be demonstrated at safe altitude with suitable airport available for single-engine landing.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Single-Engine Stalls Prohibited
cards.answer: Single-engine stalls are not to be performed during training or testing due to extreme hazard. With asymmetric thrust during a stall, strong rolling and yawing moments develop that can result in rapid entry into a spin. Recovery from a spin in a light twin-engine aircraft may be impossible. All stall training in multi-engine aircraft must be conducted with both engines operating.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - VSSE Purpose
cards.answer: VSSE (minimum intentional one-engine-inoperative speed) is the minimum speed at which intentional engine cuts may be performed. It provides a margin above VMC to account for pilot reaction time and engine failure recognition delay. Below VSSE, loss of directional control could occur before the pilot can react to a simulated engine failure. Never simulate engine failure below VSSE.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - VMC Demonstration Procedure
cards.answer: VMC demonstration is performed at safe altitude to show loss of directional control: (1) Establish heading at safe altitude with one engine at idle (simulating failure); (2) Slowly reduce airspeed while maintaining heading with rudder; (3) As speed decreases, more rudder is required; (4) At VMC, full rudder deflection cannot maintain heading; (5) Aircraft yaws toward the inoperative engine; (6) Recovery: reduce power on operating engine and/or lower nose to increase airspeed.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - VMC Recovery
cards.answer: Recovery from VMC demonstration or inadvertent VMC: (1) Immediately reduce power on the operating engine; (2) Simultaneously lower the nose to increase airspeed above VMC; (3) As airspeed increases and control is regained, power may be reapplied; (4) Maintain altitude only after sufficient airspeed is achieved. The priority is regaining directional control - altitude is secondary.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Accelerate-Stop Distance
cards.answer: Accelerate-stop distance is the distance required to: (1) Accelerate the aircraft to lift-off speed; (2) Experience an engine failure; (3) Recognize the failure; (4) Abort the takeoff; (5) Bring the aircraft to a complete stop using brakes. This distance may exceed available runway length, particularly under high density altitude conditions or on short runways. Always verify adequate runway for accelerate-stop before takeoff.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Accelerate-Go Distance
cards.answer: Accelerate-go distance is the distance required to: (1) Accelerate to lift-off speed; (2) Experience an engine failure at the most critical point; (3) Continue the takeoff on one engine; (4) Climb to 50 feet above the surface. This distance may far exceed the normal takeoff distance and may exceed available runway plus obstacle clearance areas. Accelerate-go performance is critical for route planning over mountainous terrain.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Propeller Control System
cards.answer: Most multi-engine aircraft use constant-speed propellers controlled by a governor. The propeller control allows the pilot to select the desired RPM. The feathering system typically uses an auxiliary oil pump or accumulator to drive the blades to the feathered position when oil pressure is lost (engine failure) or when the pilot selects feather. Some aircraft have separate feather buttons for emergency feathering.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Crossfeed System
cards.answer: The fuel crossfeed system allows fuel from tanks on one side of the aircraft to supply the engine on the opposite side. This is useful when: (1) One tank has more fuel than the other (balancing); (2) A fuel system malfunction exists on one side; (3) Operating on one engine and need to access fuel from tanks on the failed engine side. Follow POH procedures carefully when using crossfeed to avoid fuel starvation.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Pitch Change After Engine Failure
cards.answer: When an engine fails, the nose tends to pitch down due to loss of accelerated slipstream over the horizontal stabilizer. The propeller slipstream normally provides additional airflow over the tail, creating a downward force. When this slipstream is lost, the tail rises and the nose drops. Back pressure on the elevator control is required to maintain pitch attitude.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Roll and Yaw After Engine Failure
cards.answer: Engine failure creates immediate roll and yaw: (1) Yaw toward the failed engine due to asymmetric thrust; (2) Roll toward the failed engine due to loss of accelerated slipstream over that wing (reduced lift). The pilot must apply rudder toward the operating engine and use aileron to maintain bank. Without immediate correction, the aircraft will turn toward the failed engine.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.31(e) - Complex Airplane Training
cards.answer: No person may act as pilot in command of a complex airplane (an airplane that has a retractable landing gear, flaps, and a controllable pitch propeller) unless that person has received and logged ground and flight training from an authorized instructor in a complex airplane, or in a flight simulator or flight training device that is representative of a complex airplane, and has been found proficient in the operation and systems of the airplane.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.63(c) - Additional Aircraft Ratings
cards.answer: To add a multiengine class rating to an existing certificate, a person must: (1) Receive the required training and obtain an endorsement from an authorized instructor; (2) Meet the appropriate aeronautical experience requirements; (3) Pass the required practical test. There is no separate knowledge test required for adding a class rating to an existing certificate.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Engine Fire During Flight
cards.answer: For engine fire during flight in multi-engine aircraft: (1) Mixture - idle cutoff (starve the fire); (2) Propeller - feather; (3) Throttle - closed; (4) Fuel selector - off; (5) Fuel boost pump - off; (6) Magnetos - off; (7) Fire extinguisher - if equipped, discharge; (8) Cowl flaps - closed; (9) Airspeed - increase if fire persists (to blow out flames); (10) Prepare for emergency landing if fire not extinguished.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Engine Restart Procedures
cards.answer: If conditions permit, an in-flight engine restart may be attempted after engine failure: (1) Identify and verify cause of failure; (2) If restart is appropriate: Magnetos - on; Fuel selector - appropriate tank; Mixture - rich; Throttle - slightly open; Propeller - full forward (unfeather); (3) If engine starts, verify normal indications; (4) Slowly increase power as engine warms. Do not attempt restart if mechanical failure is suspected or fire has occurred.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.63 - Additional Aircraft Ratings
cards.answer: To add a seaplane class rating to an existing pilot certificate: (1) Receive and log ground and flight training from an authorized instructor on the areas of operation for the seaplane rating sought; (2) Obtain a logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor certifying training completion; (3) Pass a practical test for the certificate level with the seaplane class rating. No separate knowledge test is required when adding a class rating to an existing pilot certificate.

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.31(e) - Complex Airplane Requirement for Seaplanes
cards.answer: For seaplanes, a complex airplane is defined as having flaps and a controllable pitch propeller. The retractable landing gear requirement that applies to landplanes is specifically excluded for seaplanes, recognizing that seaplanes seldom have retractable landing gear. Pilots seeking to act as PIC of a complex seaplane must receive and log ground and flight training and receive a logbook endorsement.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(iii) - Seaplane Exception
cards.answer: During seaplane operations on the water, the seatbelt requirement does not apply to a person pushing off the seaplane or tying it up while the seaplane is being maneuvered at a dock. All other persons aboard must have their seat belt fastened during movement on the surface.

cards.question: 14 CFR 91.115 - Right-of-Way Rules: Water Operations
cards.answer: (a) General: Each person operating an aircraft on the water shall, insofar as possible, keep clear of all vessels and avoid impeding their navigation, and shall give way to any vessel or other aircraft that is given the right-of-way by any rule of this section. (b) Crossing: When aircraft, or an aircraft and a vessel, are on crossing courses, the aircraft or vessel to the other's right has the right-of-way. (c) Approaching head-on: When aircraft, or an aircraft and a vessel, are approaching head-on, or nearly so, each shall alter its course to the right to keep well clear. (d) Overtaking: Each aircraft or vessel that is being overtaken has the right-of-way, and the one overtaking shall alter course to keep well clear. (e) Special circumstances: When aircraft, or an aircraft and a vessel, approach so as to involve risk of collision, each aircraft or vessel shall proceed with careful regard to existing circumstances.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - USCG Navigation Rules
cards.answer: The U.S. Coast Guard definition of 'vessel' includes seaplanes while on the water. Seaplanes must comply with U.S. Coast Guard navigation rules when operating on the water, whether under power or not. Compliance with 14 CFR 91.115 ensures compliance with USCG navigation rules. Pilots should obtain and be familiar with the USCG Navigation Rules (COMDTINST M16672.2 series).

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - Types of Seaplanes
cards.answer: Flying boats (hull seaplanes): The fuselage bottom serves as the primary landing gear. Small floats near the wingtips, called tip floats or sponsons (winglike projections from the hull), provide lateral stability on the water. Floatplanes: Conventional landplanes fitted with floats (pontoons) in place of wheels. The fuselage is supported well above the water surface. Amphibians: Either type equipped with retractable wheels allowing operation on both water and land.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - Float Anatomy
cards.answer: Principal float components: Keel - strong structural member running the length of the float bottom, guides straight-line movement. Step - sharp break in the bottom surface that reduces drag during high-speed operations. Skeg - extension of the keel behind the step that prevents the float from tipping backward when on land. Chine - seam where the float sides join the bottom, guides water away from the float. Deck - top surface of the float providing access to cabin. Spray rails - metal flanges that deflect spray away from the propeller and cabin.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - Purpose of the Step
cards.answer: The step is located slightly behind the aircraft's center of gravity and provides critical hydrodynamic functions: It allows the aircraft to rotate for takeoff by serving as a pivot point. When the aircraft is 'on the step,' only a small portion of the float forward of the step contacts the water, significantly reducing drag. The step breaks the attachment of water flow along the float, preventing the excessive drag that would result if water adhered to the entire float length.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - Float Rating and Buoyancy
cards.answer: Floats are rated by the weight of fresh water they displace. Federal regulations require that floats provide buoyancy equal to 80 percent in excess of the maximum certificated weight of the seaplane. Formula: Total float displacement divided by 1.8 equals maximum seaplane weight. Example: Two floats with combined displacement of 5,000 pounds support a maximum seaplane weight of 2,778 pounds. Each float must have at least four watertight compartments, designed so the seaplane can be supported with any two compartments flooded.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - Water Rudders
cards.answer: Water rudders are retractable steering devices mounted at the rear tip of each float, connected by cables and springs to the rudder pedals. They aid in maneuvering the seaplane on the water surface. Water rudders should be retracted: In shallow water to avoid damage from striking the bottom; when objects may be present under the surface; during takeoff to prevent dynamic water forces from damaging them; during landing to prevent damage from impact forces at touchdown.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - Wave Anatomy
cards.answer: Wave terminology: Crest - the top of a wave. Trough - the low valley between waves. Height - the vertical distance from trough bottom to crest top. Wavelength - the horizontal distance between successive wave crests. Period - the time interval between passage of successive crests past a fixed point. Wind waves (sea) - waves actively being generated by wind. Swell - waves that persist after the wind stops or that have traveled outside the wind generation area.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - Wind Effect on Water
cards.answer: Three factors determine wave height: (1) Wind speed - higher wind speed creates larger waves; (2) Duration - the longer wind acts on the water, the larger the waves; (3) Fetch - the distance over which wind acts on the water surface. Calm water typically shows ripples at approximately 2 knots of wind. Small waves develop at about 4 knots. Waves begin to break and produce whitecaps at approximately 12 knots. Waves form perpendicular to the wind direction.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - Reading Wind from Water Surface
cards.answer: Wind indicators on water: Calm strip - area of smooth water along the upwind shore of a lake where wind has not yet developed waves. Wave direction - waves form perpendicular to the wind direction. Wind streaks - above approximately 8 knots, streaks form on the water parallel to the wind direction. Whitecaps - begin forming at approximately 12 knots. Pilots should check multiple wind indicators as land masses can channel and change wind direction, causing the wind to blow in different directions across a single body of water.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - Glassy Water Operations
cards.answer: Glassy (calm) water presents unique operational challenges: Taxiing and docking are easier without wind effects. Takeoff distances are longer because floats tend to adhere to the smooth water surface and no headwind component assists acceleration. Landing is hazardous because altitude above the featureless surface is extremely difficult to judge, and confusing optical illusions from reflections can disorient pilots. Special glassy water landing techniques must be learned and practiced.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - Tidal Considerations
cards.answer: Tides are the periodic rise and fall of water levels. Rising tide concerns: A beached seaplane may be lifted by rising water and float away if not properly secured. Falling tide concerns: A beached seaplane may be stranded far from the water's edge, unable to be launched until the tide returns. The severity depends on tidal range and beach topography. Always check tide tables when operating in tidal waters and plan accordingly for mooring, anchoring, or beaching operations.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - Seaplane Base Identification
cards.answer: Seaplane landing areas are identified by: Rotating beacon alternating white and yellow lights (at night and during reduced visibility). A double white flash alternating with yellow indicates a military seaplane base. On aeronautical charts, seaplane bases are depicted with a symbol similar to land airports but with an anchor symbol in the center. Tick marks around the symbol indicate availability of fuel and services. A double ring indicates military facilities.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - U.S. Buoyage System
cards.answer: When approaching from seaward (inbound): Left (port) side of channel - Green or black can buoys (cylindrical shape), odd numbers increasing toward shore, keep to your left when heading inland. Right (starboard) side of channel - Red nun buoys (conical shape), even numbers increasing toward shore, keep to your right when heading inland. Memory aid: 'Red, Right, Returning' - keep red buoys to your right when returning to port. Mid-channel buoys have black and white vertical stripes and may use letters starting with 'A' from seaward.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - Junction and Obstruction Buoys
cards.answer: Buoys with red and black horizontal bands mark junctions where waterways fork or indicate wrecks and obstructions. These buoys may be passed on either side. The color of the top band indicates the primary or preferred channel: Black top band - keep buoy to your left when inbound. Red top band - keep buoy to your right when inbound. The shape of the buoy generally matches the top band color (black top = can shape; red top = nun shape).

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - Nighttime Buoy Identification
cards.answer: Lighted buoy identification: Green/black buoys (port side) - green or white lights. Red buoys (starboard side) - red or white lights. Junction buoys - red light if red band on top, green light if black band on top. Mid-channel buoys - white light flashing Morse code 'A' (dot-dash). All colored buoy lights are flashing or occulting (never steady). Unlighted buoys may have reflective material matching the light colors of lighted buoys.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - Effects of Float Installation
cards.answer: Float installation affects aircraft performance and handling: Performance effects - Additional weight decreases useful load; increased drag reduces performance compared to wheel-equipped aircraft; lower cruise speeds; reduced climb performance. Handling effects - Directional stability may be reduced due to float vertical area forward of the CG; auxiliary fin often added to the tail for stability; less aileron may be needed to maintain a slip; rudder pressure may be required to maintain coordination in turns; water rudder cables and springs may affect air rudder streamlining.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - Operational Differences from Landplanes
cards.answer: Key operational differences: No brakes - seaplane is in continuous motion from wind and current effects; engine runup is performed while moving; coasting is used to reach docking points. Weathervaning - strong tendency to turn into the wind, more pronounced than in tailwheel landplanes; water rudders help control during taxiing; presents challenges during crosswind operations. Operational flexibility - pilot can choose takeoff and landing direction (not limited to runway alignment); usually take off directly into wind; must read wind direction from water surface.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - Rough Water Considerations
cards.answer: Rough water (waves from wind 19-24 knots or more for small seaplanes) presents significant hazards: Takeoff - floats subject to hard pounding on wave crests with potential for structural damage; increased takeoff distance; greater pilot workload. Landing - risk of damage from wave impact; difficult to judge height above waves; may need to land parallel to swell if not aligned with wind. Overall - forces can damage aircraft or cause capsizing; pilot must evaluate swell danger versus crosswind limitations; rough water operations should be reserved for emergency situations or conducted only by experienced seaplane pilots.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - Local Regulations
cards.answer: Rules governing where seaplanes may operate are determined by state and local authorities and vary widely by location. Before operating: Contact the state Parks and Wildlife Department; contact the State Aeronautics Department; check with local authorities for specific requirements; consult the Seaplane Pilots Association Water Landing Directory. Always avoid creating a nuisance, especially in congested marine areas, and avoid swimming and boating facilities.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - Seaplane Base Facilities
cards.answer: Seaplane base facilities vary widely: Common facilities include hard surface ramps for launching, servicing facilities (fuel, oil, maintenance), mooring areas, and hangar space. Information sources include aeronautical charts, Airport/Facility Directory, and boat marinas that may provide seaplane facilities. Bush operations - in remote areas, regular facilities are often limited or nonexistent; servicing becomes the pilot's responsibility; terrain and waterways are frequently hazardous; pilots should seek advice from experienced local operators.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - Water Traffic Hazards
cards.answer: Hazards from water traffic: Unpredictable craft - speedboats and personal watercraft move erratically; boat operators towing skiers may not notice landing seaplanes; swimmers are nearly invisible among waves. Lack of awareness - no equivalent of airport traffic pattern exists; many boaters are unaware of right-of-way rules; boaters may not understand seaplane maneuverability limitations and often assume seaplanes will avoid them. Curiosity - seaplanes attract interested onlookers, creating additional traffic around operations. Pilots must maintain constant vigilance and anticipate unpredictable movements.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - Water Drag Characteristics
cards.answer: Water drag characteristics differ significantly from land operations: Drag varies with the square of speed (doubling speed quadruples drag force). Unlike land operations where friction occurs only at tire contact points, water forces act along the entire float or hull length. These forces vary with pitch attitude and change constantly with wave action. No shock absorption exists (unlike landing gear), so water forces transmit directly through floats and struts to the airframe. Although water appears soft, it can transmit damaging forces.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - Buoyancy vs Hydrodynamic Lift
cards.answer: Two types of water support: Buoyancy (low speed) - the entire float length supports aircraft weight by displacing water equal to the aircraft's weight; this is the static floating condition. Hydrodynamic lift (higher speed) - upward force generated by motion through water allows the aircraft to rise higher in the water, reducing the wetted surface area. 'On the step' - the optimum balance of lift and drag; only a small portion of the float forward of the step contacts the water; the aft portion is clear of the water; minimizes drag while maintaining support; requires proper pitch attitude.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - High-Mounted Engine Effects
cards.answer: Some seaplanes (particularly amphibious hull types) have engines mounted above the fuselage, placing the thrust line well above the center of drag. This configuration produces handling characteristics opposite to normal aircraft: Applying power causes the nose to pitch down; reducing power causes the nose to pitch up. This affects both water and air operations and can lead to unexpected pitch changes. Pilots must receive additional training specific to this configuration before operating such aircraft.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - Inland vs International Waters
cards.answer: Inland waters are located inshore of the boundary line, which is marked by the outermost buoys and runs approximately parallel to shore. Seaplanes operating in inland waters must follow the Inland Rules (Pilot Rules). International waters (high seas) are located outside the boundary line. Seaplanes operating in international waters must follow the International Rules of the Sea and must carry a current copy of these rules aboard. Both sets of rules are USCG regulations that apply to seaplanes.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-23 - Conventional Inbound Direction
cards.answer: For waterways parallel to the coast where no obvious inbound/outbound direction exists, a conventional direction is established (clockwise around the continental United States): East Coast - southbound is considered inbound (red buoys on right when heading south). Gulf Coast - westbound is considered inbound (red buoys on right when heading west). West Coast - northbound is considered inbound (red buoys on right when heading north). Memory aid: Traveling clockwise around the contiguous states is considered 'inbound.'

cards.question: 14 CFR 61.31(i) - Additional Training: Tailwheel Airplanes
cards.answer: No person may act as pilot in command of a tailwheel airplane unless that person has received and logged flight training from an authorized instructor in a tailwheel airplane and received an endorsement in the person's logbook that the person is proficient in the operation of a tailwheel airplane. The flight training must include at least the following maneuvers and procedures: (1) Normal and crosswind takeoffs and landings; (2) Wheel landings (unless the manufacturer has recommended against such landings); and (3) Go-around procedures.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Conventional Landing Gear Configuration
cards.answer: In the tailwheel-type (conventional) landing gear, the main wheels are located forward of the center of gravity, and a small wheel or skid supports the tail of the airplane. The tailwheel is primarily for steering and directional control during taxiing. The term 'conventional gear' reflects historical usage when this configuration was the standard aircraft design, even though tricycle gear is more common today.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Key Handling Differences from Tricycle Gear
cards.answer: Three major handling differences exist: (1) Directional instability - the center of gravity behind the main wheels creates inherent ground instability; turns continue to tighten without opposite rudder input. (2) Built-in angle of attack - the nose-high attitude creates lift on the wings even while on the ground with a headwind, making the flight controls active during taxi. (3) Crosswind weathervaning - the exaggerated tendency to turn into the wind due to greater surface area behind the main gear. Tailwheel aircraft are less forgiving of pilot error on the ground than nosewheel aircraft.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Cause of Directional Instability
cards.answer: Tailwheel aircraft are directionally unstable on the ground because the center of gravity is located behind the main wheels. When a turn begins, the aircraft pivots on one main wheel. With the CG aft of this pivot point, forward momentum acts to continue and tighten the turn. Unlike nosewheel aircraft, releasing the rudder does not stop the turn - opposite rudder is required to return to straight travel. Taxi and turn at slow speeds to prevent serious problems and allow time for corrections.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Proper Turning Technique
cards.answer: The proper technique for making turns while taxiing: (1) Apply rudder pressure to initiate the turn; (2) Neutralize the pedals as the turn continues; (3) Apply opposite rudder to stop the turn and regain straight travel. This differs from nosewheel aircraft where maintaining rudder pressure tightens the turn as expected. In tailwheel aircraft, maintaining rudder causes the turn to tighten unexpectedly. This technique becomes natural with practice.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Ground Loop
cards.answer: A ground loop is an uncontrolled turn that occurs during taxi, takeoff, or landing roll. Causes include: a swerve allowed to continue too long; side-load on landing; taxi turn at excessive speed; overcorrection; uneven ground or soft spot. Dangers: Forces accumulate as the fuselage angle increases relative to the direction of travel; the airplane can tip until a wing strikes the ground; sideward forces may collapse the landing gear. Prevention: Counter swerves with firm rudder; use differential braking when needed; remove inputs promptly when correction begins; avoid turns at high speed.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Tailwheel Steering Mechanism
cards.answer: Most tailwheels are steerable through approximately 30 degrees each side of center and operate with rudder pedal input for normal turns. Beyond approximately 30 degrees, the tailwheel enters full swivel mode, allowing the airplane to pivot within its own length for tight maneuvering. Braking technique: Test brakes immediately when starting to taxi; apply power to start moving; retard throttle and apply both brakes smoothly; shut down if braking is unsatisfactory. Keep feet on rudder pedals and slide up to brakes only when needed.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Control Position in Quartering Headwind
cards.answer: When taxiing in a quartering headwind: Aileron - hold the control stick into the wind to reduce lift on the upwind wing and prevent the wind from lifting it. This is more critical than in nosewheel aircraft due to the built-in angle of attack. Elevator - usually hold full back to add downward pressure on the tailwheel, improving steering response. Exception: In strong quartering headwinds, holding full back elevator may allow the wind to lift the upwind wing; the elevator may need to be held closer to neutral.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Control Position in Quartering Tailwind
cards.answer: When taxiing in a quartering tailwind: Aileron - hold the stick away from the crosswind (left aileron in a right quartering tailwind). Elevator - position depends on wind strength. In strong tailwinds: full forward stick is essential as the tailwind acting on the down-deflected elevator increases downward pressure, preventing the tail from lifting and the propeller from striking the ground. In light tailwinds: propeller wash may create a net headwind over the tail, so back stick helps directional control. Test the wind and position controls where they help most.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Forward Visibility Limitations
cards.answer: The nose-high attitude of tailwheel aircraft restricts forward visibility. The engine cowling may completely block the view directly ahead, making objects in front of the aircraft difficult or impossible to see. Technique: Before starting taxi movement, make a small turn to ensure no aircraft or vehicle is under the nose. While taxiing, alternately turn the nose side to side (zigzag) or make a series of short S-turns to clear the area ahead. Perform these maneuvers slowly, smoothly, and positively.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Weathervaning Tendency
cards.answer: Weathervaning (the tendency to turn into the wind) is more pronounced in tailwheel aircraft because of greater surface area behind the main landing gear. The main wheels act as a pivot point, and wind pushing against the larger rear surface turns the airplane into the wind. Weathervaning is greatest during direct crosswind conditions. Control may require differential braking when tailwheel steering is inadequate. Maintain constant awareness of wind direction and anticipate the weathervaning tendency.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Critical Principle of Rudder Use
cards.answer: The most important principle regarding rudder use: Tailwheel aircraft are not damaged from too much rudder, but from rudder inputs held too long. Vigorous rudder inputs are sometimes required, and pilots should not fear using full rudder when needed. The problem is holding inputs after they have begun working. Remove inputs promptly when the correction begins to take effect. Limiting rudder use from fear of overcontrolling is incorrect; the risk is holding corrections too long.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Normal Takeoff Procedure
cards.answer: Normal takeoff procedure: Lower flaps if recommended; align with takeoff direction; center and lock tailwheel if so equipped; release brakes; smoothly advance to takeoff power; avoid brake pressure during roll. Tail lift: After brief acceleration, apply positive forward elevator pressure to smoothly lift the tail and improve visibility; achieve a pitch attitude that allows smooth transition to climb attitude; avoid abrupt pitch change (causes left yaw from gyroscopic precession). As speed increases: gradually reduce elevator deflection; maintain constant pitch attitude; use smooth, prompt, positive rudder corrections.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Gyroscopic Precession During Takeoff
cards.answer: When the tail is raised during takeoff, the nose-down pitch change tilts the propeller axis. Due to gyroscopic precession, this creates a left yawing moment. The amount of yaw is related to the rate of pitch change - a faster tail raise produces more yaw. Correction: Anticipate with right rudder pressure; lift the tail smoothly to minimize the yaw; avoid abrupt pitch changes. This effect occurs with any pitch change when the propeller is spinning and emphasizes the increased directional control demands of tailwheel aircraft.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Liftoff Technique
cards.answer: Proper liftoff technique: Maintain a constant pitch attitude throughout the takeoff roll. Liftoff occurs naturally when angle of attack combined with airspeed produces sufficient lift. No additional 'rotation' input is needed if the proper attitude is maintained. The ideal attitude requires only minimum pitch adjustment after liftoff. Three-point liftoff: While possible (the angle of attack with all wheels on the ground does not exceed the critical angle of attack), it results in a pitch attitude excessively close to stall and is inadvisable when flying inches above the ground. In gusty winds, add extra speed margin before liftoff.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Crosswind Takeoff Technique
cards.answer: Crosswind takeoff technique: Before liftoff - hold aileron into the wind to prevent the upwind wing from rising; apply rudder as needed to prevent weathervaning; establish corrections from the start of the takeoff roll. The tail-low attitude allows the wings to generate lift during the ground roll, and strong upwind aileron banks the aircraft into the wind, providing crosswind correction. The takeoff roll may be made primarily on the upwind main wheel. Use rudder to maintain longitudinal axis alignment with the runway. As speed increases, smoothly decrease pitch attitude and adjust aileron and rudder pressures. After liftoff, level the wings and establish appropriate drift correction (crab).

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Short-Field Takeoff Technique
cards.answer: Short-field takeoff technique is generally similar to the normal takeoff with these exceptions: Configure flaps as recommended by the manufacturer; use appropriate initial climb speed for obstacle clearance; adjust pitch after liftoff as needed for obstacle clearance. Some high-power tailwheel aircraft manufacturers recommend a three-point liftoff for short-field operations. Always review and follow the procedures specified in the Pilot's Operating Handbook for the specific aircraft.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Soft-Field Takeoff Technique
cards.answer: Soft-field takeoff procedure: Lower flaps if recommended to transfer weight to the wings; taxi onto the soft surface without stopping to avoid bogging down; keep in continuous motion while aligning for takeoff; hold full up elevator while taxiing to counteract high power settings and prevent nosing over. Takeoff: Align with intended path; apply power smoothly and rapidly; keep the tail very low to maintain a positive angle of attack and minimize drag from surface irregularities and adhesion; the wings progressively relieve the wheels of weight. After liftoff, remain in ground effect while accelerating to climb speed.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Differences from Nosewheel Landing
cards.answer: Key landing differences: In nosewheel aircraft, touchdown is followed by pitch reduction to contact the nosewheel, reducing angle of attack and rapidly transferring weight to the tires. In tailwheel aircraft, this reduction of angle of attack is not practical - it is rare for the wings to exceed the critical angle of attack in the three-point attitude. The airplane continues to 'fly' after touchdown, requiring careful attention for an extended period. The pilot must manage heading, roll, and pitch throughout the landing roll. Two landing techniques are used: three-point landing and wheel landing. Tailwheel aircraft are less forgiving of crosswind alignment errors than nosewheel aircraft.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Touchdown Alignment
cards.answer: At touchdown, the aircraft's longitudinal axis must be parallel to its direction of movement. The aircraft must not touch down while in a crab or while drifting sideways. Consequences of misalignment: Side loads are imposed on the landing gear; directional instability develops; ground loop may result; landing gear may collapse. Prevention: Eliminate crab before touchdown; eliminate drift before touchdown; use the slip (wing-low) technique for crosswind landings; precise alignment is essential. Tailwheel aircraft are much less forgiving of alignment errors than nosewheel aircraft.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Three-Point Landing Technique
cards.answer: Three-point landing technique: The main gear and tailwheel touch the runway simultaneously. The aircraft is held off until its attitude matches the landing gear geometry. Technique: Arrive on approach with proper airspeed, alignment, and configuration; round out approximately 1 foot above the surface; gently increase angle of attack to maintain flight while slowing; achieve a much steeper fuselage angle than in nosewheel aircraft; touch all three wheels simultaneously. After touchdown: Further pitch increase is impossible with the tailwheel on the ground; the airplane remains on the runway tenuously; weight shifts from wings to wheels with deceleration. Hold full back elevator after the tailwheel contacts the ground.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Three-Point Landing Errors
cards.answer: Common errors and recovery: Error 1 - Main wheels touch early with tail still up: The tail drops when main wheels contact, increasing angle of attack; the airplane may become airborne again (skip). Recovery: Re-flare and hold off until three-point attitude; if skip is large, execute a go-around. Error 2 - Held off too long with too steep attitude: The tail contacts first; if from one foot or less, the event is undramatic; the airplane pitches forward slightly onto the main wheels; rollout proceeds normally. After any touchdown: Immediately ease the elevator fully back to press the tailwheel onto the runway, prevent the horizontal stabilizer from lifting the tail, and maintain directional control. This is very different from nosewheel technique.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Wheel Landing Technique
cards.answer: Wheel landing technique: Contact the runway at higher airspeed than in a three-point landing, with a flatter pitch attitude, on the main wheels only (tailwheel remains airborne). When used: Wind conditions require more control authority; need higher speed for adequate control; many pilots prefer wheel landings in crosswinds because the higher touchdown speed keeps controls more effective. Technique: A soft touchdown is essential; immediately after wheels touch, slightly relax back elevator pressure to prevent the tail from dropping (which would cause a skip); allow the tail to lower on its own; when the tail contacts the runway, move the elevator to the full aft position; deceleration proceeds as in a three-point landing.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Bounced Wheel Landing Recovery
cards.answer: A bounced wheel landing occurs when touchdown is made at too high a descent rate. When the airplane bounces, the tail is forced down by its own weight, suddenly increasing angle of attack and lift. Danger: If the pilot pushes forward to force contact with the runway, pilot-induced oscillation can develop and become dangerous. Recovery options: (1) Initiate a go-around; or (2) Convert to a three-point landing if conditions permit. Never push forward to force contact after a bounce. The only difference between a wheel landing and a three-point landing is the timing of touchdown (earlier versus later in the flare).

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Crosswind Landing Technique
cards.answer: The preferred crosswind landing technique is the side-slip (wing-low) touchdown. This method eliminates crab and drift at touchdown. Only one main wheel makes initial contact with either the tailwheel (three-point) or alone (wheel landing). Many pilots prefer wheel landings in crosswinds because the higher touchdown speed keeps the flight controls more effective. In some aircraft, the rudder may be partially blocked by the fuselage or flaps when in a tail-low attitude. It is highly desirable to eliminate all crab and drift; touchdown must be aligned with direction of movement to prevent side loads and directional instability.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - After-Landing Roll Procedure
cards.answer: After-landing roll procedure: Elevator - hold the control as far back as possible and as firmly as possible; maintain until the airplane stops; this provides positive tailwheel steering control, tends to shorten the landing roll, and prevents bouncing and skipping. Directional control - be alert for control difficulties immediately after touchdown; any drift or crab produces a turning moment about the main wheel contact point; the airplane tends to swerve, which can lead to a ground loop. Braking - slide feet up to brake pedals when needed; maintain rudder pressure while moving to brakes; use carefully to avoid overcontrolling. The landing is not complete until the aircraft reaches taxi speed or stops.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Crosswind After-Landing Roll
cards.answer: During crosswind after-landing roll: Rudder and tailwheel steering maintain directional control and counter the weathervaning tendency. Aileron prevents the upwind wing from rising; apply more aileron as speed decreases because ailerons become less effective and the relative wind becomes more crosswind, creating greater lifting force on the upwind wing; when stopping, hold aileron fully into the wind. Weathervaning is greater in tailwheel aircraft because of the larger profile/side area behind the main gear. The main wheels act as a pivot point, and greater surface area behind the pivot produces stronger weathervaning. Pilots must know the demonstrated crosswind component of their aircraft and avoid winds exceeding capability or personal limits.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Short-Field Landing Technique
cards.answer: Short-field landing technique: Touch down firmly holding the airplane in the three-point attitude to provide aerodynamic braking from the wings. Immediately after touchdown, close the throttle and apply brakes evenly and firmly to minimize the after-landing roll. The goal is to stop within the shortest possible distance consistent with safety. The three-point attitude maximizes aerodynamic drag to assist deceleration.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Soft-Field Landing Technique
cards.answer: Soft-field landing technique: Touch down with the tailwheel contacting simultaneously with or just before the main wheels; hold the tailwheel down with firm back-elevator pressure throughout the rollout. This minimizes the tendency to nose over and provides aerodynamic braking. Braking is typically not needed on soft fields because the soft or rough surface provides sufficient deceleration. Power may need to be increased to keep the aircraft moving and prevent becoming stuck in the soft surface. The tailwheel-first or simultaneous touchdown prevents nosing over on soft terrain.

cards.question: FAA-H-8083-3 - Critical Transition Skills
cards.answer: Critical skills for transitioning to tailwheel aircraft: Rudder control - proper techniques are essential; use vigorous inputs when needed; remove inputs promptly; do not fear using full rudder - the problem is holding too long, not using too much. Speed management - slow taxi speeds prevent serious problems; slow turns are essential; allow time for corrections. Anticipation - understand the inherent instability; counter swerves early; anticipate weathervaning; plan for gyroscopic precession. Alignment - critical during landing; touchdown must be aligned with direction of movement; no tolerance for crab or drift. With proper rudder control technique, pilots transition successfully to tailwheel aircraft.

cards.question: What is human behavior?
cards.answer:
• The product of factors that cause people to act in predictable ways
• The result of attempts to satisfy certain needs
• Understanding human behavior leads to successful instruction

cards.question: How does the instructor–learner relationship affect learning?
cards.answer:
• Differences in personality affect both the learner's style of learning and the instructor's style of teaching
• Learning goes best when the styles align
• A good instructor adapts their teaching style to the needs of each individual learner

cards.question: What is motivation, and how should an instructor use it?
cards.answer:
Motivation: the reason one acts or behaves in a certain way; it lies at the heart of goals. It can be positive or negative, tangible or intangible.

Instructors should:
• Ask new learners about their aviation training goals
• Reward successes, both small and large
• Present new challenges as the learner progresses
• Remind learners of their own stated goals
• Make sure learners understand plateaus are normal and can be overcome

cards.question: List Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs (PS BECS).
cards.answer:
P – Physiological: air, food, water, sleep (fatigue)
S – Safety/Security: learner needs to feel safe, even in the airplane with the instructor
B – Belonging: affection, friendship, being part of a group (emotional safety)
E – Esteem: self-confidence and respect from others; wanting to feel valued
C – Cognitive & Aesthetic: the need to know and understand; the need to "like" something
S – Self-Actualization: realizing your full potential, doing what you were "born to do"

cards.question: Name the defense mechanisms (DR DR FCPR) with an example of each.
cards.answer:
D – Denial: refusing to accept reality ("I didn't do that")
R – Repression: pushing uncomfortable thoughts into the unconscious (fear of heights hinders learning to fly)
D – Displacement: shifting an emotion to a less threatening target (angry at instructor, "kicks the dog")
R – Reaction Formation: faking a belief opposite to the true one because it causes anxiety ("steep turns are easy")
F – Fantasy: daydreaming about how things should be ("once I'm at the airlines I won't have to worry")
C – Compensation: disguising a weakness by emphasizing strengths (great stalls, ignoring poor lazy eights)
P – Projection: blaming others for your own shortcomings ("I failed because the DPE was unfair")
R – Rationalization: a plausible, acceptable excuse for otherwise unacceptable actions

cards.question: How should an instructor handle learner anxiety?
cards.answer:
Anxiety: a feeling of worry, nervousness, or unease, often about something about to happen.

Do: reassure the learner that anxiety is normal, that they are well-prepared, and that you'll be proud of them if they do their best.
Don't: say "just relax" or "calm down."

cards.question: Normal vs. abnormal reactions to stress (PRESIM)?
cards.answer:
Normal: stress can improve performance; the learner responds quickly and precisely, within the limits of training.

Abnormal (PRESIM):
P – Painstaking self-control
R – Rapid changes in emotions
E – Extreme over-cooperation
S – Severe anger toward the instructor, service personnel, and others
I – Inappropriate reactions (laughter, singing)
M – Marked changes in mood on different lessons

cards.question: How can an instructor deal with impatience and with worry/lack of interest?
cards.answer:
Impatience: the learner wants to do things they aren't ready for. Clearly explain the goals and reasons for each step of training.

Worry / lack of interest: tailor instruction to the learner's interests as much as possible, and prevent worry by being transparent about objectives and progress.

cards.question: What are the signs of fatigue in a learner?
cards.answer:
• Inattention
• Distractibility
• Errors in timing
• Neglect of secondary tasks
• Irritability
• Loss of accuracy and control
• Lack of awareness of error accumulation

Physical discomfort, illness, fatigue, and dehydration all inhibit learning.

cards.question: What causes apathy due to inadequate instruction?
cards.answer:
Learners who lose confidence in their instructor won't learn as well, and that confidence is hard to regain. Causes:
• Poor preparation or presentation
• Material that's too complicated or too simple
• Distracting mannerisms
• Untidiness
• Expressing annoyance with the learner

cards.question: What should you know about teaching the adult learner?
cards.answer:
• Average aviation learner is about 30 years old
• Adults are typically more self-motivated
• They want more control over lesson pace — respect their need for autonomy
• Adults particularly like syllabi

cards.question: What are the basic elements of communication (SSR)?
cards.answer:
S – Source: the sender, speaker, writer, or instructor
S – Symbols: the words or signs used to compose and transmit the message
R – Receiver: the listener, reader, or learner

cards.question: What are the barriers to effective communication (COIL)?
cards.answer:
C – Confusion between the symbol and the symbolized object ("yoke" vs. "yolk")
O – Overuse of abstractions ("bring the nose to the horizon" — not specific enough)
I – Interference: physiological, environmental, or psychological factors outside the instructor's control (bathroom break, turbulence, external pressures at home)
L – Lack of common experience (age or flight-hour differences)

cards.question: How does an instructor develop communication skills (LIQIR)?
cards.answer:
L – Listening
I – Instructional communication: instruction has taken place when the instructor explains a procedure and then determines the learner exhibits the desired response
Q – Questioning
I – Instructional enhancement (continuing education)
R – Role playing

cards.question: What is learning?
cards.answer: A change in behavior as a result of experience.

cards.question: Name the learning theories (BICC).
cards.answer:
B – Behaviorism: behavior explained by observable, measurable responses to stimuli (Pavlov's dog; positive stimuli → positive result)
I – Information Processing: the mind as a computer — encoding, retaining, and retrieving information (sensory → short-term → long-term memory)
C – Cognitive Theory: focuses on what is going on inside the mind
C – Constructivism: learners don't acquire knowledge passively; they actively build it from their experiences

cards.question: What factors affect perception (G STEP)?
cards.answer:
G – Goals and values: how you see the world; things valued highly are pursued
S – Self-concept: what learners think about themselves
T – Time and opportunity: understanding may come later (performing a stall before really understanding it)
E – Element of threat: narrows the perceptual field
P – Physical organism: must be able to see, hear, feel, and respond

Insight: grouping perceptions into meaningful wholes (understanding) — insights become "building blocks."

cards.question: What are the steps of acquiring knowledge (MUC)?
cards.answer:
M – Memorization: facts, procedure steps, checklists
U – Understanding: organizing memorized facts in useful ways
C – Concept learning: grouping things that share major attributes; used to solve problems and make decisions

cards.question: State the laws of learning (REEPIR).
cards.answer:
R – Readiness: basic needs satisfied, a clear reason to learn; "teachable moments"
E – Effect: learning is strengthened by a pleasant, satisfying outcome (and weakened by an unpleasant one)
E – Exercise: things most often repeated are best remembered
P – Primacy: what's learned first is remembered best — teach it right the first time
I – Intensity: a vivid, exciting experience is learned better than a routine one
R – Recency: what's learned most recently is best remembered

cards.question: What are the three domains of learning (CAP)?
cards.answer:
