C – Cognitive: knowledge and thinking (Rote → Understanding → Application → Correlation)
A – Affective: how a person feels (Awareness → Response → Value → Organization → Integration)
P – Psychomotor: physical skills (Observation → Imitation → Practice → Habit)

cards.question: What are the four levels of the cognitive domain (RUAC)?
cards.answer:
R – Rote: can repeat back what was learned; can't apply it
U – Understanding: can explain it; puts two or more concepts together
A – Application: can apply it to the scenario that was taught (most instructors incorrectly stop teaching here)
C – Correlation: can apply it to new and different scenarios

cards.question: What are the five levels of the affective domain (ARVOI)?
cards.answer:
A – Awareness: willing to pay attention; mentally open to learning
R – Response: reacts, complies, actively participates
V – Value: accepts and sees value in the learning
O – Organization: organizes the training into their personal belief system
I – Integration (characterization): incorporates the value into their life

cards.question: What are the four levels of the psychomotor domain (OIPH)?
cards.answer:
O – Observation: watching the instructor demonstrate the maneuver
I – Imitation: performing the maneuver after the demonstration
P – Practice: repeating it to improve
H – Habit: muscle memory — performs it automatically

cards.question: What are the characteristics of learning (PEAM)?
cards.answer:
P – Purposeful: learners learn on purpose, according to their own goals
E – Result of Experience: learning comes from individual experience (only doing ground lessons ≠ learning to fly)
A – Active process: participating beats watching
M – Multifaceted: engages the mind, feelings, and physical skills at once

cards.question: What is scenario-based training, and what makes a good scenario?
cards.answer:
SBT uses real-world scenarios to engage higher-order thinking skills (ADM in aviation). SBT (HIC):
H – Has a clear set of objectives
I – Is tailored to the learner's needs
C – Capitalizes on the local environment

A good scenario:
• Is not a test
• Has no single correct answer
• Doesn't offer an obvious answer
• Engages all three learning domains
• Is interactive
• Does not promote errors
• Promotes situational awareness and decision-making
• Requires time-pressured decisions

cards.question: What are the stages of acquiring a skill (CAA)?
cards.answer:
C – Cognitive: no prior knowledge; memorizes the steps; needs full attention — teach with a clear step-by-step example
A – Associative: practice coordinates muscles with senses; verbal instruction becomes more meaningful; better with distractions
A – Automatic: a by-product of practice; performs the skill while handling other tasks — when it "clicks"

cards.question: What are knowledge of results and learning plateaus?
cards.answer:
Knowledge of results: learners should understand their own progress — show them the standards and repeat demonstrations as needed.

Learning plateau: a point (usually after the initial spike in proficiency) where progress seems to stop. Reassure the learner it's normal. Often caused by over-practice; fix by temporarily moving to another subject or better explaining the objectives.

cards.question: What are the types of practice (DBR)?
cards.answer:
D – Deliberate: aimed at a specific goal or weakness, with specific feedback — best for perfecting one part of a skill
B – Blocked: the same task over and over until it's automatic — good short-term, poor long-term
R – Random: mixes skills throughout the session — best for long-term retention

cards.question: Define distraction, interruption, fixation, and inattention.
cards.answer:
Distraction: an unexpected event that momentarily diverts the learner's attention
Interruption: an unexpected event for which the learner voluntarily suspends one task to complete another
Fixation: becoming absorbed in one task to the exclusion of others
Inattention: failing to pay attention to an important task

cards.question: What's the difference between a slip and a mistake?
cards.answer:
Slip: you plan to do one thing but inadvertently do another (plan to land on the runway, land on the taxiway)
Mistake: you plan to do the wrong thing and succeed at it (plan to land on the taxiway, land on the taxiway)

cards.question: How can errors be reduced (DR CULT)?
cards.answer:
D – Developing routines (standard procedures)
R – Raising awareness of where errors are known to happen
C – Checking for errors
U – Using reminders (out of sight, out of mind)
L – Learning and practicing (higher skill reduces errors)
T – Taking time (a comfortable pace)

cards.question: Describe the types of memory (SSL).
cards.answer:
S – Sensory memory: receives initial stimuli; selective; holds info only a few seconds
S – Short-term memory: about 30 seconds; limited to roughly 7 "chunks"
L – Long-term memory: relatively permanent, unlimited storage; usually has significance attached

Usage: knowledge not used frequently and recently tends to be forgotten. Knowledge used recently but not frequently fades faster than knowledge used frequently but not recently.

cards.question: What causes forgetting (RIFRS)?
cards.answer:
R – Retrieval failure: can't retrieve the information
I – Interference: learning similar topics interferes
F – Fading: information not used for a period of time
R – Repression: unconsciously pushing away memories with unpleasant feelings
S – Suppression: consciously pushing away memories with unpleasant feelings

cards.question: What aids retention of learning (MR LAMP)?
cards.answer:
M – Meaningful repetition aids recall
R – Recall is prompted by association
L – Learning with all the senses is most effective
A – Attitudes that are favorable aid retention
M – Mnemonics (acronyms, acrostics, rhymes, chaining)
P – Praise stimulates recall

cards.question: What are the four types of mnemonics (AARC)?
cards.answer:
A – Acronyms (e.g., ANDS)
A – Acrostics (a phrase or poem built from first letters)
R – Rhymes
C – Chaining (a story where each word cues the next)

cards.question: What is transfer of learning?
cards.answer:
Positive transfer: learning one thing helps in learning another (rectangular course → traffic pattern)
Negative transfer: learning one thing hinders learning another

cards.question: Evaluation vs. critique as a learner progresses?
cards.answer: When introducing new skills, the instructor evaluates and gives feedback. As the learner progresses, they should learn to self-critique and recognize what improvements are needed.

cards.question: What are the four steps of the teaching process (PPAR)?
cards.answer:
P – Preparation
P – Presentation
A – Application
R – Review and Evaluation (assessment)

cards.question: What are the essential teaching skills (PAMS)?
cards.answer:
P – People skills: relate well to people
A – Assessment skills: before, during, and after training
M – Management skills: plan, organize, lead, supervise
S – Subject matter expertise

cards.question: What is a course of training, and what are objectives vs. completion standards?
cards.answer:
Course of training: a complete series of lessons leading to a specific goal; usually has a syllabus, and each lesson has a lesson plan.

Objectives: the desired outcomes of a lesson or course.
Completion standards: the specific requirements that must be met to complete the lesson.
Lessons should include ADM and risk management.

cards.question: What are the three elements of a performance-based objective?
cards.answer:
1. Description of the skill or behavior
2. Conditions
3. Criteria

Performance-based objectives set measurable, reasonable standards for the learner's desired performance.

cards.question: Why is the ACS important in training, and what are decision-based objectives?
cards.answer:
ACS: gives instructors and examiners performance-based objectives. Teach ACS maneuvers using scenario-based training — don't just teach "to the ACS."

Decision-based objectives: develop pilot judgment and ADM. Once maneuvers are learned, use them in realistic scenarios to build ADM and risk management skills.

cards.question: How is lesson material organized (IDC / AMO)?
cards.answer:
I – Introduction (AMO):
  A – Attention (a story or video clip)
  M – Motivation (why it matters)
  O – Overview (objectives and key ideas)
D – Development:
  • Past to present
  • Simple to complex (e.g., airspace)
  • Known to unknown (rectangular course → traffic pattern)
  • Most frequently used to least (GPS, then VOR, then NDB)
C – Conclusion: retraces the important elements

cards.question: What are the parts of a lesson plan (OEEISC)?
cards.answer:
O – Objective
E – Elements (content)
E – Equipment
I – Instructor actions
S – Student actions
C – Completion standards

cards.question: What are the characteristics of a well-planned lesson?
cards.answer:
• Unity — it all flows together
• Scope — tailored to one topic
• Practicality — reasonable for the learner's knowledge
• Flexibility — easily adjusted to different learners
• Relation to the course of training
• Contains the four instructional steps (preparation, presentation, application, review & evaluation)

cards.question: List the training delivery methods (LGECCDD).
cards.answer:
L – Lecture
G – Guided discussion
E – e-Learning
C – Cooperative or group learning
C – Computer-assisted learning
D – Demonstration-performance
D – Drill and practice

cards.question: What are the types of lectures (IBFIT)?
cards.answer:
I – Illustrated talk: relies on visual aids
B – Briefing: concise presentation of facts
F – Formal lecture: no learner interaction
I – Informal lecture: some learner interaction
T – Teaching lecture: lots of learner interaction

Lectures are most effective with instructional aids and training devices.

cards.question: Lecture method: pros, cons, and best delivery?
cards.answer:
Good for: introducing new material, summarizing ideas, relating theory to practice.
Pros: teaches many at once, presents many ideas quickly, most economical, supplements other material.
Cons: hard to tell if everyone understands; no feedback on learner progress; poor for learning large amounts quickly.

Delivery types: manuscript, memorized, extemporaneous from an outline (preferred), impromptu.
Language: simple; avoid epithets; explain technical terms; be specific.

cards.question: What is a guided discussion, and what makes an effective discussion question?
cards.answer:
Guided discussion: learner-driven; requires some prior knowledge; the instructor guides with questions.

Effective question:
• Has a specific purpose
• Is clear in meaning
• Contains a single idea
• Stimulates thought
• Requires a definite answer
• Relates to previously covered information

cards.question: What are the steps of the demonstration-performance method (EDSIE)?
cards.answer:
E – Explanation (instructor)
D – Demonstration (instructor)
S – Student performance
I – Instructor supervision
E – Evaluation

Student performance and instructor supervision happen at the same time.

cards.question: What are cooperative/group learning and drill and practice?
cards.answer:
Cooperative/group learning: learners help each other maximize learning. Participants show higher test scores, self-esteem, social skills, and comprehension.

Drill and practice: the instructor gives opportunities to practice and apply previously learned material — should be done every lesson.

cards.question: e-Learning: what is it, pros and cons?
cards.answer:
Learning via smartphone, tablet, computer, or simulator.
Pros: time-flexible, economical software, learner-centered, easily updated, accessible.
Cons: little peer interaction, hard for the instructor to monitor, weak study material, equipment can be expensive, ineffective if instructor or learner isn't comfortable with the technology.

cards.question: What are the problem-based learning methods?
cards.answer:
Problem-based learning is the backbone of the ACS:
• Scenario-based training: not a test; more than one answer; promotes situational awareness and decision-making
• Collaborative problem-solving: two or more learners work a problem together
• Case study: analyze a real event (NTSB reports are a great resource)

cards.question: Guidelines for using instructional aids (CGOS) and why use them?
cards.answer:
C – Clearly establish the lesson objective
G – Gather necessary data (research support material)
O – Organize the material into an outline or lesson plan
S – Select the ideas to be supported with aids

Why: explain technical or abstract subjects, show relationships, and cover more material in limited time.
Effective aids are well-organized, cover key points, and are as simple as possible.
Types: marker board, supplemental print, enhanced training materials, projected material/video, interactive systems, computer-assisted learning, models/mock-ups/cut-aways.

cards.question: What is integrated flight instruction?
cards.answer: Learners are taught to perform maneuvers by both outside visual references and flight instruments, from the first time each maneuver is introduced. Emphasize roughly 90% outside / 10% inside and build the habit of scanning for traffic.

cards.question: What are blocks of learning and a training syllabus?
cards.answer:
Blocks of learning: parts of the total learning objective, built on each other through the course.
Syllabus: explains the steps and objectives through a course of training. Part 141 schools use a Training Course Outline (TCO) — a very specific, detailed syllabus.

cards.question: What are the characteristics of an effective assessment (FAST COCO)?
cards.answer:
F – Flexible: considers everything going on with the learner
A – Acceptable: presented fairly, with authority, sincerity, and competence
S – Specific
T – Thoughtful: considers the learner's need for self-esteem and approval
C – Comprehensive: the right balance of major and minor points
O – Objective: free of personality conflicts
C – Constructive: pointless unless the learner benefits
O – Organized

cards.question: What makes a good written test (DR COVU)?
cards.answer:
D – Discrimination: distinguishes between learners
R – Reliability: consistent results on repeated measurements
C – Comprehensiveness: covers the overall objectives
O – Objectivity: can be graded fairly (essays are subjective)
V – Validity: measures what it's supposed to measure
U – Usability: easy to use and understand

Question types: supply (learner writes the answer) and selection (learner picks from choices). Written tests measure fact knowledge — a low level of understanding.

cards.question: What is authentic assessment, and what are the 4 R's of learner-centered assessment?
cards.answer:
Authentic assessment: the learner performs real-world tasks and demonstrates meaningful application of skills, usually against standards or a rubric.

R – Replay: learner verbally replays the flight or procedure
R – Reconstruct: learner identifies what they could or should have done differently
R – Reflect: learner reflects on the events
R – Redirect: instructor helps relate lessons learned to past and future lessons

cards.question: What are the maneuver/procedure grades?
cards.answer:
Describe: can describe the physical components but needs help executing
Explain: can describe the components and underlying concepts but needs help executing
Practice: can plan and complete it, but the instructor must still correct errors
Perform: can plan and complete it without instructor intervention
Not observed

cards.question: How are risk management (SRM) skills graded?
cards.answer:
Explain: can explain SRM principles but must be prompted to make decisions and correct unsafe situations
Practice: applies SRM independently; instructor corrects minor errors
Manage-Decide: applies SRM and safely conducts the flight without instructor assistance

cards.question: What are the steps in choosing an effective assessment method?
cards.answer:
1. Determine level-of-learning objectives
2. List indicators of desired behaviors
3. Establish criterion objectives
4. Develop criterion-referenced test items

cards.question: What is a critique, and what are the types (ISSISW)?
cards.answer:
Critique: a summary of performance immediately afterward, covering satisfactory and unsatisfactory items.

I – Instructor/student: instructor leads, class offers criticism (keep it controlled)
S – Student-led: a learner leads the assessment
S – Small group: each group analyzes a specific area
I – Individual student critique by another student
S – Self-critique
W – Written: more thorough, a permanent record the learner can refer to; other learners don't benefit

cards.question: What are the pitfalls to avoid in a critique?
cards.answer:
• Being too lengthy
• Covering too much
• Absolute statements
• Controversies
• Getting into a situation where you have to defend the critique

cards.question: What does proper oral quizzing accomplish?
cards.answer:
• Shows how effective the training has been
• Checks retention and comprehension
• Reviews material
• Stimulates interest and thinking
• Emphasizes important points and identifies weak areas
• Promotes active participation

cards.question: What are the characteristics of effective questions (ABCAP)?
cards.answer:
A – Apply to the subject of instruction
B – Brief and concise, but clear and definite
C – Center on one idea, with one correct answer
A – Adapted to the learner's ability, experience, and stage of training
P – Present a challenge

cards.question: What types of questions should be avoided (POTBIT)?
cards.answer:
P – Puzzle: needlessly complicated (weak right brake, swerving left, right crosswind, full flaps…)
O – Oversize: too broad ("what do you do before an engine overhaul?")
T – Toss-up: more than one answer is correct ("squawk 7700 or pick a landing spot?")
B – Bewilderment: confusing and rambling
I – Irrelevant: unrelated to the topic
T – Trick: makes learning a battle of wits

Also avoid simple yes/no questions.

cards.question: How should an instructor answer learner questions?
cards.answer:
• Make sure you understand the question
• Show interest in it
• Answer as directly and accurately as possible
• Make sure the learner is satisfied with the answer
• If it's too advanced, it may be best answered later
• Admit it if you don't know — then find out

cards.question: How should piloting ability be assessed, especially before first solo?
cards.answer:
• Base it on established standards, adapted to the learner's stage of training; include SBT and visualization
• Give oral and written critique after every flight
• Before first solo, the learner must consistently perform all fundamental maneuvers
• Be present for the first solo; a handheld radio lets you terminate it if needed; require full-stop landings; debrief immediately after
• Let learners make (safe) mistakes and work their way out

cards.question: What must an instructor do before recommending a learner for a practical test?
cards.answer:
• Sign the recommendation on FAA Form 8710-1 (IACRA) and endorse the logbook (AC 61-65K has sample endorsements)
• The applicant must have received and logged training within the preceding 2 calendar months and been endorsed as prepared (61.39(a)(6))
• Never endorse a learner who isn't ready

cards.question: What are the aviation instructor's responsibilities?
cards.answer:
• Helping learners learn (challenging but enjoyable; use the laws of learning and Maslow)
• Providing adequate instruction (analyze personality, thinking, ability; set subgoals for slow learners; raise standards for overconfident ones)
• Training to established standards of performance (never lower them to please the learner)
• Emphasizing the positive (learners adopt the instructor's attitude)
• Minimizing learner frustrations
• Emphasizing aviation safety

cards.question: How does an instructor minimize learner frustration (MACKBAG)?
cards.answer:
M – Motivate learners
A – Approach learners as individuals
C – Constructive criticism
K – Keep learners informed
B – Be consistent
A – Admit errors
G – Give credit when it's due

cards.question: What are the additional responsibilities of a flight instructor (PEEPPASS)?
cards.answer:
P – Pilot supervision
E – Evaluation of learner ability
E – Endorsements for flight instruction
P – Practical test recommendations
P – Pilot proficiency
A – Additional training and endorsements
S – See and avoid
S – Student pre-solo flight process

Also: help with physiological obstacles (fear of small aircraft, strange noises, motion sickness) — don't ignore them.

cards.question: Which regulations cover pre-solo requirements?
cards.answer:
61.87(b) — pre-solo aeronautical knowledge test
61.87(d) — pre-solo flight training maneuvers, single-engine airplane
61.87(e) — pre-solo flight training maneuvers, multiengine airplane

cards.question: What records must a flight instructor keep, and for how long?
cards.answer:
61.189:
(a) Sign the logbook of each person you give flight or ground training
(b) Keep a record (logbook or separate document) of:
  (1) the name of each person you endorsed for solo flight privileges, and the date
  (2) the name of each person you endorsed for a knowledge or practical test — the kind of test, the date, and the results
(c) Keep these records at least 3 years

TSA citizenship: keep copies of the documents for 5 years, or make the A.14 endorsement in the student's and instructor's records.

cards.question: What are the elements of instructor professionalism (SADPP)?
cards.answer:
S – Sincerity: straightforward and honest
A – Acceptance of the learner
D – Demeanor (attitude)
P – Personal appearance and habits
P – Proper language

cards.question: How should an instructor pursue professional development?
cards.answer:
• FAA resources and publications
• Classes at institutions of higher education
• Industry organizations (e.g., AOPA)
• The WINGS program
• Commenting on Notices of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRMs)
• Stay current on aircraft, procedures, and certification requirements

cards.question: What should instructor ethics and conduct ensure about learners?
cards.answer:
Learners should:
• Make safety the number one priority
• Develop and exercise good judgment
• Recognize and manage risk
• Be accountable for their actions
• Operate within the limits of the aircraft, their ability, and school practices
• Follow laws and regulations

Model Code of Conduct adds: seek proficiency in aircraft control, use flight deck technology appropriately, be confident in many situations, and respect the privilege to fly.

cards.question: What are the obstacles to learning during flight instruction (FAAWIP)?
cards.answer:
F – Feeling of unfair treatment
A – Apathy due to inadequate instruction
A – Anxiety
W – Worry or lack of interest
I – Impatience to proceed to more interesting operations
P – Physical discomfort, illness, fatigue, and dehydration

cards.question: What is the positive exchange of flight controls?
cards.answer:
A three-step process so there's never doubt who is flying:
1. "You have the flight controls."
2. "I have the flight controls."
3. "You have the flight controls."
Plus a visual check that the other pilot has the controls.

cards.question: What are sterile cockpit and the use of distractions in training?
cards.answer:
Sterile cockpit: avoid non-essential activities during critical phases of flight — taxi, takeoff, landing, and below 10,000 ft.

Distractions: most stall/spin accidents happen when the pilot is distracted. The FAA encourages realistic distractions in training, and learners must be able to tell passengers when something is distracting.

cards.category: FOI · F · Risk Management & Flight Instruction
cards.question: Risk management vs. ADM?
cards.answer:
Risk management: making decisions now to affect the future.
ADM: making a choice to manage risk in the present.

cards.category: FOI · F · Risk Management & Flight Instruction
cards.question: What are the four principles of risk management (AMAI)?
cards.answer:
A – Accept no unnecessary risk
M – Make risk decisions at the appropriate level (may mean talking to the chief pilot)
A – Accept risk only when benefits outweigh the costs
I – Integrate risk management into planning at all levels

cards.category: FOI · F · Risk Management & Flight Instruction
cards.question: What is the risk management process (IAAMIS)?
cards.answer:
I – Identify the hazards
A – Assess the risk
A – Analyze risk control measures
M – Make control decisions
I – Implement risk controls
S – Supervise and review

cards.category: FOI · F · Risk Management & Flight Instruction
cards.question: How is the level of risk determined?
cards.answer:
Risk = Severity × Likelihood (probability).

Risk assessment matrix — Likelihood (Probable, Occasional, Remote, Improbable) vs. Severity (Catastrophic, Critical, Marginal, Negligible):
• Probable + Catastrophic/Critical = High
• Occasional + Catastrophic = High
• Probable + Marginal, Occasional + Critical, Remote + Catastrophic = Serious
• Most remaining combinations = Medium; Negligible severity with remote/improbable likelihood = Low

cards.category: FOI · F · Risk Management & Flight Instruction
cards.question: What is the PAVE checklist?
cards.answer:
P – Pilot: IMSAFE, hazardous attitudes, personal minimums
A – Aircraft: documents, inspections, instrumentation, preflight
V – enVironment: weather (NWKRAFT), terrain, time of day
E – External pressures: passengers, schedules, company

cards.category: FOI · F · Risk Management & Flight Instruction
cards.question: What is a FRAT and what do its scores mean?
cards.answer:
A Flight Risk Assessment Tool assigns a risk score based on the conditions of a flight.
• Red (high): cancel if the risk can't be significantly reduced
• Yellow (serious): reduce risk before departure; consider consulting an instructor or maintenance
• Green (medium): may depart, but still look for ways to reduce risk

cards.category: FOI · F · Risk Management & Flight Instruction
cards.question: When and how should risk management be introduced?
cards.answer:
From the very beginning — ground training on risk before flight training; always model safe behavior.
• Before flight: safety, preflight, checklists, positive exchange of controls, sterile cockpit
• In flight: aviate-navigate-communicate, situational awareness
• Landing: stabilized approach, go-around if anything isn't right
• After flight: review ADM and decisions

Pre-solo: instructor guides all risk assessment; learner can use a basic FRAT by first solo. Post-solo: learner leads debriefs. Cross-country: learner runs a risk analysis before every flight.

cards.category: FOI · F · Risk Management & Flight Instruction
cards.question: What is the DECIDE model and the 3P model of ADM?
cards.answer:
D – Detect the problem or change
E – Estimate the need to counter it
C – Choose a desirable outcome
I – Identify actions to reach that outcome
D – Do the necessary action
E – Evaluate the effect

3P: Perceive → Process → Perform

cards.category: FOI · F · Risk Management & Flight Instruction
cards.question: What are the SRM 5 P's?
cards.answer:
P – Plan: route, weather, fuel, publications currency
P – Plane: instrumentation, database currency, autopilot
P – Pilot: IMSAFE, psychological state
P – Passengers: can help (traffic watch) or pressure the pilot; have contingency plans for them
P – Programming: GPS, autopilot, approaches

cards.category: FOI · F · Risk Management & Flight Instruction
cards.question: CRM vs. SRM?
cards.answer:
Both use all available resources for the safest, most efficient flight.
CRM resources: other crew, cabin crew, maintenance, dispatch, ATC, onboard systems (traffic, GPS, HUD), and devices like an iPad.
SRM: only one pilot, but most of the same resources are still available — including other pilots in flight or on the ground.

cards.category: FOI · F · Risk Management & Flight Instruction
cards.question: What are the common operational pitfalls?
cards.answer:
• Inadequate fuel reserves
• Duck-under syndrome
• Descending below the MEA
• Scud running
• Loss of positional/situational awareness
• Continuing VFR into IMC
• Neglecting flight planning, preflight, or checklists
• Getting behind the aircraft
• Get-there-itis / mindset
• Operating outside the envelope
• Peer pressure

cards.category: FOI · F · Risk Management & Flight Instruction
cards.question: What are common flight instruction risks and best practices (PAVE)?
cards.answer:
Pilot: apply IMSAFE to yourself and the learner; know both proficiencies; be ready for learner mistakes. Stay current and know the aircraft well.
Aircraft: rental/school maintenance can be compromised — check airworthiness before preflighting with the learner; tandem seating hides learner actions.
enVironment: training airspace is congested; some maneuvers carry inherent risk (full stalls → spins). Involve the learner in risk assessment; switch to a sim or ground lesson if needed.
External pressures: understand the learner's life; keep schedules flexible.

cards.category: FOI · F · Risk Management & Flight Instruction
cards.question: Special considerations when teaching takeoffs and landings?
cards.answer:
Takeoffs: don't teach once you've contacted tower or taken the runway. Use realistic scenarios, but never let the learner make an unsafe climb. Spacing from other aircraft is the instructor's job — discuss it later.

Landings: excessive talking hurts — small prompts only, save the rest for the debrief. Teach landing as dynamic (aircraft type, landing type, terrain, conditions, expected performance, traffic) while following checklists and callouts. Be ready to react quickly to serious errors.

cards.question: What does "rated" mean?
cards.answer:
"Rating" (14 CFR 1.1): a statement that, as part of a certificate, sets forth special conditions, privileges, or limitations — it appears on the pilot certificate.
Type ratings: 14 CFR 61.31(a).

cards.question: What must a pilot have to ACT as PIC (appropriately rated and current)?
cards.answer:
Certificate privileges and limitations — "Are you allowed?"
• Documents: 61.2, 61.3
• Medical: 61.23 (or BasicMed, 61.113(i))
• Flight review: 61.56
• Endorsements: 61.31
• Passenger currency: 61.57(a)/(b)
• IFR currency: 61.57(c)

cards.question: When may a pilot LOG PIC time?
cards.answer:
61.51(e)(1) — certificated pilot when:
  (i) sole manipulator of the controls of an aircraft for which the pilot is RATED
  (ii) sole occupant; or
  (iii) acting as PIC of an aircraft requiring more than one pilot
61.51(e)(3) — flight instructor: while serving as an authorized instructor (and rated)
61.51(e)(4) — student pilot: sole occupant, properly endorsed, and undergoing training

cards.question: What is an "authorized instructor" and what are a CFI's privileges (61.193)?
cards.answer:
Authorized instructor (61.1): a person who holds a flight instructor certificate and is acting within its privileges and limitations.

61.193(a) — within the limits of the certificate and ratings, a CFI may give ground and flight training, conduct certain checking events, and endorse for:
• Student pilot cert • Pilot cert • Flight instructor cert • Ground instructor cert
• Aircraft rating • Instrument rating
• Flight review, operating privilege, or recency requirement (or training to maintain/improve skills)
• Practical test • Knowledge test

61.193(b) — accept a student pilot certificate application (and certain remote pilot applications), verify the applicant's identity, and verify eligibility (61.83).
61.193(c) — does not allow operations that require an air carrier/operating certificate.

cards.question: What ratings must a CFI hold to give training (61.195(b) and (c))?
cards.answer:
61.195(b) Aircraft ratings: a flight instructor certificate with the applicable category/class rating AND a pilot certificate with the applicable category/class rating (plus a type rating if (e) applies).

61.195(c) Instrument rating: to give instrument training for an instrument rating, a type rating not limited to VFR, or the instrument training required for commercial and ATP certificates, the CFI must hold an instrument rating on the flight instructor certificate (CFII), and either:
• meet (b), or
• hold a commercial or ATP certificate with the category/class ratings, if the trainee holds the category/class ratings for the aircraft.
In a multiengine airplane, the CFII must also meet (b).

cards.question: Can a CFI without an instrument instructor rating teach flight by reference to instruments?
cards.answer:
Yes. 61.195(l): a CFI may train control and maneuvering of an airplane solely by reference to the instruments (the training a private pilot applicant receives) if the CFI:
(1) holds a flight instructor certificate with the applicable category and class rating; or
(2) holds a CFII appropriate to the aircraft and a commercial or ATP certificate with the category/class ratings (trainee holds the category/class ratings).
No CFII is required under (1).

cards.question: What do 61.195(e) and (f) require?
cards.answer:
(e) Type rating: to give flight instruction (including instrument training) in an aircraft that requires a type rating, the CFI must hold that type rating on their pilot certificate.
(f) Multiengine airplane, helicopter, or powered-lift: to give training required for a certificate or rating, the CFI needs at least 5 flight hours of PIC time in that specific make and model.

cards.question: How does a CFI keep instructor privileges current (61.197)?
cards.answer:
CFI certificates issued under the current rule don't expire. Instead, privileges require RECENT EXPERIENCE within the preceding 24 calendar months, by one of:
(b)(1) Passing a practical test for a rating on the CFI certificate, or for an additional CFI rating
(b)(2) Submitting documentation of one of:
  (i) Endorsed at least 5 applicants for practical tests in 24 months, with at least 80% passing on the first attempt
  (ii) Served as company check pilot, chief flight instructor, check airman, or flight instructor in a part 121/135 operation, or a position regularly evaluating pilots
  (iii) Completed an approved flight instructor refresher course (FIRC) within the preceding 3 calendar months
  (iv) Passed a U.S. military instructor pilot/examiner proficiency check
  (v) Served as an instructor in an FAA-sponsored pilot proficiency program (WINGS): completed a phase in 12 months, 15 activities, 5 different pilots

Miss it → may not instruct until reinstated under 61.199.

cards.question: What does TIM♥BaCoN stand for?
cards.answer:
The initial-solo sequence for a student pilot:
T – TSA citizenship verification (49 CFR 1552.15(c))
I – IACRA student pilot application (61.83, 61.85)
M – Medical (61.23)
(♥)
B – (b) 61.87(b) pre-solo knowledge test — A.3
C – (c) 61.87(c) pre-solo flight training — A.4
N – (n) 61.87(n) solo flight authorization — A.6

cards.question: TSA citizenship verification (the T in TIM♥BaCoN)?
cards.answer:
Verify U.S. citizenship (unexpired passport, birth certificate, or naturalization documents). If not a U.S. citizen or national → Flight Training Security Program (FTSP).

Endorsement (AC 61-65K A.14): "I certify that [First name, MI, Last name] has presented me a [type of document presented, such as a U.S. birth certificate or U.S. passport, and the relevant control or sequential number on the document, if any] establishing that they are a U.S. citizen or national in accordance with 49 CFR § 1552.7(a)." Date/Signature/CFI No./Exp.

Instead of the endorsement, the instructor may keep a copy of the documents for 5 years.

cards.question: IACRA and medical for a student pilot (the I and M)?
cards.answer:
IACRA (iacra.faa.gov): eligibility 61.83, application 61.85. A medical is NOT required when processing the student pilot certificate application, but the student needs one before solo.

Medical: 61.23, via MedXPress (medxpress.faa.gov).

cards.question: Pre-solo aeronautical knowledge test endorsement (A.3)?
cards.answer:
Covers at least:
• Applicable parts of 14 CFR 61 and 91
• Airspace rules and procedures for the solo airport
• Flight characteristics and operating limitations of the aircraft make and model
Review all incorrect answers.

cards.question: Pre-solo flight training endorsement (A.4)?
cards.answer:
61.87(c): pre-solo flight training. The maneuvers and procedures are in 61.87(d).
"Train to (d), endorse per (c)."

cards.question: Solo flight authorization endorsement (A.6)?
cards.answer:
61.87(n): solo authorization for the first 90-day period
• Make and model specific
• Brief the student on all limitations (61.89)
• Limited to within 25 NM of the original airport; take off and land only at the original airport (per notes: 61.93)
• Expires 90 days after the training; renew under 61.87(p)

cards.question: Additional 90-day solo endorsement (A.7)?
cards.answer:
• The endorsing instructor must fly with the student
• Make and model specific
• Refer to 61.87(d) for required maneuvers
• Make sure all prior initial-solo endorsements are properly logged
• Expires 90 days after the training; must be renewed

cards.question: Solo cross-country endorsements (A.9, A.10)?
cards.answer:
61.93(c)(1)&(2) — usually one endorsement:
• The endorsing instructor must have given the XC training
• Make and model specific
• XC maneuvers and procedures: 61.93(e)
• 61.109 requires 3 hours of XC training for private pilot

61.93(c)(3) — each flight's planning review on the day of flight:
• Items to check: 61.93(d)
• Any authorized instructor can give it (the "duty desk" endorsement)
• Carefully consider limitations!

cards.question: Night solo endorsement (A.5)?
cards.answer: 61.87(o): solo flight at night. Know how "night" is defined for this regulation (14 CFR 1.1: the time between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight).

cards.question: Student solo in Class B airspace or at a Class B airport (A.12, A.13)?
cards.answer:
61.95(a) — "a = airspace": solo in Class B airspace. Ground and flight training on that specific airspace; 90-day expiration. Without it, the student must decline an ATC clearance into Class B.

61.95(b) — "b = base": solo to, from, or at an airport in Class B. Ground and flight training on that specific airport; 90-day expiration. Note the airports in 14 CFR 91 Appendix D, Section 4 ("Dirty Dozen"), where student solo operations are prohibited.

cards.question: Solo to nearby airports (A.8, A.11)?
cards.answer:
A.8 — 61.93(b)(1): solo to an airport within 25 NM of origin, for takeoff and landing practice only. The instructor must give training to/from/at that airport, including pattern ops. 61.93(c) XC training is NOT required.

A.11 — 61.93(b)(2): repeated solo XC flights to an airport within 50 NM. Instructor gives training to/from/at that airport, including pattern ops. Requires the 61.93(c)(1)&(2) XC endorsement but NOT (c)(3). Carefully consider limitations!

cards.question: What are the eligibility requirements for a flight instructor certificate (61.183)?
cards.answer:
(a) At least 18 years old
(b) Read, speak, write, and understand English
(c) Hold a commercial or ATP certificate with the category/class rating for the CFI rating sought — and an instrument rating (or privileges) if seeking airplane single-engine, airplane multiengine, powered-lift, or instrument instructor ratings
(d) Endorsement on the fundamentals of instructing (61.185) for the knowledge test
(e) Pass the FOI knowledge test (unless exempt)
(f) Pass the knowledge test on the aeronautical knowledge areas for the rating sought
(g) Endorsement on the areas of operation in 61.187(b)
(h) Pass the practical test
(i) Airplane or glider: spin endorsement and demonstrated instructional proficiency in stalls/spins
(j) Log at least 15 hours PIC in the category and class of the rating sought
(k) Comply with the other applicable sections

cards.question: Who is exempt from the FOI knowledge test?
cards.answer:
61.183(e) / 61.185(b) — no FOI knowledge test (or FOI ground training) for someone who:
(1) holds a flight instructor or ground instructor certificate under part 61;
(2) holds a teacher's certificate from a State, county, city, or municipality to teach 7th grade or higher; or
(3) is employed as a teacher at an accredited college or university.

61.191 — an applicant for an ADDITIONAL flight instructor rating doesn't retake the FOI test, but must meet the 61.183 eligibility for the rating sought.

cards.question: What is the spin requirement for a CFI-airplane or glider applicant?
cards.answer:
61.183(i):
(1) A logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor that the applicant is competent and has instructional proficiency in stall awareness, spin entry, spins, and spin recovery — after training in an airplane or glider certificated for spins; and
(2) Demonstrate that instructional proficiency. The examiner may accept the endorsement instead of a demonstration on the practical test — unless it's a retest for failing stall/spin items, in which case the applicant must be tested in an aircraft certificated for spins.

cards.question: What ground training must a CFI applicant receive (61.185)?
cards.answer:
Ground training from an authorized instructor on:
(1) Fundamentals of instructing:
  (i) the learning process
  (ii) elements of effective teaching
  (iii) student evaluation and testing
  (iv) course development
  (v) lesson planning
  (vi) classroom training techniques
(2) Aeronautical knowledge for recreational, private, and commercial certificates in the category sought
(3) Instrument rating knowledge areas, if seeking instrument instructor privileges

cards.question: What are the areas of operation for a CFI-airplane single-engine (61.187(b)(1))?
cards.answer:
(i) Fundamentals of instructing
(ii) Technical subject areas
(iii) Preflight preparation
(iv) Preflight lesson on a maneuver to be performed in flight
(v) Preflight procedures
(vi) Airport and seaplane base operations
(vii) Takeoffs, landings, and go-arounds
(viii) Fundamentals of flight
(ix) Performance maneuvers
(x) Ground reference maneuvers
(xi) Slow flight, stalls, and spins
(xii) Basic instrument maneuvers
(xiii) Emergency operations
(xiv) Postflight procedures

Multiengine (b)(2) is the same except "slow flight and stalls" (no spins) plus "multiengine operations."

cards.question: How many hours of flight training may a CFI give in 24 hours?
cards.answer: 61.195(a): no more than 8 hours of flight training in any 24-consecutive-hour period.

cards.question: What are the limitations on a CFI's endorsements (61.195(d))?
cards.answer:
A CFI may not endorse a:
(1) Student for solo — unless the CFI gave the required solo training and determined the student can fly safely (with any limitations needed)
(2) Student for solo cross-country — unless the CFI determined the preparation, planning, equipment, and procedures are adequate for the conditions
(3) Student for solo in Class B or at a Class B airport — unless the CFI gave ground and flight training there and found the student proficient
(4) Recreational pilot — unless the CFI gave the required training and found them proficient
(5) Flight review — unless the CFI conducted it per 61.56(a)
(6) Instrument proficiency check — unless the CFI tested the pilot per 61.57(d)

cards.question: What aircraft requirements apply when giving flight training (61.195(g))?
cards.answer:
(1) All training must be in an aircraft meeting 91.109 (e.g., functioning dual controls for flight instruction)
(2) For a certificate or rating: at least two pilot stations, and the same category, class, and type (if appropriate) as the certificate/rating sought
  For single-place aircraft: pre-solo flight training must be in a two-pilot-station aircraft of the same category, class, and type.

cards.question: What qualifications must an instructor have to train an initial CFI applicant (61.195(h))?
cards.answer:
Ground training — an authorized instructor who holds a ground or flight instructor certificate with the appropriate rating and either:
• has held it at least 24 calendar months and given at least 40 hours of ground training; or
• has given at least 100 hours of ground training in an FAA-approved course.

Flight training — must meet 61.183 eligibility, hold the appropriate CFI certificate and rating, and either:
• have held a CFI certificate 24 calendar months and given 200 hours of flight training (80 for glider); or
• in the preceding 24 months, trained and endorsed at least 5 practical test applicants with 80% passing first time; or
• have the 200/80 hours and graduated from an FAA-approved flight instructor enhanced qualification program (part 141/142).

cards.question: Can a CFI endorse themselves? Who may teach Category II/III?
cards.answer:
(i) No self-endorsements — for any certificate, rating, flight review, authorization, operating privilege, practical test, or knowledge test required by part 61.
(j) Category II/III training — only by a CFI who has been trained and tested in Category II or III operations under 61.67 or 61.68.

cards.question: When does a CFI's 24-calendar-month recent experience period start?
cards.answer:
61.197(a) — the 24 calendar months start from:
(1) the month the FAA issued the CFI certificate;
(2) the month the recent experience requirement was accomplished; or
(3) the last month of the current period — if the requirement is met within the 3 calendar months before that month (so early renewal doesn't lose time).

61.197(e) — a certificate issued before December 1, 2024 that hasn't expired: establish recent experience before the month of expiration shown on it, or privileges lapse until reinstated (61.199).

cards.question: How are flight instructor privileges reinstated (61.199)?
cards.answer:
File an application with the FAA and complete one of:
(a)(1) 3 calendar months or less past the end of the recent experience period: an approved flight instructor refresher course (FIRC), or one of the (a)(2) options
(a)(2) More than 3 calendar months past: a CFI practical test (61.183(h)) for a rating held, or for an additional rating
(a)(3) Military instructor pilots/examiners: proof of a U.S. Armed Forces instructor/examiner proficiency check or qualification within the preceding 6 calendar months

(b) An old flight instructor rating on a pilot certificate isn't valid; it requires the current knowledge and practical tests.
